FliperOS 0.16

English | Português

Ubuntu 24.04 (amd64) for arcade cabinets with a CRT monitor, in the style of GroovyArcade: a 15 kHz kernel, Switchres, emulators and frontends ready to play, and a setup menu (fliperos-setup) made for the tube's screen. A PC alternative to GroovyArcade, Batocera, Recalbox, ReplayOS and RGB-Pi for 15 kHz arcade CRTs.

In development: 0.16 is tested in QEMU and on a 15 kHz CRT cabinet. Full documentation in the wiki. Website: fliperos.juniorter.in (source in website/).

What's included

  • Video: 6.18 LTS kernel with the 15 kHz patches, boot at 15, 25 or 31 kHz or LCD, Switchres.
  • Emulators: GroovyMAME, RetroArch, Flycast, PCSX2, Dolphin, Supermodel, SM2-Emu (Model 2), Hypseus Singe and OpenBOR; Wine, Steam and Heroic through Setup > Games > Extras.
  • Frontends: FliperOS's own frontend by default (in the look of the Setup menu: list, full screen and grid; clones folded under each game; letter-by-letter scrolling), plus Attract-Mode Plus, EmulationStation (ES-DE) and Pegasus (built on the cabinet the first time you choose them) and Fightcade 2, whose online matches play in each game's native resolution on the tube.
  • Light gun: GunCon 2 out of the box (driver via DKMS), calibrated for the tube in Setup > Joysticks. Wheels too.
  • Setup: video, geometry, audio, network, scraper, ROM lists, MAME romset cleaning, controls and latency.
  • Folders roms, bios, media, nvram, save and config in ~ and over the network (Samba); LXDE desktop with an app store.
  • SSH on from the first boot (ssh fliperos@fliperos.local, password fliperos). Under the menus it's a regular Ubuntu, so an AI assistant can configure it over SSH.

Web panel: the cabinet from your phone

Open http://fliperos.local on a phone or PC on the same network (user fliperos, password fliperos). Nothing to install. From the couch you can:

  • pick a game and play it on the tube, with the pictures, history and buttons of each arcade game from the Arcade Database;
  • watch the cabinet live in the browser, and put the live screen and the game's marquee in OBS;
  • change colour, 480i hacks and other settings while a game runs;
  • copy games, BIOS and artwork, filter a MAME romset and download only what suits your cabinet;
  • check the system (video mode and modeline, temperatures, logs), preview the marquee (Pixelcade or ZeDMD) with no hardware, or open a terminal.

At the cabinet, hold Start and Down for a second in any game to open the on-screen menu: volume, 480i filter, geometry and colour, over the running game.

Every page in detail: Web panel.

New: your controller on the stream

The stick and the buttons light up on your live stream while you press them on the cabinet, like the input displays of fighting game streams. It's a page for an OBS Browser Source, with a transparent background: copy its address from Live > Controller for OBS and paste it in OBS.

It reads the controls of Button mapping, joysticks and keyboard encoders alike, for one or two players. You restyle it in the panel, in a CSS editor with a live preview, and a saved style shows up in OBS at once. Step by step and CSS examples: Controller on the stream.

From zero to playing: step by step

This guide goes from an empty cabinet to a game on screen. Each step says what you will see and what to press. The details behind each screen are in the wiki pages linked along the way.

1. What you need

  • A PC (amd64) for the cabinet. For arcade games up to the 90s and consoles up to the PlayStation, a 2-core CPU, 4 GB of RAM and a 16 GB disk are enough. For PS2, Model 3 and Dreamcast, a 4-core CPU with AVX2 (Core i7-7700, Ryzen 5 3600 or newer), 16 GB and an SSD. The disk you install to is erased completely.
  • A graphics card with analog output. The best fit is an AMD Radeon with VGA or DVI-I from the HD 2000 series to the R7/R9 (GCN 1.0), which generates 15 kHz natively. Intel and NVIDIA work at 15 kHz with "super resolution" modes (an Intel HD of the first generation has only OpenGL 2.1: no EmulationStation-DE, no 480i flicker filter, no Vulkan; see its limits in the wiki); an NVIDIA with VGA or DVI-I (GeForce 8 to GTX 900) gets native resolutions if it passes the low resolution test. Cards without an analog output need a DisplayPort/HDMI to VGA converter. The full list is in Video cards.
  • Intel HD: you need a monitor at a standard frequency first. The boot menu and the installation are drawn at 31 kHz, and an Intel card does not make low clocks. Install FliperOS and set the video with a regular VGA monitor (an LCD or a PC monitor), and only then power off and connect the CRT.
  • The monitor: an arcade CRT (15 kHz), a TV through a VGA to SCART/component adapter, or a 25/31 kHz monitor. An LCD also works.
  • A USB stick of 4 GB or more (it will be erased).
  • A USB keyboard for the installation. After that, the panel or a gamepad moves through all the menus.
  • A network connection (cable or Wi-Fi), to copy games from another computer and to receive updates. Optional, but it makes everything easier.
  • Another computer (Windows, Linux or macOS) to write the USB stick and, later, to copy the games over the network.

2. Download the ISO

  1. Open Releases and download fliperos-0.16.iso from the latest version (what changed is in CHANGELOG.md).
  2. If the release lists a SHA-256, compare it: sha256sum fliperos-0.16.iso on Linux, Get-FileHash fliperos-0.16.iso in Windows PowerShell.

3. Write the USB stick

The ISO must be written byte for byte. Programs that rebuild the stick's boot structure break it: Rufus in its default mode ("ISO image"), Ventoy and UNetbootin don't work.

  • Windows, macOS or Linux, the easiest: balenaEtcher. Flash from file > choose the ISO > Select target > the USB stick > Flash!.
  • Windows with Rufus: choose the stick and the ISO, click START and, when it asks, choose "Write in DD Image mode".
  • Linux: find the stick with lsblk (here /dev/sdX; the wrong device erases the wrong disk) and run:

bash sudo dd if=fliperos-0.16.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress conv=fsync

4. Prepare the cabinet's BIOS

Enter the BIOS/UEFI setup (usually Del, F2 or F10 right after power-on) and:

  1. Disable Secure Boot: the 15 kHz kernel is custom and unsigned, and with Secure Boot on it doesn't start.
  2. SATA mode on AHCI (not RAID or Intel RST); otherwise the installer doesn't see the disk.
  3. Boot from the USB stick: put it first in the boot order, or use the one-time boot menu (often F8, F11 or F12). BIOS (legacy) and UEFI both work.

Save and exit with the stick plugged in.

With an Intel HD card, keep the regular monitor (standard frequency) connected through steps 5 and 6, and connect the CRT only after the installation.

5. Boot from the USB stick

  1. Wait about 10 seconds without pressing anything. The boot menu (15 kHz, 25 kHz, 31 kHz, LCD...) is drawn at 31 kHz, so it doesn't show on a 15 kHz tube. With no key pressed, the 15 kHz entry boots by itself, which is the safe one for a cabinet. On a PC monitor or an LCD, you can pick SVGA / LCD monitor in the menu instead.
  2. The FliperOS splash appears, already at 15 kHz.
  3. Output test. FliperOS turns on one video output at a time and a voice says "Testing output VGA 1. If you can see this screen, press Enter." When the text "If you can see this screen clearly, press ENTER" is readable on your monitor, press Enter. Without Enter it moves on to the next output and repeats the round up to three times.
  4. Testing Results shows the card, the output, the mode and the frequency. Choose Validate settings (or Repeat test).
  5. Monitor type: choose your monitor from the list (for example generic_15 for a common arcade monitor or TV, arcade_15, ntsc, pal, or a specific model). The list opens on the suggestion for the boot entry. The full table of boot entries is in Install.

6. Install to the disk

The FliperOS Setup menu opens (Install to HD/SSD, Recovery Mode, Terminal, Shutdown). The arrows move, Enter confirms and Esc goes back.

  1. Choose Install to HD/SSD.
  2. Do you want to configure video? Choose Yes to adjust it now (you can also do it later in Setup > Video Setup):
  3. Monitor Type: the same monitor as in the test;
  4. Monitor Orientation: horizontal, or vertical for a rotated monitor (vertical games);
  5. Resolution: the modes your monitor and card accept (the suggestion is fine);
  6. Geometry: a grid to center the picture and fit its size on the tube. Use the arrows to adjust and Enter to save.
  7. Automatically Partition: choose the disk by model, size and type (USB/NVMe/SATA). If yours isn't listed, My drive is not listed (details) explains why (usually the SATA mode, step 4).
  8. WARNING: it shows the disk that will be completely erased. Check it and confirm (No goes back to the list).
  9. Installing FliperOS: a progress bar with the current step. It takes a few minutes.
  10. Installation completed successfully: remove the USB stick and choose Reboot now. On an Intel HD, power off instead: move the cable from the regular monitor to the CRT, then turn the cabinet on.

7. First boot of the installed system

  1. The cabinet boots straight to the splash, without text.
  2. Nothing to choose for what opens at power on: it is the FliperOS frontend (change it later in Setup > Games > Frontend). A short wizard gets the cabinet ready: Wi-Fi (only when the network cable brings no internet and there is a Wi-Fi adapter), controls (the Button mapping of step 8) and the live screen of the web panel.
  3. When you leave the frontend (Esc), the FliperOS menu appears: Start frontend, Setup, Start desktop, Exit to shell, Shutdown / Reboot. The title shows the cabinet's IP address. Every item is explained in The menus, item by item.
  4. Network: a network cable works by itself. For Wi-Fi: Setup > Network Setup, choose the network and type the password. Once connected, the IP appears in the menu title.
  5. Updates: at each boot with internet, if there is a FliperOS update, a screen describes it and asks Apply now or Not now.

8. Set up the controls

In the menus, the panel or a gamepad already acts as the keyboard: directions = arrows, button 1 = Enter, button 2 = Esc.

  1. Setup > Joysticks > Button mapping (the first boot already offers it; this is how to redo it).
  2. For each player, press what it asks for, in order: up, down, left, right, buttons 1 to 6 in panel order (1 2 3 in the top row, 4 5 6 in the bottom row), Start and Coin. The first input pressed tells which controller belongs to that player. With nothing pressed for 8 seconds, that input is skipped.
  3. The mapping goes to every emulator at once (GroovyMAME, RetroArch, Flycast, PCSX2, Dolphin, Supermodel, Hypseus and OpenBOR).
  4. Light gun (GunCon 2), wheel and pedals have their own calibrators in the same menu, and Setup > System > Quirks fixes USB devices that arrive wrong (for example a dual encoder showing up as a single player). See Controls.

9. Copy your games

Use only games you have the right to use (your own dumps, or the free homebrew from Setup > Games > Downloader > Free games).

Use the LXDE desktop. Plug a USB mouse and keyboard into the cabinet and choose Start desktop in the FliperOS menu. It is a regular desktop, and it makes all the work with games easier:

  • Folders: the file manager opens your home folder, with roms, bios, media, nvram, save and config. You see where each file goes and can create, rename and move files with the mouse.
  • Browser: Falkon (browser) in the desktop menu, to search for the torrents of your games.
  • Torrents: Transmission (torrent) opens the .torrent files and magnet links from the browser. When the download finishes, move the files from Downloads to the right folder in roms.
  • External storage: plug in a USB stick or an external disk. It is mounted by itself and gets an icon on the desktop: open it, copy the files and paste them into the right folder in roms (or bios).
  • To go back to the games: Logout in the desktop menu > back to the FliperOS menu.

Over the network, from another computer on the same network:

  • Windows: in File Explorer's address bar type \\fliperos\roms (or \\IP-of-the-cabinet\roms) and press Enter. If it asks for a login: user fliperos, password fliperos.
  • macOS: Finder > Go > Connect to Server > smb://fliperos.local/roms.
  • Linux: smb://fliperos.local/roms in the file manager.
  • Also available: \\fliperos\bios (BIOS files), \\fliperos\media (artwork) and \\fliperos\config (emulator settings).

SFTP also works: fliperos@fliperos.local, password fliperos.

Each emulator has its folder in roms. Copy the files as they come: MAME sets stay zipped and are never renamed (sf2ce.zip, not Street Fighter II.zip).

Folder Games Emulator
mame Arcade: MAME sets (.zip, .7z) and their CHD folders GroovyMAME
naomi, naomi2, atomiswave Sega Naomi and Sammy Atomiswave sets Flycast
model3 Sega Model 3 sets Supermodel
model2 Sega Model 2 sets Model 2 (SM2-Emu, Games menu; built on first launch)
dreamcast .gdi, .cdi, .chd Flycast
ps2 .iso, .chd, .cso PCSX2
dolphin GameCube and Wii (.iso, .rvz, .wbfs) Dolphin
retroarch/<core> Consoles and computers; the _info.txt in each folder lists the extensions RetroArch
openbor/Paks OpenBOR games (.pak) OpenBOR

BIOS come by themselves: Setup > Games > Downloader > Download BIOS brings the ones your games lack. Ones you bring yourself go in bios, never in a games folder: bios/mame for MAME (neogeo.zip, qsound.zip...), bios/dc for Flycast (naomi.zip, awbios.zip, dc_boot.bin), bios/ps2 for PCSX2, and the bios folder itself for the RetroArch cores.

Has a full MAME romset? Setup > Games > Cleaner > MAME ROM Cleaner keeps only the games that work and suit your cabinet (horizontal or vertical, the controls you have) and puts them in the right emulator's folder. More in ROMs, BIOS and artwork.

10. Make the frontend show the games

  1. The FliperOS frontend makes its lists by itself. When it opens, and whenever a games folder changes, it redoes them in the background. Arcade games get their real name (Street Fighter II instead of sf2), year, manufacturer and clones from MAME's data; a new set may take about a minute the first time.
  2. Artwork (screenshots, logos, videos, descriptions): the frontend fetches what a game lacks when the cursor stays on it for 2 seconds, and keeps fetching in the background while it is open. To do it all at once, use Setup > Games > Scraper, which needs internet. See Scraper.
  3. If you use Attract-Mode Plus instead: Setup > Games > Frontend > choose it (the Setup creates a system for each folder that has games; do it again every time a folder gets its first games) and run Setup > Games > AttractPlus ROM List for the real names. For games added later, run the ROM List or the Scraper again.

Details in Frontends and Adding games.

11. Play

  1. In the FliperOS menu choose Start frontend (or just turn the cabinet on: the default launcher opens by itself).
  2. In the FliperOS frontend: up/down move through the games (hold to jump letter by letter), left/right change the game list (each folder, and Arcade with all the arcade folders together) and Start switches between list, full screen and grid. Button 4 marks a favourite and button 5 opens the filters; Tab opens the options. (In Attract-Mode Plus, left/right change the system and up/down move through the games; Tab opens its configuration, where Controls binds buttons to change filters and anything else.)
  3. Press button 1 (or Enter) on a game and choose Play. The screen goes black for a moment while Switchres sets the video mode for that game, and the game starts.
  4. Insert a credit with Coin and start with Start.
  5. Leaving the game: in GroovyMAME, Esc on the keyboard. In RetroArch, Start + Coin together open its menu, then Quick Menu > Close Content. The other emulators use their own exit key or menu (Emulators). You go back to the game list.
  6. Button 2 in the game list (or Esc, and confirming) leaves the frontend and returns to the FliperOS menu, where Shutdown / Reboot turns the cabinet off safely.
  7. The cabinet's power button (a short press): with a game open, it closes the game and returns to the game list; in the game list, it turns the cabinet off safely. So from inside a game it takes two presses to power off: wait for the list to show before the second one.

12. If something goes wrong

  • No picture at boot: wait 10 seconds (the menu doesn't show at 15 kHz). On a 15 kHz-only tube, connect an LCD temporarily to choose another boot entry.
  • The installer doesn't list the disk: SATA mode on AHCI in the BIOS. My drive is not listed (details) shows what Linux sees.
  • The picture is off-center or too big: Setup > Video Setup > Geometry.
  • Two or three monitors (Darius, Punch-Out!!, F355 Challenge): Setup > Video Setup > Multiple Monitors, see Multiple monitors.
  • A system doesn't appear in the frontend: the folder needs at least one game file (the _info.txt doesn't count); then choose the frontend again in Setup > Games > Frontend.
  • A game doesn't open: turn on Setup > System > Debug mode to see the emulator's messages on screen; without it they are saved in /opt/fliperos/logs. A missing BIOS: Setup > Games > Downloader > Download BIOS.
  • No sound: Setup > Audio Setup chooses the card and the volume and plays a test.
  • Something the menus don't cover: over SSH (ssh fliperos@fliperos.local, password fliperos) it's a regular Ubuntu 24.04, and an AI assistant with terminal access can configure it for you. On a network you don't control, change the password with passwd.

More in Installed system, Frontends and Latency.

The menus, item by item

Everything in the menus, in the order it appears on screen. In any menu: arrows move, Enter confirms, Esc goes back (or choose Return). The panel or a gamepad works too: directions = arrows, button 1 = Enter, button 2 = Esc, button 3 = Space (marks items in lists with checkboxes).

FliperOS Setup (on the USB stick)

The menu that opens when you boot from the USB stick, before installing.

  • Install to HD/SSD: installs FliperOS on a disk, as in step 6. It asks for the video settings, the disk (which will be completely erased) and shows the progress.
  • Recovery Mode: repairs a FliperOS already installed on this computer, without installing again. It looks for the installation and offers:
  • Open a terminal in the installed system: a command line inside the installed system, to fix something by hand;
  • Reinstall the bootloader: puts Limine back on the disk when the computer no longer boots FliperOS (after installing Windows on another disk, for example);
  • Apply this session's video settings (new video card): changed the video card or the monitor? Boot from the USB stick, adjust the video and bring those settings into the installed system;
  • Restore system files (keeps ROMs and settings): puts the original FliperOS files back, keeping your games, saves and settings.
  • Terminal: a command line on the USB stick itself.
  • Shutdown: power off or reboot.

FliperOS menu (installed system)

It appears when you leave the frontend (Esc). The title shows the cabinet's name, its IP address and how full the disk is.

  • Start frontend: opens the default launcher (Attract-Mode Plus, for example). When you leave it, you come back to this menu.
  • Setup: all the settings, explained below.
  • Start desktop: opens LXDE, a regular desktop with a mouse, file manager, browser (Falkon), torrent client (Transmission) and app store. It is the easiest way to organize folders and copy games (step 9). To leave: Logout in the desktop menu, which opens a small menu: back to the FliperOS menu, reboot, power off or cancel.
  • Exit to shell: a full-screen command line. Type fliperos-menu to return to the menu.
  • Shutdown / Reboot: Power off or Reboot, always asking first. Use it instead of switching the cabinet off at the wall. The cabinet's power button does the same without asking, and with a game open it only closes the game.

Setup

The items come in the order of setting up a cabinet: picture, sound, network, controls, games and the rest of the system. Under the list, a balloon says what the item under the cursor is for.

  • Video Setup: how the picture comes out on the monitor. The top of the screen shows what is set now.
  • Monitor Type: the kind of monitor (arcade CRT 15 kHz, 25 kHz, 31 kHz, TV, LCD...). It decides which video modes are allowed;
  • Monitor Orientation: horizontal, or vertical (rotated clockwise or counterclockwise) for vertical games;
  • Resolution: the resolution of the menus and the frontend;
  • Geometry: a grid to center the picture and fit its size on the tube; the arrows adjust and Enter saves;
  • Reset Geometry: goes back to the monitor's default geometry;

  • Multiple Monitors: a second and a third arcade monitor, for games with 2 or 3 screens (Darius, Punch-Out!!, F355 Challenge).

    Inside: Monitor 2 and Monitor 3 (which video output each one uses), Multi-Screen Games (one screen per monitor, or everything on monitor 1), Game Screen Order (which monitor shows each screen) and Identify Monitors (turns each monitor off for 3 seconds, in order). See Multiple monitors.

When you leave Video Setup with something changed, it saves the boot settings and offers to reboot. - Audio Setup: the sound. - Default card: which sound card the system and every emulator use; - Volume: from 0 to 100 (the keyboard's volume keys also work, anywhere); - AlsaMixer: the full mixer, channel by channel; - MAME audio latency: from 0.0 to 50.0 (0 = default). Lower responds faster; raise it if the sound crackles in GroovyMAME; - Test sound: plays a sound to check the speakers; - Menu sounds: turns on and off a sound when the cursor moves and when you press Enter, like a game's select screen. FliperOS doesn't come with game sounds: put your own move.wav and select.wav in the sounds/menu folder of the network share. - Network Setup: the network cable works by itself; this is for Wi-Fi. - Connect to a Wi-Fi network: the list of networks with their signal; choose one and type the password; - Connect to a hidden network: for a network that doesn't appear in the list; - Network status: the connection and the IP address. - Joysticks: - Button mapping (all emulators): maps each player's controls once for every emulator (step 8); - Buttons layout (games of 1 to 5 buttons): where the buttons of a game go on the panel, by how many buttons the game uses: a 4-button game as 1 2 on top and 3 4 below, or 1 3 on top and 2 4 below. For GroovyMAME, the MAME cores of RetroArch, Model 2 and Model 3; - Calibrate GunCon 2 (light gun): shoot the top-left and bottom-right targets, then the center one to check; - Calibrate wheel, pedals or analog stick: the limits and center of each axis; - LPT joysticks (parallel port): old controllers on the parallel port: gamepad adapter (NES, SNES, N64, PlayStation), DB9 adapter (Atari, Amiga, Sega) or TurboGraFX interface (up to 7 joysticks). Joysticks found now shows what was detected and Turn off disables it. - Games: what puts games in the cabinet, in the order you use it. - Frontend: what opens every time the cabinet is turned on: the FliperOS frontend, Attract-Mode Plus, EmulationStation (ES-DE), Pegasus, RetroArch, the LXDE desktop or the FliperOS Setup itself. What isn't installed is installed (or downloaded) from here; ES-DE and Pegasus are built on the cabinet, which needs the network and some time. A choice the video card can't run (ES-DE without OpenGL 3, for example) gets a red X and a question before it opens.

Choosing a frontend also puts every game folder into it, so choose it again whenever a folder gets its first games. *Add a custom frontend* adds another program by its command, and *Edit or delete a custom frontend* changes or removes it. See [Frontends](#Frontends).
  • Extras: programs left out of the ISO to keep the download small, installed over the internet: Wine (needed by some Fightcade 2 emulators), Steam and Heroic (GOG games), Pixelcade, ZeDMD and game output tools.
  • Custom games: PC games, scripts and your own emulators, which the frontends show as systems. See Adding games.

  • Emulators & Games: the emulators of the desktop menu, each marked installed or not installed.

    Choose one that is not installed to install it: Model 2 (SM2-Emu, downloaded and built on the machine, several minutes), Fightcade 2 (downloaded from its site) and KOF Final Attack on Ikemen GO in 4:3 at 320x240: you point to the folder of the original game (the one with Final Attack.exe, on a USB disk or the network) and it downloads the 4:3 patch and Ikemen GO and makes a converted copy. The others come in the image. - Folders: the folders FliperOS uses (roms, bios, media, nvram, save, splashscreen) and the ones inside them: each emulator, each RetroArch core, each type of art.

    Choose one and Link this to another folder to use another folder in its place, for when the ROMs or the art are on external storage (a USB disk, a second drive): ~/roms/mame becomes a link to it and the folder used until then is kept as ~/roms/old-mame. Each folder can point to a different place. Unlink the custom folder brings the previous one back. - Downloader: - ROM/CHD MAME torrent: you paste the magnet link of a romset (and one of CHDs) and it downloads, through Transmission, only the games the ROM Cleaner filter chooses, straight into the emulator's folder. The MAME version of the romset must match the emulator; - Free games (open-source homebrew): downloads free homebrew games to the RetroArch folders, so the frontend has something to show. - Cleaner: for those who have a full romset. - MAME ROM Cleaner: you say where the romset is (a folder, USB disk or network share) and which emulator it is for (GroovyMAME, Flycast, Supermodel, Model 2, MAME 2010...).

    It keeps only the games that work and suit your cabinet (horizontal or vertical, players, buttons and controls you have, categories, with or without clones, bootlegs, prototypes and adult games), shows how many and how much space, and copies or moves them to the right folder. See the list shows the games, Change the parameters changes the filter; - MAME CHD Cleaner: brings the CHDs (the disk images some games need) of only the games that stayed.

    See ROMs, BIOS and artwork. - Scraper: downloads screenshots, covers, logos, videos and descriptions for the games found in roms. You choose the systems (or all of them), the provider (ScreenScraper, TheGamesDB, ArcadeDB, progetto-SNAPS, MobyGames, IGDB or OpenRetro, with the login saved for the ones that ask) and the kinds of media.

    Art packs by torrent brings logos and videos only for the ROMs you have. An interrupted scrape can be resumed later. Needs internet. See Scraper. - AttractPlus ROM List: makes the Attract-Mode Plus game lists of the arcade folders with each game's real name, year and manufacturer (Street Fighter II instead of sf2), clones included. Works offline. Mark the folders and confirm. - System: the rest. - Latency: shows the CPU, memory, video card and analog output of this computer. - Standard (any hardware): the default, works on any machine; - Low latency (modern CPUs): less delay between the button and the picture, for recent CPUs. If the computer is below the recommendation, it says what is missing; - Check this computer: compares this machine with the recommendation; - Recommended hardware: the list of ideal parts. See Latency. - Services: SSH, the network share, fliperos.local, the Wi-Fi radio, waiting for the network and the web panel, each one at boot, after boot or off. - Quirks (USB device fixes): fixes for USB devices that arrive wrong (a dual encoder showing up as a single player, a controller that freezes). Add a quirk asks for a name and a code; USB devices connected now shows the codes of what is plugged in; choosing a quirk in the list deletes it. Applies after a reboot. See Controls. - Password: the password of the fliperos user (login, SSH and the network share). - System Update: downloads and installs the updates of every Ubuntu package. The FliperOS updates themselves are offered at boot (step 7). - What's new: the updates installed on this machine and the changelog of each version. - Debug mode (on/off): off (the default), the boot shows only the splash and the messages of frontends and emulators are saved in /opt/fliperos/logs. On, every text appears on screen: the boot menu, the system messages and the emulator errors. Turn it on when a game doesn't open, to see why. Emulators follow it right away; the boot, after a reboot. - Lab mode (on/off): remote help. A temporary internet address to the web panel, with a terminal, for someone far away to look at a problem; it ends after 4 hours, at power off, or here. - Splash screen: the picture shown while the cabinet boots. Choose a theme to see a 10-second Preview or to Use at boot. Themes are folders in ~/splashscreen (the splashscreen share on the network); more on Gnome-look.

Build and tests

Always in Docker (CLAUDE.md explains why).

docker build -f Dockerfile.fliperos -t fliperos-builder .
docker run --rm --privileged --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/output,target=/output" fliperos-builder bash /build/fliperos-mkiso.sh --output /output/fliperos-0.16.iso

docker build -t fliperos-tests -f tests/Dockerfile tests
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/w" -w /w fliperos-tests python3 tests/test_setup.py
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/w" -w /w fliperos-tests python3 tests/test_build.py

Video cards

Which video cards FliperOS supports, and what each one gives on a 15 kHz CRT.

The difference between them is the dotclock: a 320x240 game at 15 kHz needs about 6.5 MHz, a 640x480i boot about 13 MHz. A card that generates those clocks shows each game at its native resolution.

A card that doesn't uses a super resolution: the same lines and the same refresh as the game, with the width multiplied (1280 or 2560 instead of 320). On a CRT the picture is almost the same, since the beam has no horizontal pixels. What gives it away: RetroArch draws its notifications at 2560 wide, so they come out squeezed.

Summary

Card Driver Analog output 15 kHz
AMD/ATI Radeon HD 2000 to HD 7000, R7/R9 200 and 300 (GCN 1.0) radeon or amdgpu VGA, DVI-I Native (recommended)
AMD GCN 2 and 3 with DVI-I (R7 260X, R9 380) radeon or amdgpu (GCN 2), amdgpu (GCN 3) DVI-I Reported by GroovyArcade. The R9 380 needs a kernel parameter
AMD Radeon RX and newer, Ryzen APUs amdgpu None on the card; VGA on some motherboards Native through a DisplayPort to VGA converter; super resolution through HDMI
NVIDIA GeForce 8 to GTX 900, Quadro up to K series nouveau, or NVIDIA's own driver (GTX 900) VGA, DVI-I Super resolution; native if the card passes the low resolution test
NVIDIA GTX 10 and newer (Pascal, Turing, Ampere...) nouveau None Super resolution, through a converter
Intel Gen9 (HD/UHD 500 and 600 series: Skylake to Comet Lake) i915 VGA on the motherboard Super resolution, with interlace (patch 09)
Intel HD Graphics Gen5 (Ironlake: Core i3 5xx, i5 6xx) i915 VGA on the motherboard Super resolution, 480i, seen on a CRT. Only OpenGL 2.1: no ES-DE, no filter, no Vulkan
Other Intel generations i915 VGA on the motherboard Super resolution; 480i may not work

Three cards have been seen on a CRT by the project: an AMD R7 240 (radeon and amdgpu), an Intel HD Graphics (Ironlake, i915) and an NVIDIA GTX 980 Ti (nouveau). The other lines come from the kernel patches and from what the GroovyArcade and Batocera communities report (list below).

AMD/ATI

The cards CRT_EmuDriver covers on Windows, with VGA or DVI-I: the HD 2000 series to the R7/R9 200 and 300 with GCN 1.0. The 15 kHz kernel patches cover radeon and amdgpu (DCE and DCN 1 to 3): native boot at 640x480iS and every game at its own resolution, in GroovyMAME, RetroArch and the frontends.

Good, cheap choices: HD 5450, HD 6450, HD 7750, R7 240, R7 250.

SI and CIK cards (HD 7000, R7/R9) work on both drivers; the Setup picks radeon by default and offers amdgpu (with Vulkan) in Video Setup > Video driver.

The emulators follow the driver the card runs on, checked at every session start: on amdgpu, Flycast goes to the Vulkan renderer that matches its OpenGL one (per-pixel or per-triangle) and Dolphin to Vulkan; PCSX2 and DuckStation stay on Automatic, which already picks Vulkan there. Back on radeon (no Vulkan), each goes back to its factory renderer: Flycast to OpenGL with per-pixel transparency, Dolphin to OpenGL. RetroArch stays on glcore on both: its Vulkan output can't switch the CRT's modes. A choice made in an emulator is kept until the driver changes again.

Cards with no analog output (RX 400 and newer) and the Ryzen APUs need an active converter: see Converters.

GCN 2 and 3 cards with DVI-I. Not every card after GCN 1.0 lost its analog output: GroovyArcade reports the R7 260X on DVI-I and the R9 380 on DVI-I. None of them has been tried on FliperOS.

  • R9 380 and 380X (GCN 3) only run on amdgpu, and on kernel 6.18 its new display code has no analog output (that came in 6.19). They need amdgpu.dc=0 on the kernel line, which the Setup doesn't add for them: see Black screen.
  • GCN 2, also called 1.1, on amdgpu: GroovyArcade's table says these cards (HD 7790, R7 260, R7 360) don't do interlaced modes on that driver. It wasn't checked with the amdgpu.dc=0 FliperOS uses. If the picture is lost after switching to amdgpu, the trial goes back to radeon by itself.

APUs. GroovyArcade reports Wrestler, Kabini, Kaveri and Mullins working out of the box, and Wani with amdgpu.dc=0 or an EDID. On any APU the Setup sets interlace_force_even in Switchres, which AMD APUs need.

A VGA connector isn't always analog. On some APUs and motherboards the VGA port is a DisplayPort to VGA bridge chip. It may not switch modes quickly, make low clocks or do interlaced modes, so results vary by motherboard. GroovyArcade found the ASRock DeskMini A300's to be the best so far.

ArcadeVGA cards. GroovyArcade's wiki says they "are not supported and won't work", without saying why, and other reports disagree. One forum thread has an ArcadeVGA 5000 running GroovyArcade at half speed; the documentation of another 15 kHz package says they seem to be supported.

On Windows, forum posts say CRT_EmuDriver doesn't support the 3000 and the 5000, even though the 5000 is an HD 5450 with Ultimarc's own BIOS. The cause on Linux isn't documented, and none has been tried on FliperOS. If you are buying a card, a plain HD 5450 is the safer choice.

ATOM-15 isn't needed. Flashing a supported Radeon with ATOM-15 makes it start at 15 kHz from the BIOS, which GroovyArcade's FAQ describes as protection against out-of-range signals at boot. Once the kernel has loaded, 15 kHz is there either way.

Converters

A card with only digital outputs can drive a CRT through an active converter with a DAC chip inside. A passive adapter doesn't work on a digital output.

DisplayPort is the one to use. GroovyArcade reports no lower limit for its pixel clock, so a card that makes low clocks can often show games at their native resolution. An HDMI or DVI-D link doesn't go under about 25 MHz, so it only gives super resolutions.

Recommended by the GroovyArcade community:

Converter Notes
CableDeconn DisplayPort to VGA (one sold on AliExpress, with HDMI and DVI outputs too) Very fragile VGA connector. 5 V on VGA pin 9
Cable Matters DisplayPort to VGA (product 102026) Only 3.2 V on VGA pin 9, which matters if the device after it expects 5 V

Both use a Realtek RTD2168 chip. The community found no processing of the signal and no measurable lag, apart from the mode switch.

The CableDeconn has also been reported working on a FliperOS cabinet, without a record yet of the card, the driver or the modes.

What to expect, even with these:

  • Mode switches are slower than on a native VGA or DVI-I output.
  • Interlaced modes are hit-or-miss, mostly misses. So FliperOS' default 15 kHz boot (640x480iS) may stay black: use the EDID progressive entry of the boot menu, which GroovyArcade calls the most compatible for these outputs, or a progressive mode (Black screen).
  • Some modes may be refused. If only some games go black, raise dotclock_min.

Protecting the CableDeconn's connector. Users fix a VGA gender changer to it with 4-40 hex screws, so the changer takes the wear of plugging and unplugging. Use screws of 10 or 12 mm: never longer than 12 mm.

In the Setup: the output test skips a digital output that reports nothing connected.

On HDMI or DVI-D with a CRT preset, the Setup uses super resolutions by itself, even on an AMD card: 1280x480iS at boot and dotclock_min 25.0. An LCD on those outputs isn't affected. On DisplayPort an AMD card stays native.

A converter with its own EDID. Most converters report an EDID of their own, with 31 kHz modes, so the output test takes them for an LCD ("Found a monitor that could be a LCD panel"). When you then choose a CRT monitor, the Setup replaces the converter's EDID with a 15 kHz one (generic_15_super_resp.bin, as in the EDID progressive boot entry). Without it the menu came up at 1024x768 and 48 kHz and the tube stayed black, and so did the screen after leaving a game, although the games, which set their own modes, were fine. A video=1280x480iS line alone didn't fix it: the console used it, but the frontend opens the first mode of the list, the converter's. Games stay native on a card with low dotclocks.

Seen with one CableDeconn-type converter (Ryzen 5 5600GT, amdgpu, DisplayPort), with a numbered test card for each mode and the person reading the numbers on the tube: native modes from 224 to 640 pixels wide (4.5 to 13.0 MHz) and from 712 to 2560 wide (14.5 to 52 MHz) showed, 1280x480i too. Modes between about 13.1 and 14.4 MHz (672 to 704 wide) and below 4 MHz (192 wide and less) gave no signal, though the kernel had set them. So a game of those widths can go black on this converter: raise dotclock_min. Other converters and monitors may differ.

For a third monitor on a converter, see Multiple monitors.

"With an EDID" means booting the EDID entries of the boot menu, or a monitor's file from edid/ (Install).

If yours works on FliperOS, open an issue with the card, the driver, the output and what you saw: that is what turns a line here into "seen on FliperOS".

ATOM-15: 15 kHz from power on

This rewrites your video card's BIOS chip, at your own risk. A bad result can leave the card dead, with no picture even at power on. FliperOS cannot repair that: it takes a second video card (usually not the one on the motherboard) or a chip programmer. It is an experimental community tool, not made by AMD or the card's maker.

ATOM-15, by Antonio Giner "Calamity", changes the video modes in the BIOS of an ATI/AMD card, so the computer's own startup screens already come out at 15 kHz, instead of signals out of the monitor's range until the system starts. It changes nothing after that: games and menus already run at 15 kHz without it.

Video Setup > Card firmware appears with an AMD card on the installed system, at the cabinet (not over SSH, since you have to watch the next boot).

Opening it reads the card first. The menu says what the BIOS on the card has (ATOM-15 or No ATOM-15), even if the card came that way, and saves a copy in ~/vbios. With the flash tool it reads the chip. Without it, it uses the copy the system has from this boot, in ~/vbios/card-<card>-<sum>.rom, which is only for checking: only a read of the chip, with no ATOM-15 in it, can be flashed back as the original. A card that already has ATOM-15 has nothing to apply, and Restore only appears if the original BIOS was saved on this computer.

To flash, you need the flash tool. amdvbflash is AMD's, closed, and AMD does not publish it, so FliperOS does not ship or download it. Get the 64-bit Linux version yourself (the TechPowerUp forums have it) and put the file at ~/vbios/amdvbflash. It runs as root, so use a copy you trust. It does not work with Secure Boot on.

What the Setup does, in order:

  1. The warnings, with No as the default. In UEFI mode one more: ATOM-15 is not guaranteed there, the computer's setup screen can stay black, and a patched BIOS loses the signature of its EFI part (a bricked R9 380 has been reported that way).
  2. Reads the card's BIOS twice with amdvbflash -s and compares. If it is good and belongs to this card, the backup goes to ~/vbios/original-<card>-<sum>.rom, and the Setup shows where. Copy it off the computer: if the card dies, this machine may show no picture to reach it.
  3. Makes the patched BIOS for the monitor's frequencies: ~/vbios/atom15-<card>-<range>khz.rom, with a log of each mode next to it. A BIOS that already has the hook, a card outside ATOM-15's list, or a BIOS with no room for the hook outside its EFI part is refused here, with the card untouched.
  4. Flashes it after one more question, reads it back and compares. If that fails, the original goes back right away.
  5. Reboot and test. Watch the screen from the first second. Before the frontend, a question asks if the startup screens were stable. Enter (button 1) within 90 seconds keeps it.

With no answer, or with Esc, the original BIOS is flashed back and the computer restarts. A guard service (fliperos-atom15-guard.service) does the same if the question never opens within 5 minutes, or if the test boot hung and the computer was turned off. Card firmware > Restore the original BIOS puts it back later.

A card that does not pass the power-on test never reaches the system, so none of this can undo it; that is the risk the warning is about. To flash the backup by hand from another card: amdvbflash -p <adapter> original-<card>-<sum>.rom.

How far this was tested: the patch is a translation of ATOM-15 v1.6 to Python (config/fliperos-atom15), made with the author's permission, because the original is Windows-only, with no command line. Against a BIOS written by the real atom-15.exe (R7 240, 15 kHz) all 65536 bytes came out the same (tools/atom15-check.py). Other card families, other ranges and the move of the EFI part use the same code but were not compared. The flash, the test at the next boot and the way back have only run with a fake flash tool, never on a real card.

NVIDIA

NVIDIA cards run on the open driver, nouveau, out of the box. On the installed system, Setup > Video Setup > Video driver can switch to NVIDIA's own driver (see below).

With VGA or DVI-I (GeForce 8 to GTX 900, Quadro up to the K series). Out of the box nouveau refuses every mode under 25 MHz. FliperOS's own kernel patch (10_fliperos_nouveau_analog_low_dotclock.patch) lifts that floor on the analog outputs, but whether each card's PLL actually reaches 6.5 MHz varies.

Each card's PLL has its own lowest clock, so the card is tested on the tube:

  1. boot the NVIDIA 15 kHz entry (super resolution, 1280x480iS);
  2. after you confirm the output in the video output test, the Setup shows a Switchres grid at 320x240 (6.5 MHz) for 20 seconds;
  3. black screen → a wider grid, easier for the PLL: 384x240 (7.8 MHz), 512x240 (10.4 MHz), then 640x240 (13 MHz);
  4. the first grid you see sets dotclock_min for Switchres, MAME and RetroArch (0 at 320, then 7.7, 10.3 or 12.9);
  5. none seen, or no answer → super resolutions, as before. Nothing is lost by trying.

Below the card's minimum, Switchres, MAME, RetroArch and the standalone emulators double the width: a 320x240 game comes out at 640x240. On a CRT the picture is the same. Boot modes under the minimum are not offered.

The test can be repeated on the installed system in Setup > Video Setup > Low resolutions. It only runs on an analog output with a 15 kHz monitor.

Seen on a CRT: GTX 980 Ti (GM200, DVI-I, VGA-SCART) on nouveau, with the patch. Black at 6.5 and 6.8 MHz, picture at 7.15 MHz and above: every width from 352x240 to 2560x240, plus 640x480i and 1280x480i. Community reports with lower clocks on nouveau: GeForce 8400 GS and Quadro K600 (Batocera).

Mind the speed: nouveau runs most GTX 600, 700 and 900 cards at their boot clock (it can't raise the clock of Maxwell 2, and on Kepler only by hand). For arcade and 2D consoles that is enough; for PS2, GameCube and Model 3, an AMD card is better, or NVIDIA's own driver.

NVIDIA's own driver. In Setup > Video Setup > Video driver on a card with an NVIDIA chip. Compare the two there lists what each driver gives and takes:

nouveau NVIDIA's own driver
Programs that change resolution All: menus, frontends, RetroArch, MAME, standalone emulators Only those in Xorg (MAME, the standalone emulators)
Lowest pixel clock The card's PLL (7.15 MHz on the GTX 980 Ti) Any (320x240 at 6.5 MHz), in Xorg
480i Yes In Xorg only
3D speed Boot clock: slow for PS2, GameCube Full
Cards GeForce 8 to GTX 900 with VGA/DVI-I GTX 750 to 900 (Maxwell)

Measured on the same GTX 980 Ti with driver 580: its KMS (nvidia-drm) only takes progressive modes from the EDID. It drops interlaced ones (an EDID with only 1280x480i leaves no mode at all, and the boot is black) and every mode Switchres adds ("Kernel doesn't supports user modes"). That check is inside NVIDIA's binary module, so no kernel patch reaches it. In Xorg, with ModeValidation, UseEDID false and its own modelines, every 15 kHz mode worked, as Batocera does on these cards.

Details of the switch:

  • NVIDIA driver downloads it from Ubuntu's own repository (a few hundred MB), and DKMS compiles its kernel module for the 15 kHz kernel (a few minutes). The package is nvidia-driver-580, from the GTX 900 (Maxwell, the last with DVI-I) to the current cards; it is the one checked to build on the 15 kHz kernel. The 470 of the GTX 600/700 (Kepler) does not build on kernel 6.18, so those cards and the older ones stay on nouveau.
  • Both drivers stay installed; the kernel line chooses (modprobe.blacklist=nouveau nvidia-drm.modeset=1 nvidia-drm.fbdev=1, or the NVIDIA modules blacklisted for nouveau). The package's own nouveau blacklist in /lib/modprobe.d is overridden by a file of the same name in /etc/modprobe.d.
  • The switch is on trial, like radeon/amdgpu: after the restart, press Enter to confirm the picture. With no answer in 15 s FliperOS goes back to nouveau and restarts. The boot menu (a key during the countdown) also has FliperOS - nouveau driver.
  • The low resolution result belongs to a driver, so a switch starts in super resolution. Back on nouveau, once the picture is confirmed, the Setup offers the grid again. The NVIDIA driver has no grid: its KMS doesn't take Switchres modes.
  • X uses the nvidia driver with mode validation relaxed (ModeValidation: modes without EDID, low pixel clocks, any sync range), which a 15 kHz tube needs. RetroArch, Switchres and the console use its KMS (nvidia-drm).
  • If a kernel update leaves no NVIDIA module for the new kernel, the boot tries DKMS again; with no module, it goes back to nouveau and restarts, so the screen is never left black.

Without analog output (GTX 10 and newer). Super resolution only, through an active converter. RTX 20 and 30 cards need their GSP firmware, which stays in the system (/usr/lib/firmware/nvidia).

Intel

Intel integrated graphics use the Intel 15 kHz boot entry, always in super resolution (1280x480iS): i915 doesn't generate the low clocks.

You need a monitor at a standard frequency first. The boot menu and the installation are drawn at 31 kHz, so on an Intel HD connect a regular VGA monitor (an LCD or a PC monitor), boot the media, install FliperOS and set the video with it. Only then power off, move the cable to the CRT and turn the cabinet on.

In Setup > Video Setup > Resolution an Intel card also lists 1280x240 60 Hz progressive (240p, no interlace flicker in the menus). It is not in the kernel's mode table, so the Setup writes an EDID with that mode (fliperos-1280x240.bin, 26.058 MHz, 15.66 kHz), puts it in the initramfs and points drm.edid_firmware at it. Pick the 480i entry again to go back. Seen on the tube (Core i3-540, VGA).

The same mode is in the media's boot menu as Intel 15 kHz 240p (next to Intel 15 kHz): the installer, the Setup and the frontend already come up in progressive 240p, and the installed system keeps it. The image builds the EDID (fliperos-rebuild-edids); on the installed disk it goes into the initramfs.

On Gen9 (Skylake, Kaby Lake, Coffee Lake, Comet Lake) patch 09 enables interlace, with i915.no_ytiled_scanout=1 on the kernel line. Other generations have no interlace patch: 240p works, 480i may not.

The VGA port of many motherboards is a DisplayPort to VGA bridge chip on the board, so results vary by motherboard.

What was tested

Seen working on a CRT, through the VGA output, installed from the Intel 15 kHz boot entry:

  • Card: Intel HD Graphics of a Core i3-540 (Clarkdale, Ironlake, Gen5), driver i915, kernel 6.18, Mesa 25.2.
  • Works: the boot menu and the Setup (1280x480i), the FliperOS frontend, RetroArch (each game in its own super resolution, such as 2560x224), GroovyMAME and Attract-Mode Plus.
  • Starts, games not tried: Pegasus.
  • Also seen: the 1280x240 progressive mode above.
  • Not seen on the tube: any other Intel generation, and the 3D emulators.

Limits of the Intel HD

What a user of this card has to know:

  • No native low resolutions. The card can't generate a pixel clock under about 25 MHz, so a 320x240 game is shown as 2560x240 (same lines, same refresh, wider). On a CRT the picture is almost the same. The boot, the Setup and the frontend are in 1280x480i by default: interlaced, so thin horizontal lines flicker. The 1280x240 option above is the way out, once it is checked on a tube.
  • OpenGL 2.1 and OpenGL ES 2.0 only (Ironlake; the Mesa driver is crocus). Everything that asks for OpenGL 3 does not run:
  • EmulationStation-DE does not open (it needs OpenGL 3.3 or OpenGL ES 3.0). Setup > Games > Frontend marks it with a red X and a warning, asks before choosing it, and the installer refuses to build it. Pegasus (Qt, OpenGL ES 2.0) is not affected.
  • RetroArch uses its gl driver instead of glcore: fliperos-kms-run checks the card and switches by itself. A core or a shader that needs OpenGL 3 will not work.
  • The 480i flicker filter and the software colour adjustments are off (the log says OpenGL 3.0 or newer is needed; filter off for this program). Setup > Video Setup > 480i hacks has no effect on this card.
  • No Vulkan on Ironlake. Emulators that need it (the Vulkan renderers of Flycast, Dolphin, PCSX2, DuckStation) are not usable, and the Vulkan-by-driver switch of the Setup only acts on amdgpu. Not tested; it follows from the hardware. The same goes for the 3D emulators on a card from 2010: not tried.
  • The processor must have graphics. The VGA port of a board only works with a CPU that has them: Clarkdale (Core i3 5xx, i5 6xx) does; Lynnfield (Core i7 8xx, i5 7xx) does not, and the board shows no video device at all (seen on an i7 870).
  • Changing the video card (or the CPU that has the graphics) is noticed at boot. See Changing the video card below. Recovery Mode of the media (see Install) stays as the last resort.

Changing the video card

The output test stores the card's PCI id (gpu_id in /etc/fliperos/fliperos.conf). At each boot the installed system checks that the card is still there; a card that comes or goes but is not the main one (a new CPU graphics with the AMD still in) changes nothing.

When the main card changed:

  1. Before any picture (fliperos-driver-trial.service): FliperOS writes a safe mode for the new card on its first analog output, with the monitor that was set (native boot mode on a card that makes low clocks, 1280x480iS on an Intel), drops what belonged to the old card (extra monitors, the NVIDIA grid step) and reboots once. A saved 320x240 mode on an Intel, which can't make that clock, no longer leaves the screen black. Without an analog output, or with an LCD monitor, it only marks the change.
  2. Before the frontend opens (also when the boot goes straight into a game): a question says which card it was and which it is now, and offers to redo the output test. Yes runs the same test as the installation, saves the result (kernel line, Switchres, RetroArch, Xorg) and offers a reboot. No asks again at the next boot; after three answers it accepts the card.

Installs from before this feature have no gpu_id: the first boot compares the saved driver with the cards that are there, and records the id if they match.

Setup > Video Setup > Test the video outputs asks for the same test on the next boot (it needs the screen free, without the graphic menu open).

What the Setup marks as not supported

On a card that gives less than OpenGL 3, the Setup marks the item with a red X (and (not supported) in the text menus), shows the reason (Needs OpenGL 3.3 or Vulkan, and this video card gives OpenGL 2.1 and OpenGL ES 2.0) and asks before opening it (the default is No). The check reads the card with eglinfo; without it, nothing is marked.

Where Item Needs
Games > Frontend EmulationStation-DE OpenGL 3.3 or OpenGL ES 3.0
Video Setup 480i hacks (the flicker filter) OpenGL 3.0
Games > Emulators & Games PCSX2, Dolphin, DuckStation OpenGL 3.3 or Vulkan (each project's own minimum)

Flycast, Supermodel and the other emulators are not marked: their minimum was not checked against this card.

Intel-specific workarounds in FliperOS

Three things only the Intel showed, fixed in the code:

  • The screen was not released after a program closed it. On Ironlake the Mesa leaves descriptors of /dev/dri/card0 open after pygame.display.quit(), so the process stayed the owner (DRM master) of the screen: RetroArch failed with Error when switching mode and the frontend could not reopen (kmsdrm not available). gui/drmmaster.py drops the master after the display is closed (frontend and Setup).
  • Attract-Mode Plus showed a black screen because SFML makes its buffer in ARGB8888, which Ironlake refuses to scan out (Failed to create fb). The package fliperos-attractplus carries two SFML patches: a fallback to XRGB8888 (0002) and the same drop of the master when its context is cleaned up (0003).
  • The frontend chooser marks what the card can't run (see above).

Several cards

A second card for a second or third monitor works best if it is AMD too. See Multiple monitors.

Monitors

Which preset to choose for your tube, how to centre the picture, and what sits between the video card and the monitor.

Choosing the preset

Choose it in Setup > Video Setup > Monitor Type. A preset tells Switchres which frequencies the monitor accepts, so it can make a mode for each game.

  • Arcade monitor, model unknown: start with generic_15, the narrowest range. If the picture is stable, arcade_15 and then arcade_15ex allow more games at their exact frequency.
  • Your model is on the list: use its preset.
  • TV: generic_15 if it accepts it. ntsc or pal only if the TV is strict about one standard: those run at one refresh rate only, so games made for another rate won't match.
  • Nothing fits: Custom, made on the Geometry grid (below).

Mind the "Boots at" column. A preset for a multi-frequency monitor boots at 31 kHz. On a monitor that only takes 15 kHz, 31 kHz can damage the tube, so never pick one of those just because its list of frequencies includes 15 kHz.

Preset Monitor Horizontal (kHz) Refresh (Hz) Boots at

arcade_15 Arcade, standard resolution 15.625-16.2 49.5-65 15 kHz
arcade_15ex Arcade, extended resolution 15.625-16.5 49.5-65 15 kHz
k7000 Wells Gardner K7000 15.625-15.8 49.5-63 15 kHz
k7131 Wells Gardner 25K7131 15.625-16.67 49.5-65 15 kHz
h9110 Hantarex MTC 9110 15.625-16.67 49.5-65 15 kHz
polo Hantarex Polo 15.625-16.67 49.5-65 15 kHz

The frequencies are Switchres' presets, as listed in GroovyArcade's monitor definitions, with the exact timings of each one. The last column is what lib/monitor.sh does. The project hasn't checked each preset on a real monitor: they are as Switchres defines them.

Centring the picture

  1. Put the monitor's own controls back in the middle first. In most cases Switchres gives a centred picture that fills the screen.
  2. Use Setup > Video Setup > Geometry: it stretches, shrinks and moves the picture on a grid, and saves the result as the Custom monitor (Install).
  3. Go in small steps. Too large a change makes the monitor lose sync.
  4. Finish on the monitor. No software changes the vertical size: that is the monitor's V-SIZE, or the service menu on a TV. Arcade monitors take this well; TVs are the most troublesome.

To check one mode by hand, on the cabinet's own screen (not over SSH), open the grid with the lines and refresh of a game. Tab switches between two patterns. World Rally, for example:

switchres 368 232 60 -s -l grid

What the numbers mean

A Custom monitor is one crt_range0 line in /etc/switchres.ini, 16 values:

HfreqMin-HfreqMax, VfreqMin-VfreqMax, HFrontPorch, HSyncPulse, HBackPorch, VFrontPorch, VSyncPulse, VBackPorch, HSyncPol, VSyncPol, ProgressiveLinesMin, ProgressiveLinesMax, InterlacedLinesMin, InterlacedLinesMax

Horizontally, the two porches decide the size and the position:

  • Wider picture: lower both porches by the same amount. Narrower: raise both.
  • Move left: lower the front porch and raise the back porch by the same amount. Move right: the opposite.

Vertically they only move the picture. Up: lower the front porch and raise the back porch. Down: the opposite. Switchres takes the vertical porches as minimums, so it may not move as far as you asked.

Between the card and the tube

The video card gives VGA: red, green, blue and separate horizontal and vertical sync. An arcade monitor usually expects composite sync and its own signal level, so something has to sit in between.

  • JAMMA cabinet: the Ultimarc J-PAC connects a VGA card and USB to the JAMMA connector and has a video amplifier for arcade monitors. It also works as the keyboard encoder of the panel.

Forum posts say it makes composite sync from the VGA's two sync lines and checks the frequency before passing it on. It doesn't make the 15 kHz signal: FliperOS does. - SCART TV or monitor: a VGA to SCART cable. A GTX 980 Ti was seen on a CRT that way (Video cards).

Neither the project nor the GroovyArcade wiki documents the wiring of each monitor, so follow the manual of your monitor and of the interface. Keep the tube off until the card is known to output 15 kHz if you are not sure of the boot mode.

Black screen

What to try when the tube shows nothing, or when only some games go black. Most of this comes from the GroovyArcade wiki, adapted to where FliperOS keeps each thing, so it hasn't all been tried here.

If the picture rolls or tears at a frequency the monitor can't take, turn the monitor off first. A 31 kHz signal can damage a 15 kHz tube.

Getting in without a picture

The system usually booted even with a black tube. From another computer on the same network:

  • SSH, on from the first boot: ssh fliperos@fliperos.local.
  • The web panel, at http://fliperos.local, has a terminal page (Web panel).
  • Recovery Mode on the media, when the disk doesn't boot (Install).

Debug mode in the Setup shows the boot messages instead of the splash (Installed system).

What the system sees

This lists each video output, whether something is connected, its EDID and its modes, then the card, the driver and what FliperOS saved:

for c in /sys/class/drm/card?-*; do
  echo "${c##*/}: $(cat "$c/status"), EDID $(wc -c < "$c/edid") bytes"
  cat "$c/modes"
done
cat /proc/cmdline
lspci -nnk | grep -A3 -E 'VGA|Display'
grep -E '^(driver|connector|detection|monitor|kernel_video)=' /etc/fliperos/fliperos.conf

The name in connector= must be the output your monitor is plugged into. If you moved the cable, Setup > Video Setup > Test the video outputs finds it again.

Changing the kernel line by hand

The Setup writes this line, so use it whenever you can see its menu. Without a picture, change FLIPEROS_CMDLINE in /etc/default/fliperos-boot. FliperOS has no text editor for the terminal, so these commands use sed.

To replace a part of the line, here the mode:

grep FLIPEROS_CMDLINE /etc/default/fliperos-boot
sudo sed -i 's/video=VGA-1:640x480iS/video=VGA-1:640x240S/' /etc/default/fliperos-boot

To add a parameter:

sudo sed -i 's/^FLIPEROS_CMDLINE="/&amdgpu.dc=0 /' /etc/default/fliperos-boot

Then write it to the bootloader and restart:

sudo fliperos-limine-update
sudo reboot

The next save in Video Setup rewrites the video= part.

Black from the boot

Situation Try
At the installation Another entry of the boot menu: EDID progressive, then EDID interlaced, which force every output on. To choose on a 15 kHz-only tube, see Install
Interlaced modes may be the problem (black at 640x480iS) Change video=VGA-1:640x480iS to video=VGA-1:640x240S. In the Setup it is Video Setup > Resolution
Black after moving the cable or booting without it Force the output on, with an e at the end of the mode: video=VGA-1:640x480iSe
Through a converter Interlaced modes often fail: see Converters
AMD with DVI-I that has no radeon driver (R9 380, 380X) Add amdgpu.dc=0 to the line: on kernel 6.18 amdgpu's new display code has no analog output. See Video cards
Ryzen 2200GE with random black screens Disable legacy boot (CSM) in the BIOS. Reported by GroovyArcade on this APU
Motherboard VGA on an APU or Intel It may be a DisplayPort bridge chip, which limits low clocks and interlace. See Video cards
You changed the video card FliperOS notices at boot and offers the output test: see Changing the video card

Splash shows, then black or a crash

With two video cards, the frontend may be opening on the wrong one. Set up FliperOS with only the card you will use, and disable the other in the BIOS or pull it out. To try it without opening the case, until the next boot:

lspci | grep VGA
echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:XX:00.0/remove    # XX from the line above

For monitors on two cards, see Multiple monitors.

The menus work, some games go black

Some modes are below what the card or the converter generates. dotclock_min tells Switchres the lowest clock to use. Modes under it get a wider picture with the same lines, which looks the same on a CRT.

On AMD cards the GroovyArcade wiki says 8 MHz is often needed, and lists 12 and 25 as other common values. The NVIDIA low resolution test finds this value by itself; on other cards it is by hand.

Set the same value in both files: /etc/switchres.ini for Switchres and the programs that use it, /etc/fliperos/mame/mame.ini for GroovyMAME. For 8 MHz:

sudo sed -i -E 's/^([[:space:]]*dotclock_min[[:space:]]+).*/\18.0/' /etc/switchres.ini
sed -i -E 's/^([[:space:]]*dotclock_min[[:space:]]+).*/\18.0/' /etc/fliperos/mame/mame.ini

The Setup keeps a value of yours. It only replaces its own (0, 25, or a step of the NVIDIA test). To see the mode a game gets:

switchres 320 240 60 -c

To test a resolution with a real game, the GroovyArcade wiki has tables of games by resolution and frequency. Each program's own log is /opt/fliperos/logs/<program>.log.

The picture is there but wrong

Off-centre, too large or too small: Monitors. Flickering menus: the 480i hacks in Emulators.

Asking for help

Open an issue with the output of the commands in What the system sees, your monitor, and how it is connected, converter included.

Install

From the written media to the system on disk: writing the ISO, the boot menu, the video output test and the installation through FliperOS Setup.

Writing the media

Write the ISO byte for byte to a USB stick and disable Secure Boot (the 15 kHz kernel is custom and unsigned).

The ISO uses the Limine bootloader and is hybrid (xorriso + limine bios-install): the same image boots as a CD and as a USB stick, on BIOS and on UEFI. Writers that rebuild the boot structure break it — Rufus in its default mode ("ISO image"), Ventoy and UNetbootin don't work. Use balenaEtcher, or Rufus in "DD Image mode", or dd:

sudo dd if=fliperos-0.16.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress conv=fsync

Check /dev/sdX with lsblk first: the wrong device erases the wrong disk.

Boot menu

The same options as GroovyArcade (os/groovyarcade/syslinux/syslinux.cfg). Here you only choose the range Linux boots in; the output and the monitor are decided later, by the output test.

Entry Parameters For
15 kHz (default) video=640x480iS Arcade monitor or TV, 640x480 interlaced
25 kHz video=512x384S Medium resolution monitor
31 kHz video=640x480S High resolution monitor
SVGA / LCD monitor — PC monitor or LCD (its EDID applies)
Intel 15 kHz video=1280x480iS i915.no_ytiled_scanout=1 Intel: super resolution; the parameter comes from patch 09 and enables interlacing on Gen9
Intel 15 kHz 240p drm.edid_firmware=edid/fliperos-1280x240.bin video=e i915.no_ytiled_scanout=1 Intel: 1280x240 progressive (240p, no interlace flicker), from a FliperOS EDID; the installed system keeps it
NVIDIA 15 kHz video=1280x480iS NVIDIA: super resolution; the output test then tries native modes (see Video cards)
NTSC video=720x480iS NTSC TV
PAL video=768x576iS PAL TV
EDID progressive drm.edid_firmware=edid/generic_15_super_resp.bin video=e Switchres EDID, all outputs forced. For DisplayPort or HDMI through a converter
EDID interlaced drm.edid_firmware=edid/generic_15_super_resi.bin video=e Same, interlaced

Intel HD: the boot menu is drawn at 31 kHz and the card makes no low clocks, so do the whole installation on a monitor at a standard frequency (an LCD or a PC monitor) and connect the CRT only afterwards, with the cabinet powered off. See Video cards.

The S at the end of the mode comes from the 15 kHz patch: it uses the kernel's fixed table of low-dotclock modes (drm_modes_low_dotclock.c), and i means interlaced. Every entry carries quiet splash consoleblank=0 and radeon on SI/CIK cards.

10-second timer. With no key pressed, the 15 kHz entry boots, which is the safe one for a cabinet: an LCD receiving 15 kHz only shows "out of range", but 31 kHz on a 15 kHz-only tube can damage it.

The menu itself doesn't show on a 15 kHz CRT — it is drawn in the firmware's text mode (~31 kHz), before the kernel. GroovyArcade is the same. To choose another entry on a 15 kHz-only cabinet, connect an LCD temporarily: press a key to stop the countdown, highlight the entry without pressing Enter, move the cable to the CRT, and only then press Enter. With the CRT alone, wait the 10 s. The first readable thing on the tube is the splash, already in the boot mode.

No picture at all? See Black screen.

Output test and Testing Results

Ported from gatools (video/video.sh): as soon as the media boots, fliperos-setup:

  1. forces the analog outputs on ("Lights on") and explains the test, speaking through espeak-ng;
  2. turns all outputs off and enables one at a time, writing on/off/detect to /sys/class/drm/cardN-CONNECTOR/status (an analog output with no monitor detected is forced; a digital one with nothing connected is skipped);
  3. on each one, says "Testing output V G A 1. If you can see this screen, press Enter." and shows "If you can see this screen clearly, press ENTER." for 10 s;
  4. stops at the first ENTER and goes to the Testing Results screen (gatools tests all of them and picks the best; here, whoever is looking at the screen has already decided). Without ENTER, it repeats the round up to three times.

With two cards, the console is moved to the framebuffer of the card being tested (con2fbmap), as in gatools.

On an NVIDIA card (nouveau) with the output on VGA or DVI-I and a 15 kHz boot, the confirmed output gets one more step: a Switchres grid at 320x240 (about 6.5 MHz) for 20 seconds, with "Did you see the test grid clearly?" afterwards. Yes → the card counts as generating low dotclocks (low_dotclock_pci in fliperos.conf); no or no answer → super resolution. See Video cards.

The Testing Results screen shows the GPU, driver, connector, current mode and horizontal frequency (read from the active CRTC by fliperos-video-check), whether the card generates low dotclocks, whether there is an interlaced mode, the EDID, whether the monitor was identified and whether the output will be forced at boot — with the same sentences as gatools' inform_user — and offers Validate settings or Repeat test.

Once validated, gatools' configure_from_connector applies:

  • Switchres EDID (dongle) → the monitor comes from the EDID itself;
  • otherwise, the monitor type is mandatory (the list opens on the suggestion of the boot entry);
  • the kernel line comes from the monitor: video=VGA-1:640x480iSe (the e when the output had to be forced); a card without low dotclock (Intel, NVIDIA that didn't pass the grid), or a CRT on HDMI or DVI-D → super resolution 1280x480iS (behind a converter that reports an EDID of its own, the EDID is replaced instead: see below) and dotclock_min 25.0 in Switchres; APU → interlace_force_even 1; EDID boot → drm.edid_firmware=CONNECTOR:edid/<monitor>.bin; LCD → nothing (its EDID applies).

With a DisplayPort or HDMI to VGA converter

A converter reports an EDID of its own, with 31 kHz modes, so the Testing Results screen says Monitor detection: LCD OR MODERN CRT. That is expected, not a failure. What you do:

  1. Boot menu: start with the default 15 kHz entry. If the screen stays black, restart with EDID progressive (interlaced modes often fail on converters; see Video cards).
  2. Output test: press ENTER on the output where you can see the screen (the DisplayPort or HDMI one).
  3. Testing Results: read it and choose Validate settings.
  4. Monitor Type: pick your CRT (generic_15 for a TV or an ordinary 15 kHz arcade monitor). This is the choice that matters: the Setup can't tell a CRT behind a converter from an LCD, and only your answer says it is a tube. Choosing LCD here writes no video mode and leaves the output at the converter's own 31 kHz mode.

With a CRT chosen, the Setup replaces the converter's EDID with a 15 kHz one (generic_15_super_resp.bin, the file of the EDID progressive boot entry) and forces the output on. A video= mode alone isn't enough: the menus, the frontend and the return from a game open the first mode of the list, which is the converter's own 48 kHz one, and the tube stays black. The games use native modes when the card makes low dotclocks. A cabinet installed before this rule has no boot mode saved: Setup > Video Setup > Monitor Type, choose the same monitor again, and reboot.

Everything is saved in /etc/fliperos/fliperos.conf (GPU, driver, connector, detection, monitor, range, boot mode, kernel parameters, orientation, launcher), the equivalent of ga.conf, and in switchres.ini/mame.ini.

FliperOS Setup

The media's menu (gasetup's isomainmenu): Install to HD/SSD, Recovery Mode, Terminal and Shutdown. The title shows the host and the IP.

Install to HD/SSD

  1. Do you want to configure video? — Yes opens Video Setup:

  2. Monitor Type: the 29 Switchres presets, in the gatools list, plus Custom: your own crt_range0 (the timings that really fit your monitor), made on the Geometry grid or typed in (16 values, as in switchres.ini, of the same 15/25/31 kHz band as the preset).

    It sits on top of the preset that was in use, which still gives the boot resolution, the EDID and the Xorg range; choosing a preset again discards it; - Monitor Orientation: horizontal, vertical clockwise, vertical counter-clockwise (console rotated with fbcon=rotate, panel_orientation in video=, MAME's ror/rol and the desktop through xrandr). Standing up, the Setup menu and the FliperOS frontend are laid out for the tall screen (240x320) and turned to the monitor's side; the few screens made only for a wide screen (the Button mapping panel, the ROM filter board) are shrunk to the width, between the real title and keys. The FliperOS boot screen uses its pre-rotated pictures. The console and terminal go to 640x480i standing up (60 columns, letters in proportion; in 640x240 they had 30): the boot line gets an EDID made for the monitor (edid/fliperos-vertical.bin, with Switchres' 640x240 and 640x480i), so the menu and the frontend still switch to their 640x240. A boot line that already carries an EDID stays as it is; - Resolution: only the modes of the kernel table that the monitor's range and the card accept (without low dotclock, only the super resolutions), plus a custom resolution: tested on the Switchres grid and turned into an EDID (switchres -e), like worker_custom_video_mode; - Geometry: the same geometry as GroovyArcade — Switchres' geometry.py, which draws the grid and returns the crt_range, saved as monitor custom in /etc/switchres.ini (the Monitor Type becomes Custom).

    The grid is drawn with the lines and refresh rate of the resolution chosen above (50 Hz in PAL modes; with no choice, 640x480), 8 pixels wider, like GroovyArcade's 648x480: at the exact boot mode, Switchres would have to replace the mode on screen each time an arrow reopens the grid, and the tool stopped at the first arrow.

    Downwards the image only moves while there are blank lines below it (Switchres doesn't go past the front porch); when it stops, the adjustment is the monitor's V-POS; - Multiple Monitors: a second arcade monitor on another analog output (VGA, DVI-I) of the same card, and a third, or one on a second video card or on a digital output through an active VGA converter, as an experimental option, for games with 2 or 3 screens (Darius, The Ninja Warriors and Punch-Out!! in GroovyMAME, F355 Challenge in Flycast), with a switch to turn the multi-screen mode off. See Multiple monitors. 2. Automatically Partition — lists the disks by model, size, path and bus (USB/NVMe/SATA). Not listed: the installation media itself, disks under 16 GiB, mounted or in swap, with RAID/LVM/encryption or active dependents — each one with the reason, above the list.

My drive is not listed (details) shows everything Linux sees (lsblk, the controllers and the kernel messages): an HD/SSD that doesn't even show there is hidden before Linux, almost always by the BIOS SATA mode set to RAID/Intel RST (switch to AHCI) or by Intel VMD. 3. WARNING — model, path and size of the disk that will be erased; No goes back to the disk choice. If the disk already has FliperOS, the warning suggests Recovery Mode. 4. Installing FliperOS — a single screen, with the target disk, a real progress bar (the system copy comes from the unsquashfs percentage, like gasetup's dialog --gauge), the step and short messages. Command output goes to /var/log/fliperos-setup.log. On error: step, error, View log / Retry / Return. 5. Installation completed successfully. Remove the installation CD/DVD/USB. — and Reboot now?

Partitioning: GPT, a 1 MiB BIOS boot partition, a 1 GiB FAT32 ESP, the rest in ext4. The new partitions have their old signatures wiped and the BIOS boot one is zeroed (a leftover file system from the previous disk there made limine bios-install refuse; it also runs with --force).

Limine is installed for BIOS (stage 2 in the BIOS boot partition) and for UEFI (EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI, the removable path), without touching the NVRAM.

Limine only reads FAT, so the kernel and initrd live on the ESP (/boot/efi/fliperos/), maintained by fliperos-limine-update — the equivalent of update-grub, called by the kernel and initramfs hooks. The kernel parameters are in /etc/default/fliperos-boot.

The new disk carries what was decided on the media: fliperos.conf, Switchres, MAME, Xorg, the kernel line, the configured Wi-Fi networks and the sound card.

Recovery Mode

Looks for disks with FliperOS (a FliperOS partition with the /etc/fliperos/installed marker) and offers: a terminal inside the installed system (chroot, gasetup's rescue_mode), reinstall the bootloader (the "Fix UEFI boot", for BIOS and UEFI), apply this session's video settings (graphics card replaced) and restore the system files from the media, keeping ROMs, saves, home, network, audio and video.

Installed system

What happens from boot onwards on an installed FliperOS: the default launcher, the Setup menu and what each of its items does. The desktop is covered in Desktop and theme.

Boot without text: from Limine straight to Plymouth, and the splash stays on screen until the menu or the frontend opens: fliperos-tty1 takes it down right before the launcher, the menu, the first boot or the update notice, so the login and the wait for the network (for the update check) don't leave the screen black.

Ubuntu's plymouth-quit only takes it down after 90 seconds, as a safety net, and plymouth-quit-wait doesn't hold the tty1 login.

The Limine menu is hidden (quiet: yes; a key during its 3 seconds shows it, with the diagnostics entry), the kernel and udev stay quiet (quiet loglevel=3 rd.udev.log_level=3 udev.log_level=3), the console cursor disappears (vt.global_cursor_default=0, and comes back in the shell), the automatic login writes nothing (agetty --skip-login --noissue, ~/.hushlogin) and the console stays quiet after boot (kernel.printk = 3 4 1 3 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-fliperos-console.conf: Ubuntu's 10-console-messages.conf set the level back to 4, and a kernel error after Plymouth, such as the one from the unused Intel HDMI codec, showed up on screen).

tty1 logs in by itself and follows the flow of GroovyArcade's .bash_profile (config/fliperos-tty1, called by ~/.zprofile): it opens the default launcher and, when it closes, the FliperOS menu.

The menu is a loop: Start frontend and Start desktop make the setup exit and fliperos-tty1 opens the launcher on tty1 itself, as at boot, and returns to the menu when it closes.

The setup runs as root inside sudo's pseudo-terminal; opened from there, X doesn't have tty1 as its terminal and can't switch VT (xf86OpenConsole: VT_ACTIVATE failed) — that was the cabinet's "desktop doesn't start".

If X crashes on startup, the errors from its log stay on screen until Enter (a copy goes to /opt/fliperos/logs/Xorg-failed.log). The user's shell is zsh with Oh My Zsh and the Dracula theme (Desktop and theme); ~/.bash_profile calls the same flow, for whoever goes back to bash.

Controller in the menus: with the setup menu on screen, the controller acts as the keyboard — D-pad, hat or analog stick = arrows (repeat while held), button 1 / A / Start = Enter, button 2 / B / Select = Esc, button 3 / X / Y = Space (toggles in checklists), L / R = Page Up / Page Down.

It works with arcade encoders (digital axis 0–255), gamepads and USB joysticks; light guns are left out (aiming would move through the menu).

The fliperos-padkeys service (pure Python, the kernel's uinput) only translates while /run/fliperos/padkeys exists, which the setup creates when it opens and deletes when it exits: frontends, emulators and the desktop read the controller by themselves, without a button counting twice.

First boot: nothing to choose for what opens at power on: it is the FliperOS frontend (change it later in Setup > Games > Frontend). A short wizard gets the cabinet ready:

  • Wi-Fi: only when the network cable brings no internet and there is a Wi-Fi adapter. It asks again after a failed connection, until you say no (later: Setup > Network Setup).
  • Controls: the Button mapping of Setup > Joysticks, which every emulator and the frontend use. A mapping that already exists is kept.
  • Live screen: the web panel's Live screen is installed and turned on (go2rtc from its GitHub, a pinned version checked by sha256; ffmpeg is already in the image). If it can't download, it says so and the Live screen stays in Setup > Games > Extras > Live screen.
