FliperOS updates (without a new ISO): at every boot with internet, before the launcher, tty1 asks the repository whether there are FliperOS updates (fliperos-update check, waiting for NetworkManager and, with a cable plugged in or a saved Wi-Fi network, up to 30 s for the connection, since Wi-Fi connects after NetworkManager starts; offline or with GitHub out of reach, the boot goes on as always).

Connecting to a Wi-Fi network in Setup > Network Setup runs the same check right after the connection, without waiting for the next boot. With one pending, a screen says what it brings and asks: Apply now or Not now (asked again at the next boot).

Before asking it lists the files changed on this machine that the update replaces (up to six on screen, the rest in View the files): it rehearses the update in an overlay over / and compares each file it would write with what FliperOS itself installed (/var/lib/fliperos/update/manifest, the sha256 of each file, recorded by the ISO and by each update).

Each of those files is copied to /var/lib/fliperos/update/backup/NNNN-date/ before being replaced (fliperos-update restore N puts them back), and the Setup choices (video, latency, buttons) are applied again afterwards. Personal files (fliperos.conf, button maps, ROMs, saves, frontend lists) aren't touched.

Updates are numbered and always applied in order: update N only goes in on a machine at N−1 (/etc/fliperos/patch-level), a list with a gap is refused, and if one fails nothing after it is applied (it is offered again at the next boot; log in /var/log/fliperos-update.log).

Each one is a repository commit listed in updates/index with the sha256 of its files (downloaded over HTTPS from GitHub and checked before anything is written), plus an optional updates/NNNN.sh for what isn't a file copy and its changelog in updates/notes/NNNN.md (required). They are published with tools/make-update.sh "title" [--reboot].

When an update is available, the boot screen first shows what it changes (the changelog of each pending part, with scrolling: fliperos-update notes), then the files of this machine it replaces, and asks; Read what changes in that menu shows the changelog again. After it is applied, the What's new screen lists it with its changelog.

An install older than this system gets it with curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/juniorterin/fliperOS/main/updates/bootstrap.sh | sudo bash.

What's new: after a new version or a new update, the FliperOS menu opens once on a What's new in FliperOS screen, with scrolling (up/down a line, left/right a page): the updates installed since the last time, each with its changelog (/usr/local/share/fliperos/update-notes), and the CHANGELOG sections of the versions since then (an update alone does not repeat the version sections; the first time, only this version's section). Setup > System > What's new shows it again, with every update and every version. The changelog is /usr/local/share/fliperos/CHANGELOG.md (put there by the ISO, by each update and by cabinet-push); the titles come from /var/log/fliperos-update.log, and what was already seen is whatsnew_version and whatsnew_level in fliperos.conf. A new install starts with its own version and update marked as seen. The installation media does not show it.

Colour calibration (Setup > Video Setup) sets the picture's colour: everything the card can do, plus saturation and hue by software when it can't. The fifteen settings are saved in fliperos.conf as color_NAME=:

Setting Range How it is done
Brightness −50 to +50 the card's gamma table (LUT)
Contrast 50 to 150 % LUT
Gamma 0.50 to 2.00 LUT
Colour temperature 4000 to 10000 K (6500 neutral, 9300 the bluish white of many arcade monitors) LUT: red, green and blue gains from the black-body white
Red / green / blue gain (drive) 0 to 150 % LUT
Red / green / blue black level (cutoff) −50 to +50 LUT
Red / green / blue gamma 0.50 to 2.00 LUT
Saturation 0 to 200 % the card's colour matrix (CTM); on cards without one, by software
Hue −180 to +180° CTM, or by software
RGB range card default, full, limited the connector's output_csc (radeon) or Broadcast RGB (Intel), only on cards that have it

Calibrate on the screen opens test patterns in the Video Setup mode, through the same path as the emulators: - colour bars (75 % SMPTE with near-black bars); - 16 grey steps over a continuous ramp; - black level: 1, 2, 4 and 8 % bars, for brightness; - white level: 90, 95 and 98 % boxes on white, for contrast; - red, green, blue and grey ramps; - the 24 ColorChecker patches.

Up and down pick a setting and left and right change it while you look at the tube. Space hides the bar, Enter keeps the settings and Esc goes back to the previous ones. Settings in numbers changes each setting by its number (it also works over SSH), and Back to the defaults clears them all, the RGB range included (it goes back to the card's own default).

A change made with a game open (from the web panel or over SSH) shows in that game at once: - the gamma table goes through the screen owner's own descriptor: fliperos-color, as root, takes a copy of it with pidfd_getfd (a card refuses the table from anyone but the program that owns the screen); - software saturation and hue come from the OpenGL layer, which reads fliperos.conf again when it changes.

config/fliperos-color.c (built with the image and by each update as /usr/local/bin/fliperos-color) applies the settings. Its commands: - fliperos-color caps tells what the card has: the size of the gamma table, whether there is a CTM, which range property; - apply writes the LUT, the CTM and the range through DRM; - x11 writes the LUT to every CRTC in X; - lut N prints the table and the matrix.

Where FliperOS applies them: - at boot, as soon as the splash leaves the screen (fliperos-tty1); - before each program in fliperos-kms-run and fliperos-x11-run (an X server that closes puts back the table it found); - in X, in fliperos-x11-client and fliperos-lxde, because Xorg starts with a linear table; - when the settings are saved.

Without a CTM (the cabinet's Radeon R7 240 has only the 256-point LUT, on radeon and on amdgpu), the Setup writes color_ctm=sw. Then saturation and hue go through the same layers as the flicker filter (libfliperos-deflicker.so in OpenGL, libfliperos-vkfps.so in Vulkan, in every emulator and frontend, and in the Setup's menu), and through picom on the desktop. Only the text console stays without them.

On-screen menu

Hold Start and Down for a second, or press Pause on a keyboard or Play/Pause on a wireless remote, and a menu opens over the game or the frontend. The game keeps running and stops seeing the controls until the menu closes, which also happens after 20 seconds without a press or when the game closes.

  • Volume. The volume keys of a keyboard or of a panel also show a bar for 2 seconds, without taking the controls or opening the menu.
  • 480i filter: off, light, medium or strong for the program on screen. It only shows in an interlaced mode, and the change counts on the next frame.
  • Geometry: horizontal size and position, and vertical position, with a frame and a cross over the picture. Each change is on the tube at once. Save keeps it for every game (the same crt_range as Video Setup > Geometry), and leaving without saving puts the mode back. Switchres stops at what the monitor accepts, and the value on screen goes back to that limit.
  • Colour: every setting of the colour calibration, and back to the defaults.

The arrows move and change, the first button opens and the second goes back, as in the Setup's menus. In fliperos.conf:

  • osd=off turns it off. It is also in the web panel, in Video, and it stays closed in the frontend's commercial mode;
  • osd_combo=start+down is the shortcut, with the controls of the Button mapping;
  • osd_hold=1.0 is how many seconds to hold them;
  • osd_key=119,164,201,207 are the keys, as evdev codes: Pause, and the Play/Pause, Pause and Play of a remote. 0 is no key.

fliperos-osd runs as a service. It reads the shortcut with fliperos-buttons hotkey and writes a 320x240 picture to /run/fliperos-osd/screen, which exists only while the menu is open. The layers of the frame swap draw it before the flicker filter, so its letters don't flicker either: config/fliperos-deflicker.c in OpenGL and config/fliperos-vkfps.c in Vulkan.

So the menu opens only where one of those layers is writing the FPS. On the LXDE desktop, in Fightcade's Wine emulators and in the Setup, nothing opens and the controls stay with the program. If a layer can't draw (a card below OpenGL 3), it tells the service, which gives the controls back.

The controls are taken with EVIOCGRAB only after the shortcut is released, or the game would keep those buttons held.

Settings go through the Setup's functions (--setting, --volume, --geometry), one at a time. Geometry uses Switchres's numbers (switchres -c -g). In a game on X it changes the mode through xrandr, because Xorg undoes a change made directly on the card. In KMS (RetroArch, the frontend) it uses fliperos-color timing.

To drive it without a controller, write open, close, up, down, left, right, enter or esc to /run/fliperos-osd/control as root.

Main menu (gasetup's mainmenu; the title shows host (IP) - N% used on /):

  • Start frontend
  • Setup — the items come in the order of setting up a cabinet, and a balloon under the list says what the item under the cursor is for (FliperOS's gum, patches/gum/0004-choose-balao.patch: framed at 80 columns, two lines of text in place of the key help at 40):

  • Video Setup — the same as in the installation, including Multiple monitors; saves the kernel line and offers to reboot.

    Also 480i hacks: a table of every program (emulators, RetroArch cores, Fightcade, the desktop) where each one gets 640x240, 480i with the flicker filter at its own level (with a preview on the tube), or pure 480i (Emulators).

    Changes in that table are saved as they are made; there is no Save step. Also Colour calibration (below). Also Card firmware, with an AMD card: ATOM-15 in the card's BIOS, at your own risk. Also Video driver, only with an AMD card that works with both drivers (GCN 1.0 and 1.1: HD 7000, R7/R9 200 and 300, like the R7 240).

    The card name comes from lspci, and whether both drivers take it comes from the modules' own PCI ID tables (modprobe -R on the card's modalias). radeon is the recommended choice and the default, as on GroovyArcade: 15 kHz was validated on it; OpenGL only.

    amdgpu adds Vulkan (PCSX2, Dolphin, Flycast, DuckStation); it was seen working at 15 kHz on the cabinet's R7 240 (2026-10-16), not yet on other cards. RetroArch is built with Vulkan as well, but stays on glcore: without X its Vulkan context is khr_display, which does not switch the CRT's mode.

    It goes in with amdgpu.dc=0, because the 6.18 kernel has no analog output (VGA, DVI-I) in amdgpu's new display code for these cards (that came in 6.19). Only the kernel line chooses (amd_driver= in fliperos.conf, AMD_DRIVER_KEYS in lib/bootloader.sh).

    With amdgpu set, the boot menu (a key while the system boots) gets a FliperOS - radeon driver entry, the way back if there is no picture.

    Every switch is on trial, like a resolution change on Windows: the next boot, before the frontend or the menu, asks to confirm the picture with Enter (or button 1) within 15 s, and with no answer it goes back to the driver the card was running and restarts (screen_amd_driver_confirm; state in amd_driver_trial=, amd_driver_previous=).

    The fliperos-driver-trial service covers a confirmation screen that never opens (it goes back after 2 minutes) and a trial boot that hung and was powered off (the next boot goes back at once). An installation with a driver other than the one the media is running makes its first boot a trial too.

    In the installation the item only saves the choice, and when the card has the choice and it was not made in Video Setup, the installation asks it before the disk.

    Once, the first time the main menu opens, the Setup checks the card: if it runs on the driver that is not the recommended one (and nobody chose it in the Setup or the installation), a popup offers the switch (screen_amd_driver_check, amd_driver_checked= in fliperos.conf); - Audio Setup — default card (/etc/asound.conf), volume, AlsaMixer, MAME audio latency (audio_latency in mame.ini, 0.0 to 50.0, 0 = default; GA's "Audio Latency MAME") and a sound test, and the Volume leveler, off by default: on, every system goes through a compressor (SC4 from swh-plugins, a LADSPA plugin in the ALSA default, /etc/asound.conf) that brings loud and quiet systems closer to the same volume, with no lookahead and so no added delay; on an image without swh-plugins the Setup offers to install it.

    As in GA, the volume moves Master/Front/Speaker/Headphone and leaves PCM at maximum (a card with only PCM uses PCM).

    The HDA codec stays always on (options snd_hda_intel power_save=0 power_save_controller=N): with the Ubuntu kernel's 1 s power_save it went silent and turned back on at the next sound, and each on-off popped in the speakers ("puffs" with the menu idle).

    There is no sound server: RetroArch (audio_driver = alsa), GroovyMAME (sound sdl, on the ALSA default through libfliperos-sdl-audio.so; see Emulators) and the SDL emulators (SDL_AUDIODRIVER=alsa) play straight into ALSA, so this volume applies to all of them, in KMS or X. Menu sounds: FliperOS's gum (patches/gum/0002-sons-do-menu.patch) plays a WAV when the cursor moves and another on Enter, like a game's select screen (Street Fighter Alpha 2, for example), in the menus and in the Setup's yes/no questions (aplay; a new sound cuts the one still playing, and the Enter one keeps going after the menu closes).

    The sounds are your own — FliperOS ships no game sounds: move.wav and select.wav in /opt/fliperos/sounds/menu (over the network, the FliperOS share, folder sounds/menu). With one of them there, it turns on by itself; the Audio Setup item turns it off and on (menu_sounds in fliperos.conf); - Network Setup — Wi-Fi from the list of networks (with signal) or a hidden network by typing the SSID; once connected, the IP shows in the title, next to the disk usage; - Joysticks — each player's buttons and where the buttons of 1 to 5-button games go on the panel, light gun and wheel calibration, joysticks on the parallel port. For a keyboard encoder (I-PAC and the like), Button mapping writes MAME's default keys instead. See Controls; - Games — what puts games in the cabinet, in the order of use: - Frontend — the default boot launcher; what isn't in the image is installed (or downloaded) from here. See Frontends.

    A game, straight from the boot opens a single game instead of a game list: pick the system among the folders with games, then the file; the command is the one the frontends use for that folder, saved in /etc/fliperos/bootgame and run by fliperos-bootgame.

    Leaving the game (Esc) opens the FliperOS menu, whose first item becomes Start and the game's name. Choosing a game moves every service that starts at boot to After boot (below) and turns Wait for network off, so the game reaches the screen sooner.

    Before the game the boot also skips what only serves the frontends or needs the network: the FliperOS update check (it runs when the game closes, on the way to the menu, without waiting for a network that isn't up), the creation of missing ~/roms folders and the frontends' preparation (game lists, art, 240p settings); - Emulators & Games — the emulators of the desktop menu, each marked installed or not, and the installation of the ones that don't come in the image: Model 2 (built on the machine), Fightcade 2, DuckStation and KOF Final Attack on Ikemen GO (downloaded from itch.io and patched by itself, or from a folder you bring).

    An installed one has Update, which downloads the newest version over it (Model 2: the newest source, built again; KOF Final Attack: the newest patch and Ikemen GO, converting the original game again); the ones that come in the image are updated with FliperOS. See Emulators; - Extras — installs over the network Wine (the Fightcade 2 emulators), Steam and Heroic (GOG), which are left out of the ISO so it fits in a single GitHub file. See Emulators.

    Also the Pixelcade LED/LCD marquee software, which is closed source, the ZeDMD open-source LED display and DOFLinx, the effects on the Pixelcade marquee during a game (Frontends).

    And the two programs that take the games' outputs (lamps, recoil, button lights) to hardware: Hook Of The Reaper, for light guns and controller boards (a Windows program, run through Wine), QMamehook, for serial light guns (native, built on the cabinet), and LEDSpicer, for LED boards (DIY hardware).

    Live screen brings ffmpeg and go2rtc for the cabinet screen live in the web panel and in OBS (see Web panel). Choosing an extra that is already installed offers to download it again, which updates it; - Custom games — games and programs that are not a ROM (a PC game, your own emulator, a script), in groups the frontends show as systems: a group, a name, the command and the video mode (240p, 480i or WIDTHxHEIGHT@HZ). See Adding games; - Folders — a custom folder for ~/roms, ~/bios, ~/media, ~/nvram, ~/save, ~/splashscreen or any folder inside them (an emulator, a RetroArch core, a type of art): another folder (an external disk) used in its place. See ROMs, BIOS and artwork; - Downloader — ROM/CHD MAME torrent (from a romset magnet link and a CHD one, only what the ROM Cleaner filter chooses, through Transmission), Free games (open-source homebrew) and Download BIOS (the BIOS the games in your folders lack, checked each time the menu opens). See ROMs, BIOS and artwork; - Cleaner — MAME ROM Cleaner and MAME CHD Cleaner: filter a MAME romset (for GroovyMAME, Flycast, SM2-Emu, Supermodel or MAME 2010 — the MAME 3D, for the PlayStation-based arcade games) into the emulator's folder and bring the CHDs of the games that stayed. See ROMs, BIOS and artwork; - Scraper — covers, screenshots, logos, videos and information for each ROM. See Scraper; - AttractPlus ROM List — Attract-Mode Plus game lists of the arcade folders with each game's real name, from GroovyMAME's list, clones and bootlegs included. See Adding games; - System — the rest: - Latency — Standard mode (any machine) or Low latency (modern CPUs), with a check of this machine against the recommendation and the list of ideal hardware (Latency); - Services — a table with one mark per service: Boot (starts with the computer), After boot (about 15 s after the first screen of the boot opens, the menu, the frontend or the game, so it has loaded first: fliperos-tty1 starts fliperos-services-screen.timer; if nothing opens on the screen, fliperos-services-late.timer starts them 3 min after the boot) or Off.

    The services are SSH, the network share (Samba, After boot by default: nmbd alone took about 13 s at boot), fliperos.local (Avahi), the Wi-Fi radio (only the radio: NetworkManager stays, it runs the network cable), Wait for network (NetworkManager-wait-online: off, the boot goes on without waiting for the network) and the web panel (After boot by default).

    The Downloader's Transmission is not in the table: it starts only when a download is asked for (see Downloader). What Ubuntu starts at boot and a cabinet doesn't use is masked in the image: Samba as a domain controller, gpu-manager, Ubuntu Pro and the MOTD news.

    The choice is kept in /etc/fliperos/services.conf; the Pixelcade and the ZeDMD are not in it, udev starts them when the device shows up; - Quirks — kernel fixes for USB devices that arrive wrong: controllers, guns, keyboards and disks. See Controls; - Password — the password of the fliperos user: the login, sudo, SSH and the network share (Samba keeps a password of its own, and both change together); - System Update — apt-get update and upgrade, with apt's real progress; - What's new — the updates installed on this machine (newest first) and the changelog of every FliperOS version, with scrolling (see What's new); - Debug mode — off (the default), the boot goes straight to Plymouth and the output of frontends and emulators (X, Switchres, the program itself) goes to /opt/fliperos/logs/<program>.log, rewritten on each launch: only the picture is on screen.

    On, everything shows: the Limine menu (FLIPEROS_QUIET="no" in /etc/default/fliperos-boot), the kernel and systemd messages at boot (without quiet splash or the silencing parameters) and the programs' output on the console. Programs follow immediately; the boot, after a reboot; - Lab mode — a temporary internet address to the web panel, with a root terminal, for someone helping you from far away. It ends after 4 hours, at power off, or here. See Web panel; - Splash screen — the boot screen (Plymouth).

    The themes are the folders in ~/splashscreen (\\fliperos\splashscreen over the network); picking one shows a preview on screen for 10 seconds (from the FliperOS menu, not from the desktop) or sets it for the boot: it is copied to /usr/share/plymouth/themes, becomes the default and the initramfs is rebuilt (about a minute).

    The default is fliperos-text, animated like a modern terminal (the name typing itself in, a gradient progress bar and the services starting); fliperos is in the style of the 2000s boot screens; Cogwheel, Into It and Windoze 95 also come installed.

    More themes: Plymouth Themes on Gnome-look — unpack each one into its own folder in ~/splashscreen; - Start desktop — LXDE. Logout (the menu item, the panel button and the end of the lxsession session) opens a full-screen terminal with the gum menu, in the Setup's look: back to the FliperOS menu, reboot, power off or cancel (config/fliperos-logout; the icon window of lxsession-logout was unreadable on a low-resolution screen); - Exit to shell — fliperos-menu returns to the menu. Typed in an SSH session, fliperos-menu opens the text menu (gum) there, never the graphical one on the cabinet's monitor; frontends, games and the desktop are only started from the cabinet; - Shutdown / Reboot.

The power button. A short press of the cabinet's power button (the motherboard's, or a panel key programmed to send KEY_POWER) depends on what is on screen:

On screen The button
A game opened from a frontend (Attract-Mode Plus, ES-DE, Pegasus, your own frontends) closes the game; the frontend comes back
A Fightcade match closes the match's emulator; the lobby comes back
An emulator opened from the desktop's Games menu closes the emulator; the desktop comes back
A frontend's game list, the Fightcade lobby, the desktop, the FliperOS menu, the shell, the install media powers the machine off
RetroArch or GroovyMAME as the default launcher powers the machine off (they are the launcher, there is no frontend to go back to)

From inside a game it therefore takes two presses to power off. For 3 seconds after a press the next ones don't count, so a second press given too early (or a board that reports one press through two devices) can't close the game and power off at once.

The game gets a SIGTERM, the same as closing it normally, so RetroArch still writes its saves; a game that stays open is killed (SIGKILL) by the next press. Holding the button for 4 seconds still cuts the power: that is the motherboard, not FliperOS.

How it works: systemd-logind ignores the button (HandlePowerKey=ignore in /etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/fliperos.conf; by default it would power off at every press), and triggerhappy, which already reads the volume keys, runs config/fliperos-powerkey on KEY_POWER (config/fliperos-power.triggers).

The script finds the open game through the FLIPEROS_POWERKEY variable that fliperos-session gives what it opens: frontend (the game is whatever runs below it), game (an emulator opened from the desktop) or games:FILE (the game is the PIDs listed in FILE and what runs below them). Fightcade, whose emulators are not its children, and the FliperOS frontend, whose other children (the video player, the scraper) are not games, use FILE. hold in it means the button does nothing while that game is open (the FliperOS frontend's Power closes game option, off).

Shutting down. No service holds the reboot or the power off for long: every system and user service that doesn't stop on SIGTERM gets SIGKILL after 10 seconds (DefaultTimeoutStopSec=10s in /etc/systemd/system.conf.d and user.conf.d, config/fliperos-stop-timeout.conf), instead of systemd's 90. The session on tty1 has the same 10 seconds. Only applying a pending update at power off gets more (20 minutes, in its own unit).

Volume keys: the keyboard's volume keys (or those of a panel encoder programmed to send them) work on any screen — emulator in KMS, desktop, console.

triggerhappy reads /dev/input and calls fliperos-setup --volume up|down|mute (5% steps on the Audio Setup card, saved on every press because cabinets are usually switched off at the wall); config/fliperos-volume.triggers says which keys. The LXDE panel only handles the mouse, so the volume doesn't change twice. No volume bar appears during a game (nothing draws on top of an emulator in KMS).

Web panel

The cabinet in a browser on the same network, a phone too: http://fliperos.local. Games to play, the screen live and in OBS, settings while you play, files, the ROM filter, downloads, the system status and a terminal. It has its own page: Web panel.

SSH and AI assistants: SSH is on from the first boot, and SFTP too. From another computer on the same network:

Field Value
Address (host) fliperos.local, or the cabinet's IP (shown in the FliperOS menu title)
User (login, username) fliperos
Password fliperos until you change it in Setup > System > Password
Port 22

The user and the password are the same word by default, but they are two separate things.

In the command ssh fliperos@fliperos.local, the fliperos before the @ is the user and fliperos.local after it is the address; the password is not in the command, you type it when SSH asks (fliperos@fliperos.local's password:), and nothing appears on screen while you type.

In an SFTP program (FileZilla, WinSCP) the same four fields are Host, Username, Password and Port. sudo asks for the same password, and the network share (\\fliperos\roms) takes the same user and password. After a password change only the password is different: the user is still fliperos.

Under the menus it's a regular Ubuntu 24.04, so whatever the Setup doesn't cover can be done from a terminal, and an AI assistant with shell access (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and the like) can do it for you: give it the cabinet's address and say what you want (button mapping, an emulator's settings, a frontend theme, a service) and it configures the system over SSH.

The configuration is in plain text files (/etc/fliperos/fliperos.conf, ~/config, /opt/fliperos), easy for a person or an assistant to read and change.

On a network you don't control, change the default password in Setup > System > Password (it changes the network share's too), and turn off what you don't use in Setup > System > Services.

Web panel

The cabinet from your phone or PC. Open http://fliperos.local in a browser on the same network (or the cabinet's IP) and sign in with the fliperos user. There is nothing to install on the phone or the computer.

What you can do from the couch:

  • Pick a game and play it on the tube, with the pictures, the history and the buttons of each arcade game from the Arcade Database, your favourites and the game filters.
  • See what is playing, with the FPS, and take a screenshot of the tube.
  • Watch the cabinet live in the browser, and put the live screen and the game's marquee in OBS.
  • Change settings while you play: colour, 480i hacks, services, latency mode, volume.
  • Copy games, BIOS and artwork through the browser: upload, download, new folders.
  • Filter a MAME romset and download only the games that suit your cabinet, plus the BIOS your games lack.
  • Scrape the art of your games, typing the site's login on a real keyboard, and download the art packs.
  • Install or update emulators and extras that don't come in the image.
  • Check the system: the video mode with its modeline, CPU, GPU, temperatures, network and logs.
  • Open a terminal on the cabinet, without an SSH program.

Page by page

The cabinet's state in a browser on the same network (a phone too): http://fliperos.local, or the cabinet's IP. Port 80 only forwards to the panel's own port, 8081, so http://fliperos.local:8081 works too.

You sign in with the same user and password as SSH and the network share (fliperos, changed in Setup > System > Password). Until 2026-10-22 the panel was on port 8080, which Pixelcade's own settings page also uses; with both installed one of them didn't open.

The panel has ten pages, tabs at the top, each with its own address (#frontend, #live, #romfilter, #downloads, #scraper, #install, #files, #settings, #status, #terminal); the browser remembers the last one: - Frontend: now playing with the FPS, the marquee preview beside it, games, volume and screen; - Live: the cabinet screen live, the streaming controls (service, encoder, sound) and the addresses for OBS (the live screen and the marquee). Leaving the page stops the stream, so ffmpeg on the cabinet stops too; - ROM filter: the MAME ROM Cleaner filter, for the Downloader or for a romset folder; - Downloads: the Downloader, Download BIOS and the tasks; - Scraper: the art of the games, from the FliperOS scraper or a site, and the art packs by torrent; - Install: the emulators and the extras, installed or updated; - Files: files and tasks; - Settings: colour values are sliders; - Status: now playing and the screen at the top, then video, CPU, GPU, memory, storage, network, processes and logs; - Terminal.

The status refreshes every second. What each part shows: - Now playing: the game open (emulator, file, RetroArch core) and the frontend, with the FPS and a graph of the last minute. The FPS comes from the OpenGL layer of the flicker filter, which counts the frames of whatever game is open, and for games in Vulkan (Flycast, PCSX2, Dolphin, DuckStation on amdgpu) from a small implicit Vulkan layer (config/fliperos-vkfps.c, on with FLIPEROS_VK_FPS=1) that counts their frames the same way. The minute of history stays in the browser.

The browser never keeps the panel: its pages, code, icons and fonts are sent with Cache-Control: no-store, so every visit gets the version on the cabinet, right after an update. The games' pictures and videos are checked each time (no-cache with an ETag), so new art from a scrape shows at once. - Video: what Video Setup asks (monitor, frequency, resolution, connector, orientation) next to what is on screen now: the mode, the horizontal kHz and vertical Hz, interlaced or progressive, and the full modeline of each active output, read from DRM by fliperos-video-check. - CPU: the total, each core and the load, plus the temperatures of the sensors. - GPU: the name and the driver, plus whatever the card reports: use, VRAM, clock, temperature, power. - Memory, disks and network: the speed of each interface, its IPs and the Wi-Fi signal. - Volume, which can also be changed from here (fliperos-setup --volume up|down|mute|get|set N). - Processes: the ones using the most CPU. - Logs: those of /opt/fliperos/logs, the Setup's and the updates'. - Games: the folders with games, the same ones the frontends show (fliperos-setup --systems). - The list is Attract-Mode Plus's (~/.attract/romlists/EMULATOR.txt), so arcade games show their real names, year and manufacturer from AttractPlus ROM List. Clones without their own file in a merged MAME set are listed too, since MAME opens them by name.

Files the list doesn't know (copied after it was made, or a folder without a list) show by file name. An arcade list made by AttractPlus ROM List leaves out the BIOS files.
  • At the end of the search box is the filter: FliperOS's own game filters (All Games, Most Played, the genres, manufacturers and years), the same set the Setup writes into each Attract-Mode display (fliperos-setup --filters), plus Favourites.

  • Next to it, the Clones button. Off (the default), the list shows only the original games: a clone is hidden when its original game is in the list (a clone left without its original stays, and so do favourites and the most played). On, every version shows. The choice is remembered in the browser.

    They are applied the way Attract-Mode applies them: the rules in order, exceptions, the regular expressions, sorting and the limit. The panel copies these filters; it doesn't read the frontend's displays, so a later frontend of FliperOS's own can use the same ones. - Each game opens like an accordion, one at a time. It shows what the list knows (file, year, manufacturer, genre, players, buttons, control, screen, emulation status, parent, how many times and how long it was played) and what the internet knows: - arcade games: the Arcade Database by the set name.

    That adds the full title, series, rating, the player 1 buttons drawn on the panel where Setup > Joysticks > Buttons layout puts them (colour and function, no joystick directions), the game's description and then each section of the arcade-history.com text (Technical, Trivia...), the in-game, title, marquee, flyer and cabinet pictures, and links to the video and the game's page.

    The browser can't ask the Arcade Database directly (it sends no CORS header), so the panel asks for it.

    The answer is saved on the cabinet, next to the other media: ~/media/info/<games folder>/<set>.<language>.json (~/media/info/mame/samsho.en.json). A game fetched once is never fetched again and opens without internet, and FliperOS's own frontend will read the same file. The page says when it was saved. A game the Arcade Database doesn't know is asked again after 30 days; - consoles: the box, screen and title pictures of libretro-thumbnails, by the file name (No-Intro), the way RetroArch looks for them. - The browser keeps each game's answer for 30 days (localStorage), so opening it again is instant and works offline. When the storage is full, the older half goes. - At the end are Play and Favourite. Play closes what is on the cabinet screen and opens the game; when the game closes, what was there comes back (the frontend, the desktop or the menu). Favourite keeps FliperOS's own favourites, in ~/.config/fliperos/favourites (one folder<TAB>name line per game).

    The first time the panel lists games, it copies Attract-Mode's favourites into that file (romlists/EMULATOR.tag). After that it never writes to the frontend's file, and changes made in the frontend no longer come in. - Close the game, in Now playing, closes the open game (SIGTERM, like the power button, so RetroArch still writes its saves). - Naomi, Naomi 2 and Atomiswave may all point to one folder with the whole Flycast romset. AttractPlus ROM List then keeps only each system's games in its list, by the BIOS in each set's romof chain (awbios is Atomiswave, naomi2 is Naomi 2, naomi and the GD-ROM BIOS are Naomi). Lists made before this split are redone the next time the frontend opens.

How it works: the panel writes the request to $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fliperos-web-launch (the first line is what comes back afterwards, the rest is the command), then closes the game, the frontend, the desktop or the Setup menu. fliperos-tty1 opens the request before the menu and after each session.

A newer request comes first, so switching from one game to another works. fliperos-session does not start the desktop's X again while a request is waiting. With only the desktop on screen, it takes the same path as the desktop's Games menu (fliperos-next).

Only commands that start with fliperos-kms-run or fliperos-x11-run are opened, and only files of that folder. - Screen: a screenshot of what is on the cabinet screen, shown in 4:3 as on the tube or at the frame's own size (a 2560x240 frame of RetroArch's super resolution is very wide), with Save PNG. Games, frontends and the Setup's graphical menu go through the OpenGL layer of the flicker filter.

When the panel asks ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fliperos-shot-request), the layer reads the next finished frame, before the filter, into fliperos-shot.ppm, and the panel turns it into a PNG. The LXDE desktop draws without OpenGL, so it is read from X (XGetImage). The text console and programs without OpenGL have no screenshot. - Live screen: what is on the tube, live, in the browser. It covers the game, the frontend, the menu, the desktop and the text console, with sound when Live screen sound is on. Pick 15, 30 or 60 frames per second. The card shows the size, the frame rate and the delay in the browser's buffer, and has Sound (it starts muted, as browsers ask) and Full screen. - It is installed and turned on by the first boot of the installed system. When that couldn't download it (no internet), install it in Setup > Games > Extras > Live screen (or with Install on the card): ffmpeg from apt and go2rtc (MIT, a pinned version checked by sha256). Then it is a service in Setup > System > Services (Live screen, after boot by default). - How it works: go2rtc (fliperos-stream.service) opens ffmpeg only while someone watches. ffmpeg reads the screen from DRM (kmsgrab) and encodes H.264. - Video: On AMD cards (radeon and amdgpu) the driver does not let the screen's buffer be mapped into memory, so the frame goes through VA-API's video processing, which copies and scales it on the card; the R7 240 has that part even without an encoder.

  Cards that allow the mapping read it directly (`hwdownload`). ffmpeg runs with `libfliperos-dropmaster.so` (`LD_PRELOAD`, `config/fliperos-dropmaster.c`): opening `/dev/dri/cardN` at a moment when nobody owns the screen made it the DRM master.

  Then X and the Setup's graphical menu could no longer open the video: the cabinet stayed on the text menu and the desktop failed with "exit code 1" (seen on 2026-10-22). The library gives the screen back right after the open. kmsgrab doesn't need it: as root it reads the buffers with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`.

  Without the library the capture doesn't start. Encoding runs on the graphics card (VA-API) when it has an encoder; otherwise in software with x264, ultrafast, no B-frames, a keyframe every second. The R7 240 has no encoder: its Oland chip has no VCE. On the cabinet (an i7 870) x264 keeps 60 frames per second.
- **Mode changes:** kmsgrab stops when the framebuffer changes size ("framebuffer dimensions changed"), which happens every time a game opens or closes on a 15 kHz screen. go2rtc doesn't restart the capture for someone already watching, so the viewer kept the frontend's last frame (seen on 2026-10-23).

  So the capture is two processes. The grabber (`fliperos-stream grab`) runs kmsgrab in a loop, reopening it at the new size, and always outputs raw 640x480 RGB. The encoder reads that pipe with wall-clock timestamps and never stops, so a mode change costs about a second of frozen picture with the sound still in sync.
- **Size:** never larger than 640x480. The frame is copied in RGB and scaled with nearest-neighbour to 640x480 (4:3) before it is encoded: 640x240 doubles each line, 480i stays as it is, and RetroArch's 2560x240 drops to a quarter across.

  The panel and the OBS page draw each frame on a 640x480 canvas, which the browser enlarges without smoothing (`image-rendering: pixelated`). Chrome and OBS always smooth a `<video>` when they enlarge it, and ignore that property on it.
- **Bitrate and network:** 1.5 Mbit/s at 15 fps, 2 at 30 and 3 at 60, with half a second of buffer, so a keyframe is as sharp as the other frames. WebRTC goes over TCP only (`listen: ":8555/tcp"`).

  Over UDP, the cabinet's USB Wi-Fi lost packets, and go2rtc cannot ask ffmpeg for a new keyframe, so each loss froze the picture until the next keyframe. Measured on 2026-10-23: at 8 Mbit/s over UDP, 321 lost packets and 8.6 s frozen in 20 s.

  Over TCP at 640x480, Chrome on a wired PC got 60 fps for 60 s with no loss and no freeze, with the cabinet on Wi-Fi. A two-frame buffer also hid the loss, but made each keyframe blurry.

  The Live page shows the cabinet's network (the interface of the default route) and recommends a network cable instead of Wi-Fi, highlighted when the cabinet is on Wi-Fi.
  • The browser sends its WebRTC offer to the panel (/api/stream/offer), so the panel login applies. The panel passes it to go2rtc, whose API and RTSP only listen on the cabinet itself (127.0.0.1). The video then goes straight to the browser on the local network, on port 8555 (TCP and UDP), with no STUN server outside.
  • In OBS: the card also has an address for a Browser Source (/overlay/live?key=…&fps=…, the same key as the marquee page). It shows the screen in 4:3, as on the tube, plays the sound (tick Control audio via OBS) and reconnects by itself. &fit=fill stretches it to any size; &muted=1 drops the sound.

  • Delay for OBS: while the stream plays on the page, a tip balloon under the OBS steps shows how many milliseconds to delay the camera (its source: Filters > Render Delay) and the microphone (Advanced Audio Properties > Sync Offset) so that they line up with the game.

    The figure is measured from the browser's last second of WebRTC stats: buffer and decode time, half the round trip, and the cabinet side (about two frames of capture and encoding; for the sound, the loopback period and the Opus frame).

    Chrome delays the picture to match the sound, so both settle on about the same value, roughly 300 ms on the cabinet over Wi-Fi. The stream starts with sound on; if the browser refuses, it starts muted and the button shows it. - Live screen sound (Settings and the Setup, off by default) is experimental, and on the cabinet it doesn't work yet: the live screen goes without sound. The idea is a copy of everything that plays on an ALSA loopback. - snd-aloop loads as the card FliperOSLoop, on the kernel's default timer. - asound.conf gets fliperos_tee, a route over a multi that feeds a dmix on the card and one on the loopback, both with the same format and timing. The volume leveler goes in front when it is on. - ffmpeg records the loopback's capture side in Opus. - Turning it on tests the default with a tenth of a second of silence. If it doesn't play, the setting goes back off by itself, and the game sound stays as it was. On the cabinet's HDA card it doesn't play while another program holds the card through the system's dmix. - The copy only goes into asound.conf with the loopback really there. Each session start also checks this: without the loopback the default would not open and everything would be silent. - Marquee for OBS: with Turn on the marquee page (or Marquee overlay for OBS in Settings), the marquee of the game on screen becomes a page for an OBS Browser Source, /overlay/marquee?key=…. It needs no Pixelcade or ZeDMD. - The card links to Scoreboard games in this documentation: the games with the versus scoreboard and which emulator has each (GroovyMAME, RetroArch with FBNeo, SM2-Emu for Model 2). - The page has a transparent background. It shows the game's art, the same as the ZeDMD uses: ~/media/dmd, marquee or logo (Pixelcade's art may only be used on its own hardware). Without art it shows the name.

    The opening text (the high scores, or "Now Playing") scrolls once, achievements pop up and the versus score shows each side's name and wins. &led=1 draws it as LED dots and &text=0 leaves out the texts. In OBS: width 1280, height 320.

    When the frontend is idle (30 seconds without a button press in the FliperOS frontend, or the screensaver of ES-DE and Attract-Mode Plus), the page plays the ZeDMD's logo animation (/api/overlay/idle, the 128x32 GIF). The Marquee preview below plays it too, with Pixelcade or ZeDMD picked (both play it). In the FliperOS menu, both play the animation of the item under the cursor. With no game and no system, the preview shows the animated FliperOS logo (a palm tree and a synthwave sun) instead of the name in text. The first press brings back the system. - Marquee preview mode: in Frontend, the Marquee preview card (to the right of Now playing, under it on narrow screens) has a switch and a list with Pixelcade or ZeDMD. With it on, the panel draws an LED marquee (128x32 dots, for the Pixelcade and the ZeDMD) with what that device would show for the game that is open, with no hardware: in the card, under the screen in Live, in place of the preview of the page in Live > OBS > Marquee, and in the marquee of the cabinet drawing in Frontend. Turning the mode on or changing the device checks if that device is installed on the cabinet (the same Pixelcade and ZeDMD extras of Library > Install): if not, a dialog offers to install it (a task, as in Install) and the card says whether it is installed. The preview works without it; the real display needs it. The ZeDMD looks for ~/media/dmd, then marquee, then logo; the Pixelcade for marquee, then logo; without art, the game's name. The preview also shows the scoreboard, like the OBS page: the versus score in place of the art (the preview shows it from the start of the game, even at 0 x 0, reading the detector of GroovyMAME; the LED waits for the first win), the opening text (the high scores) scrolling once and the achievements. That needs the marquee state, which fliperos-pixelcade only writes with Marquee overlay for OBS on, so turning the preview on turns it on too. Turning it on also downloads the Fightcade score detectors in the background (they used to come only with the Pixelcade or ZeDMD install, so without that hardware no game had a score). The score only works for a game opened after that: GroovyMAME turns the score plugin on when the game starts. The preview also shows the game's high scores: a HI 19,130 DAA tag on the LED panel (with Scoreboard picked) and the first three in the card. They come from the .hi file that the hiscore plugin of GroovyMAME keeps in ~/.mame/hiscore/ (it rewrites it when the table changes), read by hi2txt (the one of the Pixelcade/ZeDMD, in ~/pixelcade/hi2txt, with Java). The table address of each game is in MAME's hiscore.dat (about 5,800 sets) and hi2txt has a description for about 3,000 names: 2,444 sets have both (Pac-Man, Galaga, Donkey Kong, 1942, TMNT, Gradius...). Fighting games like sf2ce or sfa3 have no hi2txt description, so they show no high scores. When both exist, the marquee shows (Art or Scoreboard, in that same card) picks what the preview draws when a game has both: with Art the score, the scrolling text and the achievements stay out. Only games with a score detector have one (see Scoreboard games); the others just show the art. The choice of device and of art or score stays in the browser. - How it works: fliperos-pixelcade, which already gets every event (kms-run, x11-run, GroovyMAME, the Attract-Mode Plus plugin and the ES-DE scripts, installed when the page is turned on), writes the current marquee to $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fliperos-marquee. The page asks the panel for it every second; the art comes from fliperos-dmd art. - The OBS pages can't sign in, so their address carries a key, created on first use in /etc/fliperos/overlay.key (root only). New address makes another key and the old address stops working, the live screen's and the controller's included. The key only opens the marquee state, the current game's picture, the live screen and the controller. - Controller for OBS: the player's controller on the stream, /overlay/input?key=…. Its own page, with the OBS steps and CSS examples: Controller on the stream. The stick and the six buttons (1 2 3 on top, 4 5 6 below), Start and Coin light up while they are pressed on the cabinet. - It reads the controls of Setup > Joysticks > Button mapping (/etc/fliperos/buttons.map): the joysticks through SDL and a keyboard encoder's keys straight from the input devices, without taking them from the game. With no mapping, it uses MAME's default keys for players 1 and 2. - &players=2 or &players=1,2 picks the players. In OBS: width 800, height 400 for one player, 1600 × 400 for two. The background is transparent. - The card has a CSS editor with syntax colours. The preview follows each key you type, and Demo in the preview presses the buttons by itself, so the look can be tried with nobody at the cabinet. Format lays the CSS out with one property per line (Ctrl+Z undoes it). Save writes it to /etc/fliperos/input-overlay.css, and the pages open in OBS take it at once, with no need to refresh the source; Factory CSS goes back to input.css. - The classes: .pad (.p1, .p2, .active while something is pressed), .label, .stick (.up .down .left .right, and data-dir such as up-left) with .gate and .ball, and .button (.b1 to .b6, .start, .coin; .on while pressed). The sizes use --u: one panel is 200 × 100 --u. - How it works: while at least one controller page is open, the panel runs one fliperos-buttons watch at low priority. It sends the panel a line each time the pressed controls change, and the panel passes it to the pages as Server-Sent Events. It stops when the last page closes. - Settings: the Setup settings that are safe to change over the network, grouped as System, Services, 480i hacks and Colour. - System: the default launcher, latency mode, debug mode, the volume leveler and menu sounds. - Services: the whole services table. - 480i hacks: a card per program, with an explanation of each method at the top. The method is a row of buttons (640x240, 480i with filter, 480i pure), and the filter strength (light, medium, strong) shows only when the filter is on. - Colour: every colour calibration value and Back to the defaults. A slider saves while it moves, so the game on screen changes with it; the − and + on its sides move it one step per tap (a run of taps saves once, just after the last). - Each change is saved and applied at once, through the same functions as the Setup screens (fliperos-setup --settings and --setting KEY VALUE, lib/system.sh). Debug and latency rewrite the kernel line the way their screens do; their kernel part counts after a restart. - Monitor, resolution and video driver are not here, since a wrong choice can leave the cabinet without a picture. They stay in the Setup, on the cabinet screen. - Lab mode (on the Settings page, and in Setup > System > Lab mode): a temporary internet address to this panel, so someone far away can help you (a FliperOS developer looking at a problem). - Turn on lab mode gives an address like https://some-random-words.trycloudflare.com/lab?key=…. Copy puts it on the clipboard, to send by chat or email. In the Setup it shows on the screen. - Whoever opens it gets into the panel without your password: status, logs, files, screenshots, and a root terminal (su - fliperos there gives the normal user). Send it only to someone you trust. - It ends by itself after 4 hours, when the cabinet powers off, or with Turn off. Then the address and every session opened with it stop working. A new start gives a new address. - Nothing changes on your router. The cabinet opens the connection to Cloudflare, through a Quick Tunnel of cloudflared (no account). It is downloaded the first time, about 40 MB, with a fixed version and checksum, to /opt/fliperos/cloudflared. - If the web panel is off in Services, lab mode starts it until the next boot. - The live screen doesn't work through the address. Its video goes straight to the browser on the local network. - How it works: fliperos-lab start writes a random key to /run/fliperos-lab and starts fliperos-lab.service, which runs cloudflared as a temporary user with RuntimeMaxSec=4h. The address comes from cloudflared's /quicktunnel metrics. The panel's /lab?key= compares the key; wrong keys have their own limit of 5 a minute. - Downloads: the Setup's Downloader (Setup > Games > Downloader), which takes from the MAME ROM and CHD torrents only what the MAME ROM Cleaner filter picks. - The panel shows the progress and the filter that is chosen. - It adds a torrent's link (the one that comes with FliperOS, or one you paste), applies the filter and starts, and removes a torrent (optionally with what it already downloaded). - The filter itself is chosen on the ROM filter page or in the Setup. Starting from the panel deletes nothing; deleting what a changed filter leaves out stays a Setup step. - It goes through the Setup's own functions (fliperos-setup --downloader status|add|start|remove, lib/downloader.sh). - Download BIOS (on the Downloads page): the same as Setup > Games > Downloader > Download BIOS. - It shows the last check (downloaded, already there, not in the pack, failed) and the list by state. The BIOS that failed or are not in the pack open first, since they ask for something from you. - Check now runs the check as a task. Check, reading the pack again reads the BIOS pack's list again first. The box turns the automatic check off or on; that check runs each time the cabinet menu opens. - It goes through fliperos-setup --bios status|list|check [--refresh]|auto on|off (lib/downloader.sh). - Scraper: the same as Setup > Games > Scraper. - The page says what each kind of folder gets, since arcade has much more art. The folders come in two groups, Arcade (MAME sets) and Consoles. - Pick the folders (none picked means all). Scrape the games is the FliperOS scraper: what each game lacks, like the frontend does by itself, with no account. An arcade folder gets the description, screenshot, flyer, marquee and logo from the Arcade Database. A console folder gets only the screenshot and the box art from libretro-thumbnails; logos, videos and descriptions of console games come from a site (ScreenScraper covers every system). - Scrape with a site is Skyscraper. Each provider shows what it covers: every system (ScreenScraper, MobyGames), arcade only (ArcadeDB; progetto-SNAPS, only screenshots) or consoles and computers (TheGamesDB, IGDB, OpenRetro). Pick the provider, type its account (user and password, the API key, or the client ID and secret), mark what to fetch and, with a MAME folder, the clones. The account is easier to type here than with the joystick.

    The account goes to the Setup through standard input, never on a command line or in a log, and the saved password never comes back to the page. A scrape that stopped before the end (a power off) can be resumed here or in the Setup. - Art packs by torrent puts every pack with ROMs to download, as in the Setup, and shows its progress. The packs are arcade only: logos and videos of MAME, RetroArch's arcade cores, Naomi, Atomiswave, Model 2 and Model 3. - It goes through fliperos-setup --scraper status|sources|systems|source|account|media|scrape|site|resume (lib/scraper.sh) and --mediapacks auto|status. - Install: Setup > Games > Emulators & Games and Extras. - Each emulator shows whether it is installed and its version. Check for an update asks GitHub for the newest one. Those that come in the image update with FliperOS, so they have no button. - Install or Update runs as a task. Only one installation runs at a time, the live screen's included. - KOF Final Attack is downloaded from itch.io; installing it from a copy of the original game stays a Setup step. An installed Pixelcade also takes the code of the paid art pack. - It runs fliperos-emulators, fliperos-extras and fliperos-pixelcade, the same programs as the Setup. - ROM filter: the filter of the MAME ROM Cleaner (Setup > Games > Cleaner), with the same parameters, options and presets as the Setup's screen, which come from the Setup itself (fliperos-setup --romfilter, lib/romclean.sh). - It has two uses. Downloader filter: what the Downloader takes from the ROM and CHD torrents; it opens with the saved filter, and Save records it as Setup > Games > Downloader > Filter does. Clean a romset folder: a folder with a romset (a disk, a USB drive, the network folder mounted by the Setup), chosen in a folder list. - Pick the emulator (the MAME version of the romset: GroovyMAME, Flycast, SM2-Emu, Supermodel, MAME 2010) and a preset. The emulator of a romset folder is guessed from its name, as in the Setup. - The parameters are a board of tiles in groups (which games, players and controls, screen, categories and years, hardware), like the Setup's graphical filter board. Each tile shows its value with a small drawing: players and buttons lit up to the limit, the emulation lamps, a switch, the marked blocks.

    A pink dot marks a value changed from the preset or the saved filter. A yes/no tile switches with a click; the others open their options in a dialog, one choice or chips for several, with a search box on long lists such as the categories. - The scoreboard (GAMES and SIZE) stays in view while scrolling and counts what passes after every change: on the ROM torrent's list for the Downloader, on the folder for a romset. Only the latest count is kept; a new one stops the one before it. - For a folder, Preview shows what goes where (sets, size, parents, BIOS and devices, free space) and the list. Copy them, or Move them from a folder that can be written to, runs as a task with its progress. Deleting what is left over after a move stays a Setup step. - Tasks: what takes minutes (reading a torrent's link, applying the filter, scraping, checking the BIOS, installing) runs in the background. The card is on the Downloads, Scraper, Install and Files pages, and when a task ends, its card refreshes by itself. - Each task shows the step and the percentage from the Setup's progress events, and has a log and Cancel. - Only one task of each kind runs at a time, and the last 20 stay listed. - Trackball (off for now: the card is hidden and /api/trackball answers 404 unless the service has FLIPEROS_WEB_TRACKBALL=1): the phone as the cabinet's mouse, for trackball and spinner games (MAME reads the mouse for them), frontends and the desktop. - Roll with a finger on the pad. After a quick flick the ball keeps rolling and slows down by itself, like an arcade trackball, and a touch stops it. - There are three big buttons and a sensitivity slider; a mouse wheel on the pad also scrolls. - The panel creates a virtual USB mouse in /dev/uinput ("FliperOS web trackball": X, Y, wheel and three buttons) the first time it is used. It stays while the panel runs. The page sends the movement over a WebSocket (/api/trackball) once per screen frame. - A button that is held when the connection drops is released. - Terminal: the cabinet's shell in the browser, as the fliperos user, with its own zsh and the window's size: the same as SSH, without a program on the computer. - It is a login shell in a pseudo-terminal (setsid -c, so Ctrl+C and job control work). ~/.zprofile only starts the tty1 flow on /dev/tty1, so the shell opens normally. The shell runs at normal priority, not the service's Nice=15. - The page talks to it over a WebSocket (/api/terminal). Only the panel's own page can open it (the Origin must be the panel's address), and only after the login. - The screen is drawn by xterm.js 5.5.0 with its fit addon (MIT, config/web/xterm-LICENSE.txt). It ships inside the panel and loads only when the terminal opens. - Files: the folders ~/roms, ~/bios, ~/media, ~/nvram, ~/save and ~/splashscreen. You can open folders (inside one, the .. folder at the top of the list goes back up), download a file, and upload several files with their progress (also by dropping them on the list). You can also create a folder and delete a file or an empty folder. - An upload is written to a hidden .part file in the same folder and renamed at the end, so a cut upload doesn't leave a broken game under the right name. - A file that already exists is only replaced after you confirm. - What you send belongs to the fliperos user. - Nothing outside those folders is reachable (no .., no absolute paths), but links inside them work (a games folder on an external disk). The folder at the top is never deleted.

It is a service in Setup > System > Services (Web panel). By default it is After boot, so it starts about 15 s after the menu, frontend or game opens at boot.

config/fliperos-web (installed as /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-web, the fliperos-web.service unit) uses only Python's standard library, on port 8081 (--port changes it; 8080 is Pixelcade's own settings page).

It runs as root to read DRM and to check the password in /etc/shadow through libcrypt, the same way the login does. Only the fliperos user signs in. The session is an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie that lasts 12 hours.

Every POST asks for the X-FliperOS: 1 header, which a form on another site cannot send, and five wrong passwords in a minute lock that address for a minute. The page is plain HTTP, so the password crosses the network unencrypted: use it on a network you trust.

The page is in English, or in Portuguese with a Portuguese browser; the button at the top switches.

The JSON API is the same one the page uses, so it also serves scripts: POST /api/login {"user","password"}, then GET /api/status (all of it), /api/logs, /api/log?name=NAME&lines=N and POST /api/volume {"action":"up"|"down"|"mute"} or {"set":0..100}, GET /api/systems, GET /api/games?system=KEY (the romlist fields, Favourite, PlayedCount, PlayedTime, and the filters), GET /api/gameinfo?system=&game=, POST /api/favourite {"system","game","on":true|false}, POST /api/launch {"system","game"} (the set name or the file), POST /api/close, GET /api/files?root=roms&path=FOLDER, GET /api/download?root=&path=, POST /api/upload?root=&path=&name= (the body is the file; &overwrite=1 replaces), POST /api/mkdir {"root","path","name"}, POST /api/delete {"root","path"}, GET /api/settings, POST /api/settings {"key","value"}, GET /api/downloader, POST /api/downloader ({"action":"add","kind":"roms"|"chds","magnet"}, {"action":"start"} or {"action":"remove","kind","delete"}), GET /api/romfilter?target=&folder= (the parameters, presets and saved Downloader filter), POST /api/romfilter/count, /save, /scan and /run ({"target","folder","values":{KEY:VALUE},"preset"|"transfer"}), GET /api/dirs?path=, GET /api/stream, POST /api/stream/offer {"fps":15|30|60,"sdp"} (the SDP answer), POST /api/stream/install, GET /api/overlay and POST /api/overlay {"action":"newkey"}, and without login, by the key: GET /overlay/marquee?key=, /overlay/live?key=, /api/overlay/state?key=, /api/overlay/art?key=&id= and POST /api/overlay/offer?key=, GET /api/tasks, GET /api/task?id=N (with the log), POST /api/task/cancel {"id":N}, GET /api/screenshot (a PNG) and GET /api/terminal (a WebSocket: binary frames are the keys and the screen, a text frame {"resize":[columns,rows]} sets the size) and GET /api/trackball (a WebSocket of text frames {"m":[dx,dy],"w":wheel} and {"b":["left"|"right"|"middle",1|0]}).

Controller on the stream

Controller on the stream

Put your controller on the screen of your live stream. The stick and the buttons light up while you press them on the cabinet, like the input displays of fighting game streams. Viewers see every motion and every button.

It's a page for an OBS Browser Source, with a transparent background, so it sits on top of the game. You restyle it in the web panel, in a CSS editor with a live preview. A saved style shows up in OBS at once.

It needs no extra hardware or program: it reads the same controls you set in Setup > Joysticks > Button mapping.

Put it in OBS

  1. Open the web panel (http://fliperos.local) and go to Live.
  2. Scroll to the Controller for OBS card and press Copy next to the address.
  3. In OBS: Sources > + > Browser, and paste the address in URL.
  4. Width and height: 800 × 400 for one player, 1600 × 400 for two.
  5. Place it over the game, in a corner or below it, and resize it as you like: everything scales with the source.

The address carries a key, the same as the marquee's and the live screen's, because OBS can't sign in. New address, on the Marquee for OBS card (it shows with the marquee page on), makes a new key for all three; then copy the addresses again.

Options

In the panel In the address What it does
Players: Player 1 (nothing) One panel, player 1
Players: Player 2 &players=2 One panel, player 2
Players: 1 and 2 &players=1,2 Two panels side by side (also 1,2,3 and 1,2,3,4)
Demo in the preview &demo=1 Presses the buttons by itself, with no one at the cabinet

The demo only changes the preview in the panel. In OBS, leave it out of the address, or the buttons light up on their own.

What it shows

Each player has:

  • the stick: a ball that leans to the direction pressed, diagonals too;
  • six buttons: 1 2 3 on top and 4 5 6 below, the panel order of Button mapping, on the curve of a Vewlix panel;
  • Start and Coin;
  • the P1 / P2 label.

The buttons follow the Button mapping, not one game's labels: button 1 is the panel's button 1 in every game.

Change the look (CSS)

The card has a CSS editor next to the preview, with syntax colours. The preview changes at each key you type.

  • Save writes the CSS to the cabinet, and the pages open in OBS take it at once. No need to refresh the source.
  • Format lays the CSS out with one property per line. Ctrl+Z undoes it.
  • Factory CSS goes back to the default style.

The factory CSS is commented part by part, and the best start is to edit it.

The classes

Class What it is
.pad One player's panel; also .p1, .p2, and .active while something is pressed
.label P1, P2...
.stick The stick; gets .up .down .left .right while pressed, and data-dir such as up-left
.gate, .ball The base of the stick and its ball
.buttons The six buttons
.button Each button: .b1 to .b6, .start, .coin; .on while pressed
.system Start and Coin
body.players-2 Two panels (also players-3, players-4)

Sizes use --u: one panel is 200 × 100 --u, and --u grows with the OBS source. Write sizes as calc(var(--u) * 26) and the style fits any source size.

Examples

Add these at the end of the CSS and press Save.

Other button colours (here, the Sega Astro City pattern):

:root {
  --b1: #ff5555;
  --b2: #f1fa8c;
  --b3: #8be9fd;
  --b4: #ff5555;
  --b5: #f1fa8c;
  --b6: #8be9fd;
}

Unpressed buttons hidden, only the presses show:

.button { opacity: 0; }
.button.on { opacity: 1; }

No Start and Coin:

.system { display: none; }

A dark box behind each panel:

.pad {
  background: rgba(25, 26, 33, 0.7);
  border-radius: calc(var(--u) * 8);
}

The whole panel lights up while anything is pressed:

.pad.active .gate { border-color: #ff79c6; }

If nothing lights up

  • The page says "wrong overlay address": the key changed (New address). Copy the address again from the panel.
  • Nothing lights up, or the wrong button does: check Setup > Joysticks > Button mapping. The page shows exactly what that map says; with no map it uses MAME's default keys for players 1 and 2.
  • A controller plugged in after the page opened: it's picked up in about 2 seconds; a keyboard encoder too.
  • The page stays blank: the cabinet is off or out of the network. The page reconnects by itself when it comes back.

How it works

While at least one controller page is open, the web panel runs one fliperos-buttons watch at low priority. It reads the Button mapping controls: joysticks through SDL, and a keyboard encoder's keys straight from the input devices, without taking them from the game.

Each change of the pressed controls is one line of JSON, which the panel sends to the pages as Server-Sent Events. A saved CSS goes the same way (event: css), so the open pages fetch it again.

When the last page closes, the reader stops. The CSS lives in /etc/fliperos/input-overlay.css; without it, the page uses the factory input.css.

The page, the events and the CSS are at /overlay/input, /api/overlay/input/events and /api/overlay/input/css, all opened by the address's key. More of the web panel: Web panel.

Frontends

The FliperOS frontend

The default since 2026-10-23: the game list in the look of the Setup menu (Press Start 2P, Dracula colours, the animated background), drawn at 320x240 and stretched to the screen mode. It ships in the image (fliperos-setup/gui/fliperos-frontend, Python and pygame) and is the fliperos row of the session table.

It shows the same thing as the Web panel, from the same code: - the games of each folder, from FliperOS's own lists (~/.local/share/fliperos/lists, in the format of Attract-Mode's romlists; Attract-Mode Plus is optional). The arcade ones carry the name, year, manufacturer, clones and category from MAME's XML (the AttractPlus ROM List, fliperos-romclean romlist); - the game filters the Setup writes into every Attract-Mode display (fliperos-setup --filters), plus Favourites; - FliperOS's own favourites (~/.config/fliperos/favourites) and the game information saved in ~/media/info.

The lists follow the folders. When the frontend opens, and whenever a games folder changes (games copied over the network or from a USB disk), it asks the Setup to redo the lists in the background (fliperos-setup --romlists). New arcade sets get their MAME names right away: when MAME's list is not cached yet, GroovyMAME's -listxml is read once (about a minute).

Vertical monitor. With Video Setup > Monitor orientation on a vertical setting, the frontend is laid out standing up (240x320) and turned to the monitor's side when shown, the same side GroovyMAME turns the games to (ror for clockwise, rol for counter-clockwise). In the list the picture goes on top and the games below; the grid has three rows of 3:4 thumbnails; the controls guide stacks the stick above the buttons.

Three views (Start switches them): - List: the games on the left, the picture, logo and information on the right. A game with clones has a "+" on its left: button 1 unfolds the clones under it, each with what differs in its name (the region, the set, bootleg). - Full screen: the game's video or picture behind (it slides to the next game with the cursor; the videos of the 3 games before and after are opened ahead, held on their first frame), the name and information in front, and on the right the list as four stacked thumbnails, with arrows above and below while there are more games that way; the column slides to its new place. The pictures of the games around the cursor are read ahead, so changing game is instant. The clones come right after their parent: each clone thumbnail carries a CLONE badge with an up arrow in its top-right corner, the title shows what differs in its name after the title, and button 2 goes back to the parent. - Grid: three thumbnails a row, two rows, all the same size: 4:3 with the game's screenshot (or its cover), 3:4 when Video Setup has the monitor vertical. The chosen one has a pink frame that slides to it, and the rows slide too. Every visible game plays its video at once, silent except the chosen one; the videos of the 3 rows above and below are opened and held on their first frame, so a new row starts playing at once. A scrollbar in the corner, with a small arrow above and below it while there are more rows that way. The clones come right after their parent, with the same CLONE badge as in full screen; button 2 on a clone goes back to the parent.

The game's video. In the three views, the game's video (~/media/preview/<folder>/<set>.mp4) plays with its sound, half a second after the cursor stops on it; without a video, its picture shows. In any view, a game missing some of its art (screenshot, cover, marquee, logo or video) gets the missing pieces scraped by itself when the cursor stays on it for 2 seconds, once per game; they land in the same ~/media folders the scraper uses. The logo comes from the Arcade Database too (its "decals"); what it lacks comes one file at a time from the archive.org packs of Setup > Games > Scraper > Art packs by torrent, without downloading the pack.

Automatic scrape. While the frontend is open, it fetches in the background, one game at a time, what each game in the folders still lacks: - arcade: the information, screenshot, flyer, marquee and logo from the Arcade Database; - consoles: the cover and screenshot from libretro-thumbnails; - videos and the logos still missing: the torrent packs of Setup > Games > Scraper > Art packs by torrent, only the files of the games you have (fliperos-setup --mediapacks auto, checked every 6 hours). A pack that keeps its files in one .zip per letter (the MAME videos) would download whole letters, gigabytes for a few videos: it stays out of the torrent, and the frontend fetches each file from inside the zip over HTTP instead.

It pauses while a game is open. A game is tried once every 30 days (what a source does not have stays missing): ~/.local/share/fliperos/scrape-state.json. Tab > Frontend options shows a progress bar, how many games are left and the torrents' progress.

Genre, controls and buttons show with Arcadeflow's icons when Arcadeflow has been downloaded (it can't ship in the image). In the list they come without text, in one row: the genre, the number of players, the control (a pistol for light-gun games, which Arcadeflow has no icon for) and the buttons. They shrink a little when the row doesn't fit.

Below them, out of commercial mode, the list shows the game's synopsis (the start of its arcade-history text, saved by the scrape in ~/media/info), scrolling slowly upwards with a transparent fade at the top and the bottom. It starts two seconds after the cursor stops on the game, and goes around from the end to the start. Console games have no synopsis, and with the monitor upright there is no room for it. In commercial mode the coin indicator takes its place.

Controls. The first time the frontend opens, it starts in Frontend controls (below), so you can say what each button does; back leaves it. From then on, a guide shows the controls each time the frontend opens; any button closes it.

The guide draws the controls as Frontend controls left them: the joystick and the panel buttons in the panel's shape, each button in its function's colour, both centred in the window. A button with no function is left out of the drawing, and so is the joystick when no direction has one.

These are the defaults: - Up and down move through the games; past the last one comes the first again, and before the first the last (holding stops at the end, the next press goes around). Holding speeds up, and after 3 seconds the letter mode starts: the letter big in the middle of the screen, the cursor jumping from letter to letter (slowly at first, faster after a short hold). - The letter mode stays after letting go: each tap of up or down moves one letter. - Two seconds without touching anything (or any other button) end it, on the first game of that letter. - Left and right change the game list (each games folder, and Arcade with all the arcade folders together); the screen slides to the new one. A strip of tiles shows the lists around the chosen one: each tile has the system's written logo (the same as the marquee's, from the Arcadeflow theme, made once and kept in ~/.cache/fliperos/syslogo), filling 80% of a tile as wide as the logo needs, with the emulator's icon sitting on the bottom right corner; under it, the number of games. Without Arcadeflow, or a system it doesn't know, the tile is square with only the emulator's icon, and the list's name is written under it. The same logo also replaces the list's name at the top of the screen. Each game list remembers where the cursor was, also after the frontend is closed or the cabinet turned off. In the grid they move through it, and change the game list only when the chosen game already touches that side; a tab below the thumbnails names the next one. - Button 1 opens the game's menu: Play, Favourite and "+". The "+" page has the game's information from the Arcade Database, saved on the cabinet, in two pages. The first has the cover, year, genre, players and control, the player 1 buttons drawn on the panel where Buttons layout puts them (with their colour and what they do, the same drawing as the controls guide; the joystick directions are left out) and the game's description. A blinking arrow on the right leads to the second: the game's pictures, maker, series, screen, status, language, set and rating, and the rest of the arcade-history.com text (Technical, Trivia...). A value too long for its line shows with "..." and then scrolls inside it, like a marquee. - Button 2 goes back; from the list, it asks whether to return to the FliperOS menu. - Buttons 3 and 6 move a page up and down. Button 4 marks or unmarks the favourite. Button 5 opens the filters; the filter belongs to the romlist (each one keeps its own, and changing romlist brings back its filter). - Tab (keyboard) opens the game options: - Classify: genre, players, buttons, control, year, maker, rotation and series, saved in ~/media/info/<folder>/<set>.user.json; the filters use them; - Rename, with an on-screen keyboard; - Scrape this game: its information, pictures, logo and video, right away; - Delete this game: after a YES/NO question, its file goes away from the folder (for MAME, also the CHD folder of the same name); its art in ~/media stays. A clone kept inside its parent's zip has no file of its own to delete.

Under them come the frontend options. The game options and the frontend options are one list that scrolls with the chosen line (always whole lines, never cut in half), with the Auto scrape box fixed at the bottom; the card is 200 pixels tall, so it fits on the tube. Each option is saved at once in ~/.config/fliperos/frontend.json: - View: list, full screen or grid, with left and right (Start also switches it). - Show clones and Hidden games (the list of hidden games; button 1 brings one back). - Frontend controls: a screen with the frontend's functions (games up and down, list left and right, select, back, page up and down, favourite, filter, view mode and game options). Each one has a Panel column and a Keyboard column; left and right switch between them.

Select asks for the new one: press the panel control (a button, a direction or Start) or the key. A button or key that another function already had swaps: that function gets the old one. The same one again, or Delete, leaves the function with none; any function can have none.

Nothing pressed for 8 seconds keeps it as it was (Esc, or the panel's back button when choosing a key, cancels). The last line has **Reset** and **Save** side by side (left and right). Reset brings back the functions' defaults (the exit shortcut and the panel layout stay); **Save** saves and leaves the screen, like back. Each change works at once and is saved in `frontend.json` (`controls`).

**Exit game** is the shortcut that closes the open game. In the Panel column, select asks for the buttons: hold two or more together for a second, and in a game the same buttons held for a second close it. In commercial mode the coin can't be one of them. In the Keyboard column, select asks for the key: press it within 8 seconds (back on the panel cancels).

A key the panel itself sends (a keyboard encoder) is refused, since each button does one thing. Delete turns either one off.

**Panel layout** (left and right) is the shape of the panel that the guide draws: **6 buttons** in two rows (where Buttons layout puts them), **4 in line** like a Neo Geo MVS, **3 in line**, **2 in line** or **2 stacked**. The guide draws only the buttons that shape has, and in this screen a button it doesn't have shows dimmed (its function then works only from the keyboard).

The coin stays the coin (commercial mode). A key that the panel itself sends (a keyboard encoder: the `k:` entries of the Button mapping, or MAME's keys without them) can't be a keyboard key.
