Leaving the screen with select or back off the panel shows a warning: without them the menus only open from the keyboard.
  • Power closes game: on (the default), the cabinet's power button closes the open game; off, it does nothing while a game is open. With no game open it always powers off.
  • Commercial mode and, with it on, Minutes per coin (1 to 60, left and right).

The exit key and buttons are read alongside the game by fliperos-buttons hotkey, without taking anything from it. The frontend closes the game and what runs under it (the X server, the emulator) with SIGTERM, and SIGKILL after 4 seconds.

Commercial mode (Tab > Frontend options), for a cabinet that charges by the time played: - Without time, the customer can browse the games but not choose one: button 1 shows INSERT COIN. - Each coin (the panel's COIN, also during a game) adds the minutes chosen in Minutes per coin to the time left. The time runs by the clock, also on the menu and with the cabinet off. Turning commercial mode off clears the time left: turned on again, it starts with no coin. - When the time runs out during a game, the game closes and the frontend says TIME IS UP. - The indicator: without time, a coin going into a slot and INSERT COIN blinking, in a frame. With time, a clock with the minutes left (the seconds, in red, in the last minute). In the list it sits under the game's control icons; in full screen in the top left corner; in the grid in the bottom right corner (the logo, the texts and the icons move up a little, the icons in two lines). - It is a kiosk: the controller's button 2 never closes the frontend. The Esc key of a real keyboard (the operator's) still asks whether to go back to the FliperOS menu.

The power button. With no game open, the cabinet's power button powers off; with a game open it closes the game (Tab > Frontend options > Power closes game). The frontend tells fliperos-powerkey which process is the game through the file named in FLIPEROS_POWERKEY=games:FILE ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fliperos-frontend.game): its other children, the video player and the scraper, are not a game. Before this, the button killed the video and never powered off.

The buttons are the panel's own, from Setup > Joysticks > Button mapping (/etc/fliperos/buttons.map). Without a mapping, a common pad works, and so does a keyboard encoder in MAME's layout.

A game opened from the frontend gets the screen, the sound and the controls, and counts in Attract-Mode's play statistics (the Most Played filter).

Setup > Games > Frontend

The default launcher, the one that opens when the computer starts; one that isn't installed can be installed from the FliperOS repository, which ships inside the image (/opt/fliperos/repo, below). Whatever doesn't have a package yet shows as not available yet.

Fightcade 2 doesn't come from a package: it is downloaded on the spot from its website (Fightcade 2). At 240p: on a 15 kHz monitor the frontends run at 320x240, and each one's default is designed for 720 lines or more — the text ends up 4 to 8 pixels tall.

That's why the Setup writes a configuration once (whatever is changed later in the frontend itself stays; with the frontend open, it applies next time): both get a FliperOS 240p theme, made for 240 lines and in Dracula colors: the system at the top, the game list in a 12-pixel font, the game image with year, publisher and description.

In EmulationStation (ES-DE) it is config/esde-theme-fliperos, installed in /usr/share/es-de/themes/fliperos-240p-es-de (Theme in es_settings.xml), without the menu background blur and without the new-version notice: the systems as a list of names, the game video (if any) in place of the image, and in the footer only the buttons that fit in 320 pixels.

In a wide-pixel mode (640x240 on a 4:3 tube) the FliperOS ES-DE package draws the interface at 320x240 and stretches it twice horizontally (packaging/patches/emulationstation; fliperos-kms-run sets ESDE_STRETCH_X from the mode), so text and images keep their proportions on the tube, as Arcadeflow does.

In the themes that ES-DE ships, even with the large font, the list text is thin and low-contrast and the footer help ends up about 6 pixels tall. In Pegasus it is config/pegasus-theme-fliperos, installed in /usr/share/pegasus-frontend/themes — left/right switch systems, L2/R2 skip ten games.

Grid, Pegasus's default theme, shows the covers at 320x240 but leaves the description 4 pixels tall.

Pixelcade marquee

A Pixelcade LED or LCD marquee shows the game you have selected in the frontend and the game you open. Setup > Games > Extras > Pixelcade installs it.

Pixelcade's software (pixelweb) is closed source, so it isn't in the image: the Setup downloads it from Pixelcade's GitHub (alinke/pixelcade-linux-builds), along with the artwork (a few hundred MB), into ~/pixelcade.

Choosing Extras > Pixelcade again, once it is installed, offers to update the program and the artwork, or to install the paid art pack: type the license code you got from Pixelcade and the Setup downloads the pack.

~/pixelcade is the folder Pixelcade's own guides use, so the same can be done by hand: cd ~/pixelcade && ./pixelweb -install-artpack <code>.

The events below are the ones of Pixelcade's own EmulationStation scripts (alinke/pixelcade-linux), with the same calls to pixelweb.

  • Service: fliperos-pixelcade.service keeps pixelweb running as the fliperos user and starts it when the marquee is plugged in (99-fliperos-pixelcade.rules, USB IDs 1b4f:0008 for V1 and 2e8a:1050 for V2). The serial port belongs to the dialout group. Pixelcade's settings page is at http://<cabinet IP>:8080.

If no marquee is connected, pixelweb searches for about 30 seconds and then exits. The service tries 3 times and then stops until the marquee is plugged in. When it starts, the marquee shows the FliperOS logo; when the computer shuts down or restarts, it shows "Bye". - Game opened: every game from every frontend and emulator goes through fliperos-kms-run or fliperos-x11-run. These call fliperos-pixelcade launch in the background, so a game never waits for the marquee. The game is the last argument: a file in ~/roms, or the set name for GroovyMAME and Model 2.

When there is no game (a frontend, an emulator's menu) nothing happens. First a text scrolls once: the game's high scores, or "Now Playing" and the game's name. Then the game's marquee stays. - High scores: for arcade games, the text is the top three scores (#1 19,130 DAA #2 ...). They come from the game's .hi file, the newest one among ~/.mame/hiscore (GroovyMAME's hiscore plugin) and the RetroArch saves folder (/opt/fliperos/saves/retroarch, where the MAME and FBNeo cores write theirs).

The hi2txt program reads the file, as in Pixelcade's installer. Extras > Pixelcade downloads it (pinned by hash) into ~/pixelcade/hi2txt and installs Java from apt (default-jre-headless), which it needs. A game that hi2txt doesn't know shows its name instead. - Game closed: the helper waits for the game to end and then shows the game's marquee the way the frontend selection does. That matters in Pegasus, which doesn't report what is selected. - Game selected: in ES-DE, through its custom event scripts (~/ES-DE/scripts/game-select and system-select, with Custom event scripts and Browsing custom events turned on; browsing doesn't wait for them).

In Attract-Mode Plus, through FliperOS's Pixelcade plugin, which is copied to ~/.attract/plugins and turned on in plugins.cfg. Pegasus has no event hooks, so it only shows the game that was opened.

The service writes these frontend settings at every boot; if the frontend is open at that moment, they wait for the next boot. - Screensaver: when the FliperOS frontend is idle for 30 seconds, or the screensaver of ES-DE (screensaver-start and screensaver-end scripts) or Attract-Mode Plus starts, the marquee plays the FliperOS logo animation (the same as the ZeDMD's, copied to ~/pixelcade/console/fliperos-idle.gif). Without it, the marquee goes into Pixelcade's attract mode, a playlist you set up on the settings page. When it ends, the marquee shows the selected game or system again. - FliperOS menu: in the menu that opens when the frontend closes, the marquee follows the cursor. Each of the five items has its own animation in the style of the default logo: a synthwave sun with an animated icon and the item's name in neon chrome, with glitches. The items are FRONTEND (a joystick), SETUP (two gears), DESKTOP (a monitor with windows and a mouse), SHELL (a terminal typing) and POWER (the power symbol pulsing). Entering an item keeps its animation through the submenus. The graphic Setup sends each move of the cursor (fliperos-pixelcade menu ITEM); the text Setup sends the item when you enter it. The ZeDMD, the Pixelcade, the web panel's preview and the OBS page all play it (tools/marquee-logo-anim.py, marquee-menu-ITEM.gif among the web panel's files). - Achievements: with RetroAchievements turned on in RetroArch (cheevos_enable = "true"), each unlocked achievement shows on the marquee, and then the game's marquee comes back.

RetroArch has no event for this, so fliperos-kms-run opens it with --verbose and the helper reads the [RCHEEVOS] Awarding achievement lines from /opt/fliperos/logs/retroarch.log. In debug mode the log goes to the screen and no achievement is shown. - Pixelcade LCD over USB: the LCD marquee (USB ID 1d6b:3232, firmware 6.3 or newer) appears as a network card.

The udev rule keeps it out of NetworkManager and starts fliperos-pixelcade-lcd@<interface>.service, which gives the card the address 169.254.100.2 (the LCD is 169.254.100.1), sets lcdMarquee and lcdUsbConnected in ~/pixelcade/pixelcade.ini, writes the LCD's name there and restarts the service. This is what Pixelcade's installer does; it has not been tested with an LCD marquee yet. - Visual Pinball: a program whose name starts with vpinball draws the display itself, over the same serial port. When it opens, pixelweb (and dmdserver) close and let go of the port; when it ends, the services open them again. FliperOS doesn't ship Visual Pinball. - Changing the system in the FliperOS frontend: when you switch the game list (left and right), the system's written logo (NAOMI, ATOMISWAVE, SEGA MODEL 3...) slides in on the marquee from the side the list moved to, with the previous one leaving, and blinks twice. It is the same slide as the frontend's screen.

The logos are the ones of the Arcadeflow's displays menu: each is a character of the theme's font, drawn when needed by fliperos-syslogo from ~/.attract/layouts/Arcadeflow (the Setup downloads the theme; Arcadeflow has no license, so none of it is in the image). Without the theme, or for a system that isn't in it, the marquee shows the system's art as before.

The ZeDMD gets the frames straight from fliperos-dmd slide. The Pixelcade only shows files, so the logo goes in a GIF in ~/pixelcade/console (fliperos-logo-*, replaced at each switch). fliperos-syslogo export DIR writes every logo as a PNG.

The marquee preview of the web panel and the marquee page for OBS draw the same logo with the same slide and blinks (the panel serves it as a PNG, /api/marquee/logo?name=), as long as marquee_overlay is on; the preview turns it on by itself. - Systems: the arcade folders (mame, naomi, naomi2, atomiswave, model2, model3, and the MAME and FBNeo cores) use Pixelcade's mame artwork. The RetroArch cores go by their system (snes, genesis, psx...). Other folders go by their name.

DOFLinx (effects during the game)

DOFLinx shows the score and effects on the Pixelcade marquee while a game runs. It is closed source and large (about 230 MB to download), so it is a separate extra: Setup > Games > Extras > DOFLinx, after Pixelcade. It follows Pixelcade's own setup, which covers the FBNeo arcade games in RetroArch.

  • What is installed: the Linux program from DOFLinx's GitHub (DOFLinx/CurrentExecutable) into ~/doflinx, the DOFLinx.ini and colours.ini that Pixelcade publishes, with FliperOS's folders, in ~/doflinx/config, and the per-game files, which pixelweb -update-doflinx downloads into ~/pixelcade/DOFLinx.

If you change DOFLinx.ini, a later install keeps your file and saves the new one as DOFLinx.ini.latest. - RetroArch: DOFLinx finds the running game and reads its memory through RetroArch's Network Command Interface. The install writes /etc/fliperos/retroarch/doflinx.cfg (network_cmd_enable, port 55355), which fliperos-kms-run adds to RetroArch. Without DOFLinx the interface stays off. - Service: fliperos-doflinx.service runs it as the fliperos user after pixelweb answers. - It has not been tested with a marquee yet.

ZeDMD (open-source LED display)

ZeDMD is an open-source LED display you can build yourself: an ESP32 board driving HUB75 LED panels, 128x32 (two 64x32 panels) or 256x64. Setup > Games > Extras > ZeDMD installs support for it.

It needs ZeDMD firmware 5.1.0 or newer. Older firmware, like the one that works on Batocera 41, doesn't connect to FliperOS. ZeDMD firmware version says how to check yours and how to update it.

The display gets the same events as the Pixelcade marquee: the game selected in ES-DE or Attract-Mode Plus, the system selected in ES-DE, the game opened from any frontend or emulator (with the high scores or "Now Playing" scrolling first), the game closed, the screensaver, the RetroAchievements and "Bye" at shutdown.

Pixelcade and ZeDMD can be installed together. The high scores need hi2txt and Java, which come with Extras > Pixelcade.

  • What is installed: dmdserver from libdmdutil (the Visual Pinball DMD library, pinned version and hash) into ~/zedmd, and the python3-pil package. Neither is in the image.
  • Service: fliperos-zedmd.service runs dmdserver as the fliperos user, listening on 127.0.0.1:6789.

The udev rule (99-fliperos-zedmd.rules) names the ESP32's USB serial adapter /dev/zedmd and starts the service when it is plugged in (CP210x 10c4:ea60, CH340 1a86:7523, CH9102 1a86:55d4, ESP32-S3 native USB 303a:1001). With another adapter, dmdserver searches every USB serial port. If no ZeDMD is found, the service tries 3 times and then stops until one is plugged in. - What it shows: fliperos-dmd sends a 128x32 picture (dmdserver scales it up for a 256x64 panel).

It looks in ~/media in this order: dmd/<games folder>/<rom>.png or .gif (dmd/mame/sf2.gif; the same folders as ~/roms) (art made for the display; GIFs play animated), then the scraped marquee and logo images (Setup > Games > Scraper).

Without any picture it shows the game's name, taken from the Attract-Mode or ES-DE game list. A name that doesn't fit in one line keeps scrolling in big letters until the next event, like an LED sign; the web panel's marquee preview and the OBS page do the same. A system picture goes in ~/media/dmd/<system>.png. - Screensaver and startup: when the service starts, and whenever the frontend is idle, the display plays a looping 3D vector animation in two flat colors (cyan and magenta) on black, with 1-pixel lines: the screen opens like a CRT, the camera dives through a wireframe tunnel with spinning wireframe cubes, and out of a flash of light the FliperOS letters appear as extruded line art, each one spinning like a coin while it is drawn, over a scrolling floor. The word sways, a scan line swaps the two colors, it makes a full turn to show its depth, and it flies back into the distance as the screen closes. It goes on until the next game or system event. tools/zedmd-vector-anim.py renders it (config/zedmd-fliperos.gif, 128x32, 8 seconds).

Idle means 30 seconds without pressing a button in the FliperOS frontend (FLIPEROS_IDLE_SECONDS, 0 turns it off). The first press brings back the logo of the selected system. ES-DE and Attract-Mode Plus start the same animation with their own screensaver timers. The pictures in ~/media/dmd and ~/media/marquee are no longer cycled; fliperos-dmd attract art still does it. - Artwork: Pixelcade's artwork is licensed only for Pixelcade hardware, so FliperOS doesn't use it on the ZeDMD.

ZeDMD firmware version

FliperOS talks to the display through dmdserver from libdmdutil 0.11.0, which brings libzedmd 0.10. That library only understands ZeDMD firmware 5.1.0 or newer. The newest release is 5.1.8.

The firmware changed its USB handshake twice, and each time the new library stopped talking to the older firmware:

Firmware Works with FliperOS
3.x and 4.x No. 3.6.0 was tried on a user's cabinet: it never answers
5.0.x No. Its handshake reply is shorter than libzedmd 0.10 expects (read from the code, not tried)
5.1.0 and newer Yes. 5.1.8 was tried on the same cabinet: a 128x32 ESP32 board with a CH340 USB adapter

Coming from Batocera. Batocera 41 has an older libzedmd, which still talks to firmware before 5.1. Batocera 42 and 43 have the new one, like FliperOS: the ZeDMD 5.1.0 release notes told Batocera users to wait for Batocera 42.

So a ZeDMD that works on Batocera 41 but not on 42 or 43 has old firmware, and FliperOS won't see it either until it is updated. After the update it no longer works on Batocera 41.

Seeing the version. The display shows it at the bottom right of its logo when it powers on (every version does). Once it connects, the service log has it too: journalctl -u fliperos-zedmd shows ZeDMD 5.1.8 found: device=/dev/zedmd, width=128, height=32.

What old firmware looks like. The display stays on its logo. The log shows ZeDMD handshake response error, result: 0, then Unable to connect to ZeDMD on /dev/zedmd and No DMD displays found, three times, and the service stops.

A ZeDMD 5.x gives the same messages while its settings menu is open: it only talks over USB after Exit in that menu.

Updating the ZeDMD firmware

FliperOS doesn't update the display by itself. It is done once, from FliperOS or from a PC.

  1. From the latest ZeDMD release, download the zip for your board and panels. ZeDMD-128x32.zip is for an ESP32 with two 64x32 panels, ZeDMD-256x64.zip for HD, ZeDMD-128x64.zip for a single 128x64 panel, and the ZeDMD-S3-N16R8_… ones for an ESP32-S3 N16R8. The ZeDMD README describes each one.

The zip has ZeDMD.bin: the firmware and its files in one image, written at address 0. 2. On FliperOS, in a terminal (SSH, or the web panel's Terminal), with the display plugged in:

sudo systemctl stop fliperos-zedmd sudo apt install esptool esptool --chip esp32 --port /dev/zedmd -b 460800 --no-stub write_flash 0x0 ZeDMD.bin

Ubuntu's esptool comes without esptool's helper program (the "stub"), hence --no-stub: the ESP32's own ROM writes the flash. It takes about 2 minutes and ends with Hash of data verified. For an ESP32-S3 the chip is esp32s3.

From a Windows PC, the ZeDMD project's ZeDMD_Updater2 does the same. 3. On the first start after the update the display opens its settings menu, and it doesn't talk over USB while the menu is open. Set RGB Order until the top left shows red as red, green as green and blue as blue, then pick Exit. Without buttons, unplugging the display and plugging it back also leaves the menu.

The update doesn't keep the old RGB order and brightness. 4. Start the service again, since it gave up after its 3 tries: sudo systemctl reset-failed fliperos-zedmd, then sudo systemctl start fliperos-zedmd. The log should show ZeDMD 5.1.8 found.

Two warnings in the log are normal. With 5.1.8 on the original ESP32 the log says The ZeDMD USB package size of 32 is a very low value and The ZeDMD panel minimal refresh rate of 30 is a very low value. Those are the firmware's defaults, and pictures and scrolling text are fine with them.

If animations stutter, the ZeDMD README suggests a USB package size of 512 for the original ESP32 (USB packet size in the display's menu).

Keeping the old firmware. To go back to it later (to use the display on Batocera 41 again), save the flash before updating. Ubuntu's esptool can't do it: with --no-stub, read_flash stops at 2 MB with CRC or checksum was invalid, because in that mode it doesn't tell the ROM the flash size.

Espressif's own esptool, which has the stub (pipx install esptool, or its releases), reads the whole flash with esptool --chip esp32 --port /dev/zedmd read_flash 0 ALL zedmd-backup.bin (not tried here). It goes back the same way as the update: write_flash 0x0 zedmd-backup.bin.

Versus score on the LED display

During a two-player match the display shows the score: the matches each side has won since the game opened. On a ZeDMD the score stays on the display (GUILE 3 x 1 KEN, with each side's character when the game tells it, or P1 and P2).

On a Pixelcade a text scrolls each time someone wins a match, and then the game's marquee comes back. The score appears with the first win: until then (the game's demo, the character select, the first match) the display keeps the game's picture.

It works in GroovyMAME, for about 200 arcade ROM sets, and in RetroArch with the FBNeo core, for about 100: the ones Fightcade has a detector for. The full list is in Scoreboard games.

What was checked on a FliperOS cabinet, with Fightcade's own detectors and no picture on the tube:

  • GroovyMAME: Street Fighter II' Champion Edition, The King of Fighters '98, Mortal Kombat II and Street Fighter III 3rd Strike, one of each kind of detector, played by a script. The wins of both players and the characters came out right, and so did the 128x32 picture sent to the display.
  • RetroArch (FBNeo): Street Fighter II' CE, KOF '98 and 3rd Strike left in their demo. The memory the detectors describe was read right (the match start and the characters). No match was played there, because nothing can press the buttons of a RetroArch without picture, so a win has not been seen counted in RetroArch.

  • A real LED display (ZeDMD or Pixelcade) showing the score has not been seen yet.

  • Where the score comes from: the game only draws it on the screen, so it is read from the game's memory. The map is Fightcade's detectors, one file per game saying where a match starts, where each side wins and which character each side chose.

It is the map Fightcade uses to know who won each online match. Its repository has no license, so the files aren't in the image: Extras > Pixelcade and Extras > ZeDMD download them (a pinned version) into ~/.local/share/fliperos/versus-detectors. fliperos-versus fetch downloads them again. The repository keeps a reference copy of the same version in third-party/fightcade-detectors (not installed by anything). - Which games: the CPS1 and CPS2 games (Street Fighter II, Alpha 3, Marvel vs. Capcom...), the Neo Geo ones (The King of Fighters, Garou, Samurai Shodown...) the CPS3 ones (Street Fighter III, JoJo, Red Earth) and the ones whose detector uses the CPU's own addresses (Mortal Kombat II and many others; these only in GroovyMAME). A clone uses its parent's detector. - How it is read: for a game with a detector, the groovymame command turns on the fliperos-versus plugin.

The plugin evaluates the detector every frame, the way Fightcade's emulator does (a condition counts after 30 frames in a row), and writes the result (fliperos_wins1, fliperos_wins2, fliperos_char1, fliperos_char2) to a file in the session's runtime folder, which fliperos-versus follows.

These are not MAME outputs and don't go through port 8000: in today's MAME a script can't create new outputs, only use the ones the game declares. - Points: the detectors don't have each player's points. For those there is /etc/fliperos/versus-games.conf, a table of addresses read directly (the format is explained at its top; your own lines go in ~/config/versus-games.conf). It is empty for now, so the display shows the wins only. When a game has its points there, they appear below the wins. - RetroArch: with the FBNeo core, the emulator the detectors were written for.

fliperos-kms-run turns on RetroArch's Network Command Interface for a game with a detector (/etc/fliperos/retroarch/versus.cfg), and fliperos-versus reads the game's memory ten times a second (READ_CORE_RAM) and evaluates the detector itself.

It covers the CPS1, CPS2, Neo Geo and CPS3 games; a detector that uses the CPU's own addresses can't be read there. The MAME cores (mame2010, mame) don't let the memory be read, so there is no score in them: use GroovyMAME or FBNeo for those games. - The FBNeo core comes in the image from 0.9.1. On an installed system, get it in RetroArch: Online Updater > Core Downloader > Arcade (FinalBurn Neo). Its games go in ~/roms/retroarch/fbneo, in FBNeo's own ROM sets.

The Fightcade ROMs (~/roms/fightcade) are Fightcade's alone: the frontends don't list them, and the core's folder is not linked to them (an earlier FliperOS made that link by itself; it is removed at the next boot, and the folder is empty again).

To play a set in the core, copy it to ~/roms/retroarch/fbneo; a set that changed between Fightcade's FBNeo 0.2.97.44 and the current core may not open in the core. - Console sets in the FBNeo folder. The core only looks for a .zip among the arcade sets, unless the folder it is in has the name of a system (megadrive, sms, nes, pce, tg16, sgx, msx, coleco, sg1000, gamegear, spectrum, fds, snes, ngp, channelf); a Mega Drive game loose among the arcade sets closed with romset is unknown.

Fightcade ROM packs often come like that, with every system in one folder.

FliperOS finds the system of each set in FBNeo's own lists (/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-fbneo; a name that exists in more than one system is settled by the CRCs inside the .zip) and opens the game through a link in ~/.cache/fliperos-fbneo/<system>/, with its parent set and the system BIOS (spectrum.zip, msx.zip, coleco.zip...) linked next to it, so nothing has to be moved.

This happens when a frontend or the Games menu opens the game; a set loaded by hand in RetroArch's own menu still has to be in a system folder. A set that is in none of FBNeo's current lists still shows romset is unknown. - Model 2 (SM2-Emu): for Virtua Fighter 2, Fighting Vipers, Sonic the Fighters, Last Bronx and Dead or Alive, the emulator itself reads the memory, with FliperOS's patch, and publishes the rounds each side has taken among the game's outputs (P1_Wins, P2_Wins on TCP port 8000, see DIY hardware).

With a display installed, fliperos-x11-run turns that port on for these games and fliperos-versus follows it. A match is counted for the side with more rounds when they go back to zero, which the game does when the next match starts, so the win appears then; there are no characters.

Checked with the real emulator up to the rounds arriving and with a scripted feed for the count; not seen in a match on a cabinet. fliperos-versus watch model2 <game> shows the values. - Sides: versus_side=2 in /etc/fliperos/fliperos.conf puts player 2 first, for the cabinet on that side. - Checking a game: open it and run fliperos-versus watch mame <game> over SSH: it prints the wins and the characters as they change, to compare with the screen. - The count starts again when the game closes. Only with a Pixelcade or a ZeDMD installed; without one, nothing is turned on.

APT repository

Attract-Mode Plus comes from a dedicated APT repository of prebuilt .debs, like GroovyArcade's groovy-ux-repo (packaging/build-deb.sh, packaging/make-repo.sh, Dockerfile.packages, recipes in packaging/packages/). The build carries the repository into the image (/opt/fliperos/repo, deb [trusted=yes] file:/opt/fliperos/repo ./, option --repo) and already installs Attract-Mode Plus; without it, the cabinet's apt said "Unable to locate package".

The config/fliperos-sessions.conf table says, for each launcher, whether it runs in KMS or X (from galauncher's videodata.conf table) and which package it comes from.

EmulationStation and Pegasus: built on the cabinet

ES-DE and Pegasus are not in the image or in its repository. The first time you choose one in Setup > Games > Frontend, the Setup says it will be built on that machine and asks for confirmation. It needs the internet.

What happens (config/fliperos-frontend-build, installed as /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-emulationstation and fliperos-pegasus; the name picks the recipe):

  1. It installs the build tools of the recipe (packaging/packages/<package>.sh, the same recipe the CI uses, kept in /usr/local/share/fliperos/packaging).
  2. build-deb.sh downloads the official source at the pinned version, applies FliperOS's patches (ES-DE: the 2x horizontal stretch in packaging/patches/emulationstation; Pegasus: its own KMS patch) and compiles.
  3. The .deb is installed with apt, which brings the runtime libraries from Ubuntu.
  4. The build tools that were not on the system before are removed.

ES-DE needs OpenGL 3.3 or OpenGL ES 3.0. A card that gives less (an Intel HD of the first generation has OpenGL 2.1 and ES 2.0) can't open it: the Frontend screen marks it with a red X and the reason, asks before choosing it, and the installer refuses to build it (fliperos-emulationstation unsupported prints the reason). See Video cards.

Everything the build prints goes to /var/log/<package>-build.log. It needs about 4 GB free in /var/tmp. Choosing the frontend again rebuilds it. A recipe marked PKG_ON_DEMAND=1 is left out of build-deb.sh --list-iso, which is the list the CI builds for the image.

Scoreboard games

Every game shows on the LED display (ZeDMD or Pixelcade) and in the marquee preview of the web panel: its artwork or name when it is selected and when it opens, see Frontends. This page lists the games that also have more data, and which data each one has.

The data

  • Artwork or name: every game. The ZeDMD looks for ~/media/dmd, marquee and logo; the Pixelcade for marquee and logo; without art, the game's name.
  • Wins: the rounds or matches each side has won in the session, in Versus score on the LED display. It comes from a Fightcade detector (fightcade-detectors, commit de9e7a9), read from the game's memory by GroovyMAME or by the FBNeo core of RetroArch, or, for Model 2, published by the emulator itself.
  • Characters: the detector also tells who each side is playing; without it the scoreboard shows the wins only.
  • Points (each player's score): the code reads them from a line of config/versus-games.conf, but no game has one yet: a game only goes in after its address was watched in a real match.
  • High scores: the top of the high score table, for GroovyMAME. The address of the table of each game is in MAME's hiscore.dat; the hiscore plugin keeps the .hi file and hi2txt decodes it. Only the sets in both lists are here.

What was checked. Wins and characters were seen in a played match on the test cabinet, in GroovyMAME, for sf2ce, kof98, mk2, sfiii3nr1 and sfa3 (in sfa3 the characters were read too). sfa2 was played and the detector did not count a win. The other sets are listed because their detector reads as one this code handles, not because each was played. The high scores were checked with a test .hi file of pacman (the decoding gives the right score); no game was played with a real table. Nothing here was seen on a real LED display yet.

Wins and characters. The list is the set of games Fightcade has a detector for, crossed with the sets each emulator has: 230 ROM sets. The set name is the one the detector was written for: a clone without a detector of its own has no scoreboard. Fightcade's other detectors (89) are for console games and for hacks that neither emulator has under that name.

  • GroovyMAME: 199 sets (the ones in MAME 0.289).
  • RetroArch (FBNeo core): 103 sets (the ones in the core's game list). Detectors written as CPU addresses can't be read there.
  • Model 2 (SM2-Emu) is outside the Fightcade list: the emulator itself publishes the rounds each side has taken, with FliperOS's patch, for vf2, fvipers, schamp, lastbrnx and doa (DIY hardware). The scoreboard shows the session wins, without the characters.

High scores. 2388 sets have both the address of the table (hiscore.dat, 5856 sets) and a description in hi2txt (2971 names): Pac-Man, Galaga, Donkey Kong, 1942, TMNT, Gradius and so on. 17 of them also have wins. Most fighting games have wins but no high scores: hiscore.dat has a table but hi2txt has no description for them (sf2ce, sfa3), or the other way round (kof98, mk2).

Files. The last column links to the file that holds each game's data: the Fightcade detector (third-party/fightcade-detectors/<set>.inf, a copy kept in this repository), the SM2-Emu patch that publishes the Model 2 rounds, and the line of the game in MAME's hiscore.dat (the address of its high score table; pinned to MAME commit 6df80b6). hi2txt's description of each game is inside its hi2txt.zip, which the cabinet downloads, so it has no link.

This page is generated by tools/scoreboard-games.py.

Emulators

OpenBOR beat 'em ups its own Xorg 320x240
Supermodel Sega Model 3 its own Xorg 640x240@57.524 at 15 kHz, 496x384 on the others
Model 2 (SM2-Emu) Sega Model 2 its own Xorg same
Fightcade 2 (downloaded through the Setup) online matches: FBNeo, SNES9x and FBA (Wine), Flycast its own Xorg the lobby at 512x448 (interlaced at 15 kHz); the matches in the game's native resolution: each FBNeo/FBA game in its own mode (384x224 for CPS, via GroovyMAME and Switchres), SNES9x at 256x224, Flycast at 640x240
Steam, Heroic (GOG, Epic, Amazon), through Setup > Games > Extras PC games inside the LXDE desktop the desktop's

Dedicated pages: Fightcade 2, ROMs, BIOS and artwork (the folders in ~) and Controls (buttons, SDL, calibration).

All of them appear in LXDE's Games menu (Desktop and theme).

RetroArch uses crt_switch_resolution 4 (the Setup's /etc/switchres.ini) at each game's native width when the card generates low dotclocks (the "s" in the output test result: radeon/amdgpu, and an NVIDIA that passed the low resolution grid), like GroovyArcade; the 2560 super resolution is only for cards that don't (Intel, the other NVIDIA).

At 2560 RetroArch draws its notifications at that width, and on the tube they came out squashed (video_retroarch_super, saved by the output test and at installation).

RetroArch's video is the glcore driver (OpenGL 3.2 core) and its audio is sdl2, which goes straight into ALSA; both come from the system retroarch.cfg (/etc/fliperos/retroarch), which is applied on top of the user's on each launch.

From there also come input and joypad in linuxraw (the kernel's /dev/input/js*; fliperos-controllers generates the automatic controller profiles for udev and linuxraw), RetroArch without on-screen notifications and a single Esc to close the game (confirm_quit off; the default asks for a second Esc, with a notice that would not show).

On cards with only OpenGL 2.x (Radeon X300 to X1950, Intel up to 1st-generation Core, GeForce FX/6/7) glcore doesn't open: fliperos-kms-run asks Mesa (eglinfo) and, on those, passes gl instead.

GroovyMAME at native resolution. GroovyMAME runs in X, like GroovyArcade's X mode: called from the console (by fliperos-launch, by the boot session, by a frontend or in the terminal), the groovymame command opens in an Xorg of its own (fliperos-x11-run) and, with modesetting 1 in mame.ini, GroovyMAME's Switchres creates and switches each game's mode through XRandR — on the cabinet, MvC at SR-1_384x224@59.64, full screen.

Commands without a screen (-listxml, -listclones, -verifyroms, -showconfig, -createconfig, -version...) run directly, without starting X. As in GroovyArcade's galauncher.xinitrc, fliperos-x11-client starts openbox before the program (config/openbox-x11-run.xml: no borders, no shortcuts): it is what fits the full-screen window to the new screen on each mode switch through XRandR; without it the window kept the size of the mode it opened in (the UI in a quarter of the 640x480 screen, the game out of place).

Opened without a game (the UI), groovymame passes -noautosync -waitvsync: the game chosen in the UI runs in the same process, and GroovyMAME's emusync in X (emusync_linux.cpp from gm0289sr222f) uses the /dev/dri/card0 that it closed when leaving the UI (osd_deinit closes the fd and doesn't reset it; "drmCrtcGetSequence(-1)") — with autosync, syncrefresh removed the throttle and the game ran too fast.

Opened directly with the game (frontends, command line), vblank works and autosync stays.

In KMS this didn't work on this installation: with modesetting 0 and SDL_KMSDRM_REQUIRE_DRM_MASTER=0 Switchres applied the game's mode, but SDL kept drawing at the size of the boot mode (in radeon's debugfs framebuffer, GroovyMAME's frames at 320x240 with the screen at 384x224) — the game came out stretched, squashed or in the middle with black bars, depending on the resolution chosen in the Setup; with modesetting 1 the mode wasn't even applied ("No way to get master rights") or the screen went black ("Could not queue pageflip: -13").

RetroArch, in KMS, creates its frames already at the game's size (384x224) and switches correctly. On an earlier installation, fliperos-rootfs.sh replaces the old modesetting 0 with 1.

The other reason for the doubled width is the screen's aspect: with aspect auto GroovyMAME takes the aspect from the current mode, and booting at 640x240 gives 8:3 — twice 4:3, so Switchres doubled the width of every game ("SR(0): 768x224").

mame.ini ships with aspect 4:3, like GroovyArcade (-aspect "4:3"); the Setup only goes back to auto when the chosen monitor is an LCD.

GroovyMAME: the release and the groovymame command. The build no longer compiles GroovyMAME (it took over an hour): it uses the official Linux release (gm0289sr222f, MAME 0.289 with Switchres 2.22f, verified by sha256), in /usr/local/libexec/groovymame, with the libraries it needs (Qt6 is the debugger's).

The groovymame command — the one fliperos-launch, the frontends and the terminal call — is config/fliperos-groovymame, which passes -inipath /etc/fliperos/mame: the release's default is .;ini, relative to the folder it is opened from, so a ~/.mame/mame.ini doesn't apply; what applies is /etc/fliperos/mame/mame.ini (owned by the fliperos user), which the Setup writes.

It also preloads libfliperos-sdl-audio.so (config/fliperos-sdl-audio.c). MAME 0.289 routes each game's speaker to the output SDL calls the default and saves that choice in the game's cfg (sound_map).

SDL 2.30's ALSA backend cannot name a default and lists only the hw: devices, so MAME took the card's raw hw: device: no dmix shared with other programs, not the card picked in the Setup, and no sound on the live screen. The library reports ALSA's default as SDL's default.

On the first game with it, the command also removes the old sound_map entries from ~/.mame/cfg once (marker .fliperos-sound-default). MAME's portaudio module is no fix: it never lists default either, and opens the card's hw: device, silent while another program holds the card.

The release only ships the binary; like GroovyArcade's package, the build puts in /usr/local/share/groovymame the source files of the same tag (commit 953db38): plugins (hiscore), the uismall.bdf font, bgfx, artwork, language, ctrlr, keymaps and hash.

mame.ini is made like GroovyArcade's: GroovyMAME's own -createconfig (every option of the version, at its default), with those of config/mame.ini on top, each on its own line (config/fliperos-mame-ini, at build time).

The GroovyArcade options (gasetup's -createconfig): plugin hiscore, skip_gameinfo 1, video opengl, switchres_ini 1, sound sdl, aspect 4:3 — plus the Setup's latency (lowlatency, autoframedelay, framedelay); the UI font stays MAME's own (uifont default), because GroovyArcade's pixel font (uismall.bdf) was too small on the cabinet.

modesetting 1 is also GroovyArcade's, with GroovyMAME in X (the "GroovyMAME at native resolution" paragraph).

What GroovyMAME writes goes to ~/.mame (cfg, hiscore records), ~/nvram/mame (nvram) and ~/save/mame (savestates); ui.ini gets GroovyArcade's infos_text_size 1.00 and font_rows 20, together with the Dracula colors — GroovyArcade uses 19, but MAME only accepts 20 to 40 and replaces 19 with the default 30, which at 224 lines leaves the font 7 pixels tall and unreadable; with 20 it is 11.

On an earlier installation, fliperos-rootfs.sh only adds to mame.ini and ui.ini the keys they don't have yet (what was already saved stays, theme included); among the paths, the relative ones (the ., cfg, snap of a plain -createconfig: relative to the folder GroovyMAME is opened from, they filled the home folder with cfg and nvram) are removed, and with no absolute one left, the one from config/ applies.

The cfg/nvram left in the home folder moves to ~/.mame; when both exist, each file keeps its newest version. On a system installed earlier, fliperos-rootfs.sh moves the compiled binary to /usr/local/libexec and puts the shortcut in its place.

Reset Geometry. Setup > Video Setup > Geometry saves the geometry measured on the grid (crt_range0 with monitor custom in /etc/switchres.ini, and switchres_ini 1 in mame.ini). The Monitor Type then shows Custom, where a crt_range0 can also be typed in.

Reset Geometry, or choosing a preset in Monitor Type, undoes it: Switchres goes back to the chosen monitor's preset, which applies to GroovyMAME (switchres_ini 1, as in GroovyArcade) and to RetroArch's mode 4, which read the same file.

Multiple monitors (2 or 3 screens). Setup > Video Setup > Multiple Monitors adds a second and a third arcade monitor on the other outputs of the same card (analog; digital through an active converter is experimental).

With Multi-Screen Games on, GroovyMAME opens each screen of Darius, The Ninja Warriors or Punch-Out!! on its own monitor, and Flycast does the same with the NAOMI multi-board games (F355 Challenge, Airline Pilots, Sega Strike Fighter) on 3 monitors. The other emulators and the frontends stay on monitor 1. Details in Multiple monitors.

Nothing interlaced at 15 kHz, by default. On a 15 kHz tube no fliperos-x11-run emulator opens at 480i unless it is chosen for it in 480i hacks (the exception is the Fightcade 2 lobby, which doesn't fit in 240 lines; its matches do): the 480-line ones and the 384-line ones (Model 2 and 3) run at 640x240 progressive, stretched to 200% horizontally — 640x240 has 8:3 pixels, and the 4:3 image only fills the tube when stretched: Flycast rend.ScreenStretching=200 (300·W/4H), PCSX2 AspectRatio = Stretch, Dolphin AspectRatio=3, Supermodel -fullscreen -res=640,240 -stretch, Hypseus -x 640 -y 240 -ignore_aspect_ratio (options at the end of the line: Hypseus reads the game and the player first), and Model 2 (SM2-Emu) with aspect_mode = stretch set on every launch when the mode is wider than 4:3 (its settings file starts at 4:3).

On the cabinet Flycast opened at 640x480i: the setup saves frequency=15k, and the script only recognized 15, so every emulator fell into the 31 kHz column.

Cards without low dotclocks (Intel, NVIDIA that didn't pass the grid; see Video cards). They cannot generate the ~12 MHz pixel clock of a 640x240 mode at 15 kHz, so the Setup writes dotclock_min 25.0 to /etc/switchres.ini.

With it, fliperos-x11-run asks for the super resolution width (super_width, 2560) instead of the table's, as RetroArch does: the lines and the frequencies are the same, only the pixels are thinner.

The stretch and the sizes given to the emulators follow that width (Flycast rend.ScreenStretching=800, Supermodel -res=2560,240, Hypseus -x 2560). Otherwise Switchres would double the width by itself until it passed the minimum, and the emulators that are given the table's size would draw in part of the screen. Fightcade's per-game modes don't go through this yet.

No loading screen in Flycast. While a game loads, Flycast shows the box art and a "Loading..." window with a progress bar. FliperOS builds it with a patch (config/flycast-patches) that keeps the screen black until the game starts, as on the arcade board; a load error still shows. If a newer Flycast no longer takes the patch, the image build warns and leaves it out, and the loading screen comes back.

No text on launch. The output of X, Switchres and the emulator goes to /opt/fliperos/logs/<program>.log (the last run of each), and between the desktop and the emulator the screen stays clean; the Setup's Debug mode shows everything.

The mouse cursor only appears in emulators with a mouse UI — PCSX2 (game list, BIOS wizard), Dolphin, Flycast and Fightcade —, which hide it themselves during full-screen play; the others open with Xorg -nocursor.

GroovyMAME: what's missing. When a game stops at "System media audit failed", the reason is in /opt/fliperos/logs/groovymame.log, and groovymame -verifyroms GAME lists the missing files — BIOS and device ROMs come in zips separate from the game. A missing BIOS is brought by Setup > Games > Downloader > Download BIOS (ROMs, BIOS and artwork). By hand, everything goes in ~/roms/mame (BIOS can also go in ~/bios/mame), from the same MAME version (0.289).

PCSX2 is the official AppImage (pinned by version and sha256, extracted to /opt/pcsx2): its current code requires SDL3 and Qt 6.10, which Ubuntu 24.04 doesn't have. Dolphin is compiled from the stable version (the official Linux distribution is the Flatpak, which would bring ~1 GB of runtime).

PCSX2: performance and controls. fliperos-x11-run opens PCSX2 with mesa_glthread=true (Mesa's OpenGL thread, which takes the sending of commands to the card off the main CPU thread; to run without it, export mesa_glthread=false). Per-game tweaks go in that game's ini, ~/.config/PCSX2/gamesettings/<serial>_<crc>.ini.

PCSX2: default video. The first PCSX2.ini (config/pcsx2.ini) comes with the settings chosen on the cabinet's CRT: texture filtering Nearest (filter = 0), no bilinear smoothing on the output (linear_present_mode = 0), VSync on and used for timing, 3 software-renderer threads, and the renderer left on Automatic (Vulkan on a card that has it, OpenGL otherwise). PCSX2 warns that Nearest is an "unsafe setting"; set Bilinear (PS2) back in a game that draws wrong.

Turning on UserHacks = true there disables the fixes PCSX2's GameDB applies to that game. The panel's D-pad also works as the left analog stick (LUp/LDown/LLeft/LRight in PCSX2.ini point to the controller's D-pad when they are empty or on the keyboard): many PS2 games only move with the analog stick.

Supermodel: game choice and speed. Opened without a game (from the desktop menu), fliperos-launch opens a terminal (Alacritty) with the list of games in ~/roms/model3, by the names in Supermodel's Games.xml; Enter opens the chosen one, Esc exits.

Supermodel's bottleneck is the emulated PowerPC CPU, not the video: games on the Step 1.5 (100 MHz) and Step 2.x (166 MHz) boards were slow on an i3 (Virtua Fighter 3tb at 35 fps).

For them fliperos-x11-run passes -ppc-frequency=75, which emulates the CPU at 75 MHz (Virtua Fighter 3tb at 59 fps); Step 1.0 games (66 MHz) stay as they are. FLIPEROS_SUPERMODEL_PPC=100 changes the value, and FLIPEROS_SUPERMODEL_PPC=0 turns it off. If a game shows internal slowdown or wrong parts, raise the value for it.

RetroArch cores. Seven come compiled, to work without network: FCEUmm (NES), Snes9x, Genesis Plus GX (Mega Drive/Master System), mGBA, PCSX ReARMed (PS1), MAME 2010 and, from 0.9.1, FinalBurn Neo (the arcade core in which the versus score reaches the LED display through RetroArch, see Frontends; its games go in ~/roms/retroarch/fbneo, in FBNeo's own ROM sets).

MAME 2010 is the MAME 3D: MAME 0.139, which runs the PlayStation-based (PSX) arcade games well (ZN-1/ZN-2 — Street Fighter EX, Rival Schools —, Namco System 11/12 — Tekken, Tekken 3, Soul Calibur —, Konami GV/GQ, Taito G-NET...).

Any other can be downloaded in RetroArch itself, in Online Updater > Core Downloader (from the libretro buildbot): cores, .info files and controller profiles live in /opt/fliperos/retroarch, owned by the fliperos user, so the menu saves without root.

The factory .info files and profiles are pinned by commit (libretro-core-info, retroarch-joypad-autoconfig).

MAME 2010 is compiled without the _FORTIFY_SOURCE that Ubuntu's gcc turns on by itself (ARCHOPTS=-U_FORTIFY_SOURCE): MAME 0.139 writes 9 bytes into a char[8] when starting the H8/3002 CPU, and with the check glibc closed RetroArch (buffer overflow detected) on every Namco System 12 game (Tekken 3, Tekken Tag, Soul Calibur), System 23 and ND-1.

Running a program at 640x240

On a 15 kHz monitor, 480 lines only exist interlaced (480i), and interlacing flickers. At 640x240 progressive the program draws its 480 lines in 240: it loses half the vertical resolution, but the image is stable — that's how FliperOS runs Dreamcast, PS2, GameCube/Wii and laserdisc at 15 kHz.

The one doing this is fliperos-x11-run: it opens the program in an Xorg of its own, and Switchres creates the requested mode within the ranges of the monitor chosen in Video Setup.

Three ways, from the one-off to the permanent:

  1. On the spot, in the console (Setup > Exit to shell, on the cabinet):

sh /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run --mode 640x240@60 program [arguments]

Any mode works (WIDTHxHEIGHT@HZ, e.g. 320x240@60, 640x240@59.94, 384x224@59.64).

  1. In the desktop menu: a shortcut in ~/.local/share/applications/my-program.desktop. fliperos-launch --mode leaves the desktop, opens the program in the requested mode and returns to the desktop when it closes (with the same confirmation as the menu's emulators):

ini [Desktop Entry] Type=Application Name=My program Exec=/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-launch --mode 640x240@60 /path/to/the/program Categories=Game;

  1. Always for that program: a line in /etc/fliperos/emulator-modes.conf (command name, mode at 15 kHz, mode on the other monitors). From then on any path that goes through fliperos-x11-run — the menu, a frontend, the console without --mode — uses that mode:

myemulator 640x240@60 640x480@60

A new image doesn't overwrite this file once it has been edited.

In a frontend (Attract-Mode and others), the emulator command becomes /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run --mode 640x240@60 emulator "[romfilename]" (or without --mode, with the line in the table).

The image has to be stretched. 640x240 is an 8:3 screen in pixels, which the tube shows as 4:3. A program that "keeps the 4:3 aspect ratio" would use only half the width (320 columns) and come out squashed in the middle.

Set the program to stretch/fill the screen — for Flycast (rend.ScreenStretching = 200, via -config), Dolphin (AspectRatio = 3, via -C), PCSX2 (AspectRatio = Stretch, in PCSX2.ini from the second launch on) and Model 2 (aspect_mode = stretch) fliperos-x11-run already does it by itself. The math, for another mode: stretch by 300 × width ÷ (4 × height) percent.

GroovyMAME and RetroArch don't go through here: they switch modes by themselves on every game. In GroovyMAME, interlace 0 in /etc/fliperos/mame/mame.ini makes Switchres never choose an interlaced mode (480-line games come out at 240p).

In RetroArch, the MAME 2010 core already ships that way: CRT SwitchRes reads a switchres.ini of the core only, on top of /etc/switchres.ini, in ~/.config/retroarch/config/MAME 2010/MAME 2010.switchres.ini (from config/retroarch-switchres), with interlace 0 — a 640x480 game (Namco System 12) opens at 640x240 progressive, with the image shrunk vertically, instead of 480i.

The same file named after another core (config/<Core>/<Core>.switchres.ini) does the same for it; to go back to 480i, interlace 1 and without the # FliperOS line at the top (updates only rewrite the file that has it).

480i hacks: 640x240, filter or pure 480i

Setup > Video Setup > 480i hacks is a table with one row per program and three columns, one mark per row, like the Services table. It sets how each program shows games with more than 240 lines on a 15 kHz tube:

  • 640x240: the 640x240 progressive mode described above. No flicker, half the lines.
  • 480i filter: true 480i (the program's 640x480 line in emulator-modes.conf, which Switchres makes interlaced on the tube) with the flicker filter at that program's level.
  • 480i pure: true 480i without the filter. Sharpest, with the flicker.

Marking 480i filter on a row opens that program's level (light, medium, strong) and Preview on the screen. The preview opens a test screen at 640x480i through the same path as the emulators.

It is made to flicker: one-pixel stripes and a checkerboard, small text, thin frames and a grid, a moving line and a scrolling marquee. The arrows change the level while it is on the tube, and Enter keeps it (off makes the row pure). To choose another level for a row already on the filter, mark pure and then the filter again.

Row 640x240 means 480i means Default
Flycast, PCSX2, DuckStation, Dolphin, Hypseus Singe fliperos-x11-run opens the 640x240 line of the table the 640x480 line 640x240
Supermodel, SM2-Emu (384 lines) 640x240 at 57.524 Hz 496x384 at 57.524 Hz, interlaced 640x240
GroovyMAME interlace 0 in mame.ini: Switchres never picks an interlaced mode interlace 1 480i filter
RetroArch PS1, SNES, Mega Drive, FBNeo interlace 0 in the core's own switchres.ini interlace 1 480i filter
RetroArch MAME 2010 the same, interlace 0 (the shipped file) interlace 1 640x240
Fightcade Flycast its Flycast matches at 640x240 640x480, with or without the filter (picom, see below) 640x240
Desktop none (the resolution comes from Screen Resolution) picom with or without the filter 480i filter
Other programs none custom games and anything else in a 480i mode 480i filter

The default of each row is what that program already did. The choices are saved in fliperos.conf: - mode480_PROGRAM=240p|filter|pure, which fliperos-x11-run and fliperos-fightcade read; - deflicker_PROGRAM=light|medium|strong|off, which the filter reads; - deflicker= for the Other programs row.

PROGRAM is the command name in emulator-modes.conf, or the RetroArch core without _libretro.so. The core files are written as ~/.config/retroarch/config/<Core>/<Core>.switchres.ini without the # FliperOS header, so updates leave them alone. Everything counts from the next game.

480i flicker filter

When a game does run interlaced (480i on a 15 kHz tube), a line one pixel tall exists in only one of the two fields, so it is drawn 30 times a second and flickers. The filter blends each line with its neighbour before the frame goes out. Then every detail is in both fields: the flicker goes away and the image is a little softer. - Medium, the default, averages each line with the next one. That is RePlayOS's "Interlaced Flicker Reduction", which samples between two lines. - Light (15/70/15) keeps more detail. - Strong (a third each from the line above, the line and the line below) hides the most. - Off leaves the picture sharp, with the flicker.

The level is per program, in the 480i hacks table above.

The filter finds the level from the first of these that is set: 1. a file named by FLIPEROS_DEFLICKER_FILE, re-read every 30 frames (the preview); 2. FLIPEROS_DEFLICKER; 3. the open RetroArch core: deflicker_pcsx_rearmed=. The filter lists the loaded libraries every 30 frames to see which *_libretro.so is open. It does not wrap dlopen, which would change where each program looks for its own libraries; 4. the program: deflicker_flycast=. The name comes from FLIPEROS_DEFLICKER_APP, which fliperos-x11-run sets to the table name, or else from the process; 5. deflicker=.

It works below the emulators, so no emulator needs a shader of its own.

libfliperos-deflicker.so (config/fliperos-deflicker.c, built with the image and on each update into /usr/local/lib/fliperos) is loaded through LD_PRELOAD by fliperos-kms-run (RetroArch and the other KMS emulators) and by fliperos-x11-client (the emulators in their own Xorg).

It is not loaded into Xorg or into Switchres: fliperos-x11-run takes it out of an LD_PRELOAD inherited from a frontend, and fliperos-x11-client puts it back on the emulator alone. The library catches the frame swap (glXSwapBuffers, eglSwapBuffers, including lookups through dlsym and GetProcAddress, as SDL does).

It copies the frame, draws it back through a three-tap vertical filter and restores the GL state the emulator had. It checks the CRTC mode of every card (/dev/dri/card0 to card7, since the monitor's card is not always card0) through DRM every 30 frames: in a progressive mode (240p, 31 kHz, LCD) it does nothing.

Programs in Vulkan (PCSX2, Dolphin, DuckStation and Flycast on amdgpu) get the same filter from the implicit Vulkan layer config/fliperos-vkfps.c, on with FLIPEROS_VK_FPS=1. Before each present, in an interlaced mode, it copies the image and draws it back with the same weights and the same level. They stay on Vulkan: the layer asks the swapchain for what it needs and allocates nothing until the first filtered frame.

The layer was tested on Mesa's software driver (lavapipe) with the Khronos validation layers on (tools/vkfps-test.sh), and on the cabinet's R7 240 (RADV on amdgpu) in a real interlaced Xorg. There, one-line stripes gave the expected values at each level, and Flycast and PCSX2 ran in Vulkan with it, at the same speed with and without the filter and with no GPU errors. The level changes from the web panel with the game open. Dolphin and DuckStation have not run with it yet. The software saturation and hue of the colour calibration go through it too, for cards without a colour matrix.

The LXDE desktop draws without OpenGL, so it gets the same filter through picom with a window shader (config/fliperos-desktop-deflicker --watch, started by fliperos-lxde, at the Desktop row's level deflicker_desktop=). It checks the screen mode every 2 seconds and runs picom only while it is interlaced, so a change in Screen Resolution counts at once. Ubuntu's own picom autostart (/etc/xdg/autostart/picom.desktop, without the shader) would take the screen first, since only one compositor runs at a time: fliperos-lxde puts /etc/fliperos/xdg first in XDG_CONFIG_DIRS, where a picom.desktop with Hidden=true hides it.

The programs that cannot take the library get the same picom over their whole Xorg: fliperos-x11-client starts it for Fightcade (its lobby is Electron, and FBNeo, SNES9x and FBA are 32-bit Wine programs) and for any wine or .exe command. The Fightcade lobby (512x448, interlaced on a 15 kHz tube) uses the Other programs level; while a Flycast match is open, fliperos-fightcade switches it to the Fightcade Flycast row's level (deflicker_fightcade-flycast=). The Wine matches run at 240 lines, so there picom has nothing to filter and stays off.

For testing: - FLIPEROS_DEFLICKER=off|light|medium|strong overrides the level. - FLIPEROS_DEFLICKER_FORCE=1 filters in any mode. - FLIPEROS_DEFLICKER_DEBUG=1 prints the level it picked (with the program and the core) and the size and GL profile it filters. - tools/deflicker-test.sh builds the library and checks the result on a software-rendered Xvfb. It covers the per-program and per-core levels, the desktop shader and the preview with its arrows.

Emulators & Games

Setup > Games > Emulators & Games lists the emulators of the desktop menu (RetroArch, GroovyMAME, Flycast, PCSX2, Dolphin, Supermodel, OpenBOR, Model 2, Fightcade 2, DuckStation) and KOF Final Attack, each marked installed or not installed — the same file the desktop menu looks at (TryExec) to show the shortcut.

Next to each installed one is its version, read from files without opening the emulator (fliperos-emulators versions): the /usr/local/share/fliperos/emulator-versions the image build writes (the pinned version, or the date and commit of the master branch built that day), the AppImages' metainfo (PCSX2, DuckStation), Fightcade's VERSION.txt, the commit of the SM2-Emu source and, on an older image without the file, GroovyMAME's version text. Choosing an installed one asks GitHub what the update brings (fliperos-emulators latest NAME, a few seconds; without network it only shows the installed one): Up to date, or Update: X. For the image's emulators that is the version the next FliperOS image pins (from the repository's fliperos-mkiso.sh) or the newest master commit; Fightcade doesn't publish its version before the download.

Choosing one that is not installed installs it (config/fliperos-emulators):

  • Model 2: installs what is missing from the compiler and clones and builds SM2-Emu as the user, the same build the desktop menu does on the first click (fliperos-sm2emu --deps and --build). Chosen again when installed, it updates and rebuilds.

When a system update brings other FliperOS patches for it (config/sm2-emu-patches), the update rebuilds it by itself (fliperos-sm2emu --outdated, log in /opt/fliperos/logs/sm2-emu-build.log; if the build fails the previous one stays), so it also reaches whoever only plays from a frontend. - Fightcade 2: downloaded from its site, with Wine (Fightcade 2). - DuckStation (PlayStation): its license (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) doesn't allow it in the image, so the official AppImage is downloaded from its GitHub (the latest release) and unpacked in /opt/duckstation (config/fliperos-duckstation). Chosen again when installed, it updates.

Its games go in ~/roms/duckstation (created once it is installed; a ~/roms/psx from before is moved there), and it also lists the ones in ~/roms/retroarch/pcsx_rearmed; the BIOS is the one in ~/bios, the same as RetroArch's.

Each launch (fliperos-x11-run) sets full screen, AspectRatio = Stretch To Fill and the BIOS folder; the first one also skips its setup wizard and puts both panels on SDL (Cross/Circle/Square/Triangle on A/B/X/Y, as in PCSX2).

Its renderer stays on Automatic, which picks Vulkan where there is one (amdgpu, Intel; radeon has none, and it uses OpenGL); the 480i flicker filter works on either.

A renderer chosen in DuckStation itself stays. Esc or Select+Start opens its menu. Opened from a frontend it closes with the game (-batch); from the desktop menu it opens in Big Picture. Not seen on the CRT yet. - KOF Final Attack (Ikemen GO, 4:3): below. - The others come compiled in the image; one that is missing (an image built without it) can't be installed from here.

KOF Final Attack

The King of Fighters: Final Attack is a MUGEN game in 16:9. The 4:3 patch converts it to Ikemen GO in 4:3 at 320x240 with one sprite pixel per screen pixel, for the CRT.

The installer offers two ways to get the game:

  • Download from itch.io: the free game from its page (United By Games, a 1.4 GB zip) is downloaded, unpacked, patched and deleted by itself. It asks for 7 GB free (the zip, the unpacked game and the converted copy).
  • Use a folder I have: the folder of the original game (the one with Final Attack.exe) on a USB disk, over the network share or in the home folder (the folder above it also works).

The installer (config/fliperos-kof) downloads the patch, which downloads Ikemen GO and a portable PowerShell (the conversion scripts are PowerShell), and makes the converted copy in ~/roms/ikemen/kof-final-attack (about 2 GB; 3 GB free are asked for).

The original folder is not changed: the patch works from a Patch 4x3 folder inside it, removed at the end, and a folder that can't be written to (a read-only disk) is copied to the disk first. Installing again replaces the copy only after the new one is ready.

It opens from the desktop menu (Games > KOF Final Attack) or with fliperos-kof on a terminal, in its own Xorg at 320x240@60 (fliperos-kof in emulator-modes.conf). It is not in the frontends' game lists.

Laserdisc (Hypseus Singe)

Laserdisc games live in /opt/fliperos/roms/hypseus, which is ~/.hypseus (over the network: \\fliperos\FliperOS\roms\hypseus): the ROM in roms/<game>.zip, the laserdisc video in vldp/<game>/ with the framefile <game>.txt, and Singe games in singe/<game>/. To open on the CRT (640x240 at 15 kHz, full screen):

/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run hypseus lair     # Dragon's Lair
/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run singe timegal    # a Singe game

in the console or as a frontend command. Hypseus has no menu of its own (it needs the game name), which is why it has no shortcut in Games. It is Hypseus Singe v2.12.1 (the 3.x series requires SDL3, which Ubuntu 24.04 doesn't have), installed as the project's README says (hypseus/singe are its scripts, hypseus.bin the program).

OpenBOR

The games (.pak) go in /opt/fliperos/roms/openbor/Paks (over the network: \\fliperos\FliperOS\roms\openbor\Paks). The Games > OpenBOR menu opens OpenBOR's own menu, which lists the paks.

Old paks. OpenBOR is version 4. Many mods were made for 3.0 (build 6391) and stop as soon as they load in 4 (the log in Logs/OpenBorLog.txt says An Error Occurred, e.g. Unable to load image file '...gif': 4 no longer takes GIF sprites).

FliperOS also ships 3.0 build 6391: when 4 refuses a pak, the openbor command (config/fliperos-openbor) opens 3.0 right away and writes the pak in openbor/v3/paks.txt; when every pak is on that list, 3.0 opens directly. 3.0 runs in openbor/v3, with its own Saves and Logs (the .cfg files of one version don't work in the other) and the same Paks and ScreenShots; the controls of the Setup go to both.

To try a pak in 4 again, remove its line from paks.txt. The 3.0 binary is in the repository (config/openbor-legacy, rebuilt by tools/build-openbor-legacy.sh), so updates bring it too.

Model 2

SM2-Emu is the Sega Model 2 emulator (native, BSD). It is not compiled into the image. Games > Model 2 is always in the menu. The first click opens a terminal and asks to clone and build it (the network, once; a few minutes).

What is missing from the compiler (glslc, ninja, the X and ALSA headers the vendored SDL3 needs) is installed then, with sudo. The tree stays in ~/.local/src/sm2-emu, owned by the user.

After that, the same screen lists the .zip files in ~/roms/model2 by the names in games.xml, and Update Model 2 at the bottom pulls and rebuilds. Esc cancels and the desktop stays. A set that cannot be loaded stays on that screen, with the missing chip named in the header, instead of closing back to the desktop.

It opens in its own Xorg, full screen, in the same mode as Supermodel. At 15 kHz that is 640x240, and each launch sets aspect_mode = stretch so the frame fills the tube. VSync is on by default (vsync = true, set on the first launch); turning it off in F10 sticks.

Chips are matched by CRC32, so the zip has to be a MAME Model 2 set: one made only for the old Model 2 Emulator can be missing a chip, and that chip is named on the game list (and in /opt/fliperos/logs/sm2-emu.log).

A gamepad is read by button position through SDL, with the keyboard live beside it (5 and 6 insert coins, 1 and 2 start, arrows and Z X C V are player 1). F9 quits back to the desktop; F10 is the emulator's own settings.

It is CPU-bound on one core. FliperOS builds it with link-time optimization. The speed work below started as FliperOS patches and is part of SM2-Emu itself since 0.9.41, so they left config/sm2-emu-patches (installed to /usr/local/share/fliperos/sm2-emu-patches); a patch put there is applied before compiling.

The one there now publishes game state as outputs: the recoil, ammunition and life of the gun games for light guns, the round wins of the fighting games and the credits (DIY hardware).

Most of the time on the 2B and 2C boards went to the geometry coprocessor waiting for its next command: the Model 2C MB86235 re-ran a read of its empty input FIFO every cycle, and the Model 2B SHARC spun in a one-NOP DO ... UNTIL NOT FLAG0_IN loop.

Nothing else runs during that slice, so each repeat leaves the machine in the same state. The emulator now skips to the end of the slice instead. The i960 also fetches instructions straight from ROM and work RAM, without a virtual bus call.

The emulated machine is unchanged: a 600-frame run gives the same final state and the same audio, bit for bit, on House of the Dead, Last Bronx, Sonic Championship and Virtua Fighter 2.

On the cabinet's i3-540 (headless, one core), the speed went from 0.93× to 2.34× on House of the Dead (2C), 0.71× to 1.65× on Last Bronx (2B), 0.80× to 2.35× on Sonic Championship (2B), 0.85× to 2.84× on Fighting Vipers (2B) and 2.42× to 3.15× on Virtua Fighter 2 (2A).

The F10 settings menu stays readable on a 640x240 screen (also upstream now): the overlay no longer shrinks its font below the native 13 pixels, and the Settings window fits between the menu bar and the status bar, scrolling what does not fit.

A patch that no longer applies to a newer SM2-Emu is skipped, and the build goes on without it. When a FliperOS update brings a different set of patches, the next Games > Model 2 offers to update: it pulls SM2-Emu and rebuilds (the network, a few minutes), because a patch that left FliperOS now comes from upstream.

Since 0.9.43 the settings menu is translated, and the build also asks for the HarfBuzz and fontconfig headers. The quick check of a set before it opens uses a throwaway NVRAM, so it does not overwrite the game's saved one. OpenGL 4.3 needs a GPU that can open that context (that cabinet's R7 240 opened a 4.5 core context).

Steam and GOG

Neither ships in the image (they would take over 500 MB, and are useless without network): Setup > Games > Extras installs them. Steam: Ubuntu's steam-installer; on first launch Valve downloads the client (hundreds of MB, needs network).

GOG: there is no official Linux client; the Setup installs Heroic Games Launcher (official .deb, with a pinned hash) (GOG, Epic and Amazon; the same as on the Steam Deck), which runs Windows games with the Wine/Proton it downloads itself.

Both open inside the LXDE desktop (they are X programs), from the Games menu. Their UIs were made for larger screens: on a 15 kHz CRT at 640x480 they are cramped — on a 31 kHz monitor or an LCD they are much better.

Fightcade 2

Fightcade 2 (online arcade and console matches, with rollback) is closed-source freeware with no clear permission to redistribute — it isn't in the image or in the repository.

In Setup > Games > Frontend it shows as Fightcade 2 (not installed): when chosen, the Setup downloads the official Linux package from its website (about 160 MB, https://www.fightcade.com/download/linux), with a progress bar, to /opt/fliperos/fightcade — a user-owned folder, because Fightcade updates itself by writing there.

In the sessions table the package column is fetch:fliperos-fightcade (a program downloaded from its website, not a .deb), and the line's "binary", /opt/fliperos/fightcade/fightcade, only exists after the download. Once installed it can be the boot launcher and shows in Games > Fightcade 2 in LXDE.

/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-fightcade fetch downloads it again on top (repair): the ROMs and settings stay.

  • ROMs in ~/roms/fightcade, one folder per emulator it uses: fbneo (the .zip files of FBNeo 0.2.97.44, with neogeo.zip; console games in subfolders megadrive, nes, sms...), flycast (Naomi, Atomiswave, Dreamcast), snes9x and fc1 (the Fightcade 1 games, FB Alpha 0.2.96.74 romset).

The ROMs folders inside Fightcade become links to them (config/fliperos-roms); the folders exist even before installing. RetroArch's FBNeo core shares the fbneo folder while its own (~/roms/retroarch/fbneo) has no games. The romsets are the ones each emulator asks for, not those of the current MAME. - Arcade memory in ~/nvram/fightcade/flycast: the package brings the memory of many Naomi and Atomiswave games (emulator/flycast/data, which becomes a link to this folder). The .net files are the ones used online.

At installation, the system's Flycast (~/nvram/flycast) also gets a copy of this memory, without the .net files, for the games that have none of their own yet. What you have played stays. - Lobby screen: the lobby is a desktop page (a 1280x800 window) and doesn't fit in 240 lines, so it is the only program in the modes table that opens interlaced at 15 kHz: 512x448 (fightcade 512x448@60 in /etc/fliperos/emulator-modes.conf; wider pixels than 640x480 for bigger text, and an interlaced 15 kHz mode can't have much fewer lines), with the page scaled down in proportion to the height (--force-device-scale-factor, 100% at 600 lines, 0.75 at 448; FIGHTCADE_SCALE sets another value, and Text > Zoom In/Out, Ctrl+= and Ctrl+-, adjusts it on the fly). - Matches in the game's native resolution: on a 15 kHz tube, every FBNeo and FBA (Fightcade 1) game plays in its own original resolution, like GroovyMAME does in GroovyArcade — Street Fighter II (CPS) at 384x224 at 59.637 Hz, Neo Geo at 320x224, and so on — with a modeline made for it by Switchres.

Nothing is scaled: each pixel of the board is one pixel on the tube, with no stretching to 320 or 640 and no 16:9 window.

How it works: when FBNeo or FBA opens, fliperos-fightcade pauses it (before Wine reads its settings), takes the game's size and refresh from GroovyMAME's -listxml (the romset names are the same; the answer is cached in ~/.cache/fliperos/fightcade-modes), adds the mode to the output with Switchres and turns on the emulator's ArcadeRes option (bVidArcaderesHor in fcadefbneo.ini, bVidArcaderes in FBA's); then it lets the emulator go on, and Wine switches the screen to the game's mode.

It works the same in an online match and in Test game. Vertical games, games GroovyMAME doesn't know and widths the modeline can't make exact use the table's mode instead (fightcade-fbneo and fightcade-fc1, 320x240), at the game's own refresh rate when GroovyMAME knows it.

The screen and the emulator run at the same rate: the emulators run each game at its original speed (bForce60Hz 0, which FliperOS sets once in FBA, where it comes turned on), and the output keeps only one mode of each size, because the emulators ask Wine for a size, not for a refresh rate (CPS2 and CPS3 are both 384x224, at 59.637 and 59.599 Hz). FIGHTCADE_NATIVE=0 turns it off. - The other emulators also open in their native modes from the table: SNES9x at 256x224 at 60.0988 Hz (the console's own mode, fightcade-snes9x) and Flycast at 640x240, stretched to 200% like the system Flycast (fightcade-flycast).

fliperos-fightcade checks every second whether one of its emulators is open: if so, Switchres computes the modeline and xrandr switches the screen to its mode; when it closes, it goes back to the lobby's.

For each emulator to fill the mode, its file (created from the package's default) gets full screen at that size on each launch, following the table, and, only the first time (whatever is changed later in the emulator itself stays), the game already in full screen (bVidAutoSwitchFull 1, fullscreen = yes, SNES9x's EmulateFullscreen) and, on a tube, a 4:3 monitor instead of the package's 16:9. On the other monitors (25/31 kHz, LCD) the matches stay in the lobby's mode. - Pure picture: scanlines, bilinear filtering, shaders, motion blur, hardware gamma and SNES9x's hi-res blending are turned off once (each emulator keeps what you change later), with VSync on. - Keys: it needs a keyboard and mouse (the login, the lobby). Ctrl+W (Window > Close) closes Fightcade and returns to the menu; Alt+Tab switches between the lobby and the match's emulator and Alt+F4 closes the front window (config/openbox-fightcade.xml). - Wine: the FBNeo, SNES9x and FBA emulators are 32-bit Windows programs; they run in Wine, which isn't in the image: downloading Fightcade through the Setup installs it first (or Setup > Games > Extras), with a prefix of their own (~/.local/share/fliperos/wine-fightcade), without the Mono/Gecko window. 32-bit Wine's Direct3D draws through 32-bit OpenGL (libgl1:i386, libgl1-mesa-dri:i386, libglx-mesa0:i386, installed together with Wine): without it FBNeo stops at "Couldn't initialise DirectX9 Alternate video output".

The prefix is created the first time the lobby opens (about 15 s), not on the first match. Fightcade's Flycast (Flycast Dojo) is native, but ships as an AppImage, which asks for FUSE: the launcher exports APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN=1, and it extracts itself to /tmp on each launch and runs from there.

Every time the lobby opens, Dojo receives the system Flycast's video and control options (~/.config/flycast/emu.cfg): every rend.* and pvr.* option — no linear interpolation, Texture Filtering on Force Nearest, per-pixel transparency, resolution — except the stretch, which follows Dojo's own mode, and the whole [input] section (both controllers on ports A and B), plus the controller mapping files. Whatever you change in those options in the system Flycast also applies to Dojo.

Checked on a virtual screen with package 2.1.45: download, repair, the lobby open, FBNeo opening in Wine, Alt+Tab and Ctrl+W; and, on an Xorg that accepts new modes, the mode switch — a game requested through Fightcade's own fcade:// takes the screen to 320x240 in 1 s, Flycast to 640x240 in full screen, and the lobby comes back on close.

On the cabinet's 15 kHz tube, a CPS game in FBNeo opened in its native 384x224, pixel for pixel. Not checked: an online match (needs an account).

ROMs, BIOS and artwork

The folders in ~

ROMs in ~/roms. The collection lives in /home/fliperos/roms (\\fliperos\roms over the network), with one folder per emulator — mame, ps2, dreamcast (Flycast's discs), naomi, naomi2 and atomiswave (Flycast's arcades, one system per folder: in the frontends each one is a system, with its own platform in the Scraper), model3, dolphin, openbor/Paks, hypseus, model2 (a link to the emulator's folder in Wine) — and one per RetroArch core in ~/roms/retroarch/<core> (every core RetroArch knows: those in the core info files, ~330), each one with an _info.txt naming the system and the extensions.

fliperos-roms creates whatever is missing at every login, so a new core from the Online Updater gets a folder.

RetroArch opens its file browser in ~/roms, GroovyMAME looks in ~/roms/mame, Flycast in ~/roms/dreamcast, naomi, naomi2 and atomiswave (Dreamcast.ContentPath) and PCSX2 lists ~/roms/ps2 (if no folder has been chosen yet).

/opt/fliperos/roms became a link to ~/roms: the old paths still work, and an earlier installation had its ROMs moved there (only renamed, without overwriting anything).

BIOS, artwork and settings. Next to ~/roms, fliperos-roms creates (at every login, only what is missing, each folder with its own _info.txt):

  • ~/bios (\\fliperos\bios) — RetroArch's system folder (system_directory): the loose files in it and the subfolders the cores look for.

~/bios/dc is the one for Flycast and the Flycast core (dc_boot.bin, dc_flash.bin, naomi.zip, awbios.zip...; Dreamcast.BiosPath in emu.cfg and FLYCAST_BIOS_PATH in fliperos-x11-run), ~/bios/ps2 the one for PCSX2 (its bios folder, ~/.config/PCSX2/bios, becomes a link there, with whatever it already had) and ~/bios/mame is in GroovyMAME's rompath (BIOS and devices such as neogeo.zip and qsound.zip; they still work from ~/roms/mame).

/opt/fliperos/bios became a link to ~/bios. FliperOS ships no BIOS, but you don't have to look for them: Download BIOS brings the ones the games in your folders need. BIOS of your own can still go here. - ~/media (\\fliperos\media) — the frontends' artwork and text, one folder per type and, inside, the same folders as ~/roms (mame, model2, naomi, ps2, retroarch/snes9x...), so the art of a games folder is in the folder of the same name: snap (screenshots), preview (videos), logo (wheel), box (covers and flyers), marquee and texto (each game's description, .txt).

Setup > Games > Scraper writes there, and the frontends read from there: Attract-Mode through the emulator's artwork lines, ES-DE through MediaDirectory, Pegasus through metadata.pegasus.txt and GroovyMAME's game list through mame.ini (snapshot_directory) and ui.ini (covers_directory, flyers_directory, marquees_directory, logos_directory).

Artwork placed by hand with the ROM name (snap/mame/sf2.png for ~/roms/mame/sf2.zip) also shows in Attract-Mode, ES-DE and GroovyMAME.
