An installation from before this layout, with one folder per scraper platform (snap/arcade, snap/snes), is moved by itself the next time the launcher opens: see Adding games. - ~/config (\\fliperos\config) — links to the configuration of each installed emulator and frontend: retroarch, groovymame (/etc/fliperos/mame, with mame.ini and ui.ini), flycast, pcsx2, dolphin, supermodel, openbor (the .cfg files in ~/roms/openbor/Saves), hypseus, model2, attractmode, es-de, pegasus and skyscraper.

Each link appears once the program has created its configuration (usually after being opened once); a deleted one comes back at the next login, and one left without a target (the program was removed) goes away. - ~/nvram (\\fliperos\nvram) — what the arcade games remember without power: dip settings, credits, the scores a game saves and what it has unlocked. It has one folder per emulator and per RetroArch core that keeps this, as in ~/roms:

  • mame: GroovyMAME, one folder per game set (nvram_directory in mame.ini). To start a game from zero, delete its folder.
  • flycast: Flycast, the Naomi and Atomiswave memory of each game (kofxi.zip.nvmem, mvsc2.zip.eeprom) and the Dreamcast memory cards (vmu_save_*.bin). All systems share one folder because Flycast keeps a single one.
  • model2: SM2-Emu, with its save states in states.
  • model3: Supermodel.
  • hypseus: Hypseus Singe.
  • fightcade/flycast: the Flycast of Fightcade 2, separate from the system's. See Fightcade 2.
  • retroarch/<core>: mame2010 and fbneo from the start. Other cores of the MAME family get theirs at the login after their first game, with what they have already saved.

Each emulator still writes to its usual path, which becomes a link to its folder here, with what it had inside. An installation from before these folders has its game sets moved from the root of ~/nvram to ~/nvram/mame at the next login.

To use a file that unlocks content, close the game and put the file in the folder of its emulator with the name that emulator writes: ~/nvram/mame/tekken3/at28c16, ~/nvram/flycast/kofxi.zip.nvmem. - ~/save (\\fliperos\save) — what you save while you play, one folder per emulator: retroarch (the game saves, .srm, and the save states), mame (the save states) and ps2 (the PCSX2 memory cards).

An installation from before these folders is moved by itself at the next login: ~/.mame/nvram, ~/.mame/sta, /opt/fliperos/saves/retroarch and ~/.config/PCSX2/memcards become links to the new folders, with what they had inside, so the old paths keep working. - ~/splashscreen (\\fliperos\splashscreen) — the boot splash themes (Plymouth), one folder per theme with its .plymouth file.

The bundled ones (fliperos, fliperos-text, cogwheel, into-it and windoze95) are copied there when missing and follow the new versions of the image while left untouched (a hidden .bundled file keeps the copy's checksum); to change one, copy its folder with a new name.

Setup > System > Splash screen previews them and sets the one used at boot (Installed system). More themes: Plymouth Themes on Gnome-look.

Custom folders

Setup > Games > Folders shows the whole structure: ~/roms, ~/bios, ~/media, ~/nvram, ~/save and ~/splashscreen and, inside them, the folder of each emulator (~/roms/mame, ~/roms/model2), of each RetroArch core (~/roms/retroarch/mame2010), of each Fightcade emulator, of each BIOS subfolder and of each type of art (~/media/snap, and inside it the same folders as ~/roms: ~/media/snap/mame, ~/media/snap/model2, ~/media/snap/retroarch/mame2010).

Any of them can have its own custom folder: another folder used in its place, for when the ROMs, the art or the BIOS are on external storage (a USB disk, a second drive; the disks are mounted by themselves in /media/fliperos/<label>, where the folder browser opens).

So the MAME 2010 sets can be on one disk, the Model 2 videos on another (~/media/preview/model2) and the Model 2 sets somewhere else. Each line says whether the folder has a custom folder, or how many of the folders inside it have one. ~/config is left out: it only holds links.

  • Link this to another folder — the folder becomes a link to the chosen one and the folder used until then is renamed next to it, with old- in the name and everything in it: ~/old-roms, ~/roms/old-mame, ~/roms/retroarch/old-mame2010, ~/media/old-snap. Nothing is copied or deleted.

fliperos-roms then creates in the custom folder what is missing, and the default frontend reads the game folders again. Everything that looks in the folder — the emulators, the frontends, the Scraper, the network shares — goes through the link; the old- folders are not listed as systems.

On a folder that already has a custom folder, Change the custom folder only swaps the link. - Unlink the custom folder — the link goes away and the old- folder gets its name back; if it was deleted, a new empty folder is created. Nothing is deleted from the custom folder.

Nothing about this is saved in a file: the state is what is on the disk, so a link made or removed by hand (SSH, the desktop) counts the same.

A link you made yourself shows as a custom folder; a link whose disk is not connected shows as not found, and at login that folder is left alone while the others are created as usual; a link deleted by hand brings the old- folder back at the next login (or when Setup > Games > Folders is opened, also when an empty folder had already been created in its place).

A folder with files in it is never removed to make room: if there is already an old-mame when a custom folder is added, the current one is kept as old2-mame.

On an installation from before SM2-Emu, ~/roms/model2 was a link to the folder of the old Model 2 Emulator (Wine): the games in it move to a plain ~/roms/model2, and that folder is deleted (config/fliperos-roms). A file that could not be moved keeps the old folder, with it.

MAME ROM Cleaner

In Setup > Games > Cleaner, with the MAME CHD Cleaner. From a folder with a MAME romset, it copies (or moves) into the emulator's folder the games that pass the filters, with the parent, the BIOS and the devices they need.

It works like ROMLister: it joins the XML of the romset's MAME version with catver.ini (categories and adult games), nplayers.ini (how two people play) and Controls.dat's controls.xml (the buttons the game really uses), and filters by what the cabinet has.

For the Naomi, Naomi 2 and Atomiswave games the controls and the buttons come from Flycast's own game table instead: MAME's XML gives nearly all of them the board's generic panel (an 8-way joystick and 6 buttons), steering wheel and light gun games included, so with only joysticks marked in Controls those games no longer pass.

Where the romset is: in a folder on this machine (disk, USB stick; the menu's own folder browser: Enter opens, .. goes back, Use this folder chooses) or in a network shared folder (Windows, NAS: the Setup asks for the computer, the user and the password and lists its shared folders; it is mounted read-only at /mnt/network with cifs-utils, the password goes in a file only root can read, never on the command line, and is only kept, in /etc/fliperos/netshare.cred, if you ask — lib/netshare.sh).

That way the whole romset stays on the home computer and the cabinet takes only what it uses.

For which emulator: GroovyMAME (the XML is groovymame -listxml; games go to ~/roms/mame and BIOS and devices to ~/bios/mame, which is also in the rompath: outside the games folder they don't show as games in the frontends), Flycast (the same romset and the same XML, only its systems: Naomi, Naomi 2 and Atomiswave, each in its own folder, ~/roms/naomi, ~/roms/naomi2 and ~/roms/atomiswave, with the BIOS — naomi.zip, naomi2.zip, awbios.zip and the special ones — in ~/bios/dc and without MAME's devices, which Flycast doesn't use; a set's system is that of the first BIOS in the romof chain), SM2-Emu and Supermodel (the same romset and XML, only the Sega Model 2 games — the model2 driver, Model 2/2A/2B/2C — into ~/roms/model2, or the Model 3 games — the model3 driver — into ~/roms/model3; neither uses BIOS, and of MAME's devices only SM2-Emu's I/O boards go along, model1io.zip and model1io2.zip, which Daytona USA, Desert Tank and Virtua Cop need beside their zip and which the Model 2 game list hides; as in Flycast, MAME's emulation status doesn't filter; a folder with model2, model3 or supermodel in its name already suggests it), MAME 2010 / MAME 3D (0.139, the one in RetroArch's mame2010 core, which runs the PlayStation-based (PSX) arcade games well — ZN-1/ZN-2, Namco System 11/12, Konami GV/GQ, Taito G-NET: Tekken 3, Soul Calibur, Street Fighter EX —, so its filter starts with the PlayStation-based hardware preset; a folder with 2010 or MAME 3D in its name already suggests it; the XML ships in the image at /usr/local/share/fliperos/mame2010.xml.xz, pinned by commit and sha256; games and BIOS in ~/roms/retroarch/mame2010, where the core looks for them) or another version (an XML from mame -listxml).

What was read from the XML stays in /var/cache/fliperos (a minute with GroovyMAME's; the next read takes a second).

The parameters screen shows each parameter with its current choice; Enter opens its options — choose one (radio, (*)) or check several (checkbox, [x]: Space or button 3 toggles, a checks all, Enter confirms) — and returns to the screen with the choice made.

The parameters: games (coin-op machines only, or everything), emulation (working, with imperfect, or everything), categories (the genres of catver.ini, with how many sets each has; slot machines, pinball, computers and consoles start unchecked; Mahjong, which catver.ini keeps inside Tabletop, is a category of its own and also starts unchecked, in every preset but Everything), adult games (* Mature * in catver.ini), players, play mode (from nplayers.ini: single player, two or more alternating, two or more simultaneous, not stated), buttons (those of controls.xml when it knows the game — Metal Slug has 4 in MAME and uses 3 —, otherwise MAME's), panel controls (8, 4 and 2-way joystick, two joysticks per player, trackball, spinner, paddle, rotary, analog, pedals, light gun, keyboard, mahjong; a buttons-only game always passes; the 0.139 types, joy8way, vjoy2way, doublejoy8way, and the current ones, joy and doublejoy with ways), screen (horizontal, vertical), resolution (low, up to 288 lines, the only progressive one on a 15 kHz tube; medium; high — from the XML's pixclock/htotal or, without them, from the lines), clones (the best version of each game, parents only, or all) and the preferred region, bootlegs, prototypes, decades, vector games, games with CHD (keep, remove, or only those), board (Neo-Geo, CPS-1, CPS-2, CPS-3, the PlayStation-based ones — ZN-1/ZN-2, Namco System 10/11/12, Konami GV/GQ/573/Twinkle, Taito G-NET, from the Sony CPU in the XML — the Midway Mortal Kombat boards, Sega Model 2, Sega Model 3, Sega Naomi, Sega Naomi 2 and Sammy Atomiswave; with no board checked every board goes, except Naomi, Naomi 2 and Atomiswave, which run better in Flycast and only go to GroovyMAME when checked).

The three data files ship in the image, in /usr/local/share/fliperos/romclean (config/romclean in the repository): catver.ini 0.289 from progetto-SNAPS, nplayers.ini 0.278 from NPlayers (CC BY-SA 3.0) and controls.xml 0.141.1 from Controls.dat.

To use newer ones, or the ones that came with your romset, put them with the romset: the Setup looks first in its folder, in the one above and in the folders subfolder (the MAME UI's), and only then in the system folder, which an update rewrites.

The screen says which ones it found and their version (Data files); without one of them, its parameters don't show.

Presets: Joystick cabinet (arcade only, up to 2 players and 6 buttons, joysticks, one version of each game, no bootlegs, prototypes or adult games), Everything that works, PlayStation-based hardware (the MAME 3D games) and Everything.

Whatever the chosen games use goes along: the parent (in a merged romset the clone is in its zip), the BIOS and the devices with ROMs (romof, cloneof, device_ref), also those of the games already at the destination.

Before touching anything, the summary (how many go and their size, the free space, how many aren't in the XML, which are left alone) and the list; the copy shows its progress, each file arrives as .part and only then gets its name (an interrupted copy never passes as complete), whatever is already at the destination with the same size stays — repeating resumes where it stopped — and what arrives is owned by the owner of the emulator's folder.

Move (only from a writable folder) takes the files out of the romset and then asks whether to delete what's left; Flycast's sets never enter that list, so the same romset can be cleaned for Flycast afterwards — except in a MAME 2010 romset, which Flycast can't read: there the Naomi and Atomiswave sets the filter leaves out are deleted like the others, instead of staying in the core's folder where the frontend would list games MAME 0.139 doesn't run (config/fliperos-romclean, lib/romclean.sh).

MAME CHD Cleaner

CHDs usually come in a separate, huge collection.

This item looks at the games already in the emulator's ROM folder (~/roms/mame; for Flycast, ~/roms/naomi and ~/roms/naomi2; for MAME 2010 / MAME 3D, the core's folder), checks in the MAME XML which ones use a disk and copies, from the CHD folder (one subfolder per game, on this machine or in a network folder), only theirs, into the ROM folder (<folder>/<game>/<disk>.chd, where MAME and Flycast look for them).

A clone's disk that is the same as the parent's comes from the parent's folder; a disk without a dump doesn't count.

From each folder only the disks those games use are taken: in a merged collection the parent's folder also holds the disks of every other version, and they stay behind (the Downloader does the same, so they are never downloaded).

The screen shows how many games use CHDs, how many folders were found and their size, the free space and the list of what wasn't found; you can include the clones inside the zips (merged romset) and change the ROM folder.

The copy shows its progress and resumes where it stopped; from a writable folder you can also move (fliperos-romclean chds).

Downloader

Setup > Games > Downloader gathers what downloads games: ROM/CHD MAME torrent, Free games and Download BIOS.

The torrent screen, in order: the Filter (the same parameters screen as the ROM Cleaner, for GroovyMAME, Flycast, SM2-Emu, Supermodel or MAME 2010 / MAME 3D (the PlayStation-based arcade games), saved apart, only for the torrent; until one is saved, the Joystick cabinet preset), the ROM set magnet link (required), the CHD set magnet link (optional; both come filled in with the links shipped in the image, MAME 0.289 ROMs and MAME 0.288 CHDs, both merged, from /usr/local/share/fliperos/downloader-magnets: Enter uses them, or paste another; under the field, Web browser opens a browser to find a magnet link and .torrent file picks a .torrent on a USB disk, the network share or the home folder), the Download folder (the folder browser; by default the emulator's, ~/roms/mame with the BIOS in ~/bios/mame — elsewhere the BIOS go with the games; for Flycast, the folder of naomi, naomi2 and atomiswave) and Start the download, which needs the ROM link — the CHDs are those of the games the romset brings.

It downloads only what the filter chooses — the games, with their parents, BIOS and devices, and the CHDs of those games — never the whole set; the Setup says so when a link is pasted. Before marking anything, Start checks that the whole download fits on the disk; if not, it says how much is needed and how much is free.

Where the sets are in the torrent is found from the file list: at its top or in any subfolder (MAME 0.289/ROMs (merged)/, next to Software Lists, readmes or extras) — the folder with the most .zip/.7z sets, or, for CHDs, with the most <game>/<disk>.chd folders; the Setup shows which folder and how many sets, and the rest of the torrent is never downloaded.

A torrent without any (the CHD link pasted as the romset) is refused. Transmission does the download: its own transmission-daemon (fliperos-transmission.service, as the fliperos user, at low CPU and disk priority, RPC only on 127.0.0.1:9092; the stock transmission-daemon.service is masked).

It is set for speed (fliperos-downloader config, at each start): up to 150 peers per torrent and 500 in all (Transmission's default, 50 and 200, left most of a big romset's peers out), a 64 MB write cache, no speed limit, DHT, PEX, local peer discovery, µTP and UPnP on, and a stalled torrent leaves the queue after 5 minutes. The disk priority is the lowest normal one (best-effort 7): the "idle" class it had only wrote while nothing else read the disk, and the frontend's videos read it all the time.

It never starts at boot: the Setup (or the web panel) starts it when a link is added or a download (or an art pack) is started, and it quits by itself when its last torrent ends. A download stopped by a shutdown shows as stopped and goes on with Start the download.

The link is added running (paused, Transmission doesn't look for peers) and, as soon as the file list arrives, stopped with no file marked; the list goes through fliperos-romclean (scan --names, chds --names --with), only the chosen files are marked, and what is already in the emulator folders isn't downloaded again.

The terminal shows a progress bar (size, peers, speed, time left); any key returns to the menu and the download goes on, even with a game open. When a torrent ends, each file goes to the download folder (the BIOS to ~/bios/mame, the CHDs in <game>/) and the torrent leaves Transmission without seeding.

When the filter changes (or a new MAME version), with links set up, the Setup says how many ROMs and CHDs it adds (and their size) and how many it deletes, with the list, and asks before applying; only what the downloader brought is ever deleted, never files put there by hand.

Removing a link can also delete what it brought. A parent, BIOS or device that a game still in the folders uses (the ROM folders of the filter and GroovyMAME's rompath) is never deleted: neogeo.zip stays while there is an MVS game, even one copied by the ROM Cleaner (fliperos-romclean uses).

State in /var/lib/fliperos/downloader (config/fliperos-downloader, lib/downloader.sh). Afterwards, AttractPlus > ROM List updates the game names in the frontend.

Free games

Setup > Games > Downloader > Free games downloads open-source homebrew into the RetroArch core folders (~/roms/retroarch/<core>), so the frontends don't start empty and to test video, sound and controls without anyone's ROMs: the 240p Test Suites for NES, Game Boy and GBA, Thwaite, Nova the Squirrel, Libbet and the Magic Floor and µCity.

Each file comes from the project's own releases page, with a pinned sha256 and the license in the list (GPL and zlib, checked in each one's repository); only those for installed cores, and what is already there stays. The image ships nobody's ROMs or BIOS (config/fliperos-freeroms, lib/freeroms.sh).

Download BIOS

Setup > Games > Downloader > Download BIOS brings the BIOS that the games in your folders need and ~/bios doesn't have yet. It looks at every folder of ~/roms that has files:

  • RetroArch cores (~/roms/retroarch/<core>): the firmware listed in the core's own .info file (PCSX ReARMed asks for scph5501.bin, Flycast for dc/dc_boot.bin, FBNeo for fbneo/neogeo.zip), into ~/bios at the path the core asks for. The optional ones come too: without them a core falls back to an imitation BIOS (HLE) or doesn't open part of its games (Sega CD, Famicom Disk System);
  • MAME sets (~/roms/mame, naomi, naomi2, atomiswave, and the arcade cores): the BIOS and devices those sets use, from the MAME XML (fliperos-romclean uses): neogeo.zip, qsound.zip… go to ~/bios/mame, the Naomi and Atomiswave ones to ~/bios/dc, FBNeo's to ~/bios/fbneo, and those of the other MAME cores next to their games;
  • PCSX2 (~/roms/ps2) and Flycast (~/roms/dreamcast): their BIOS in ~/bios/ps2 and ~/bios/dc.

The files come from a reference BIOS pack, the Batocera v36 full BIOS pack on the Internet Archive (/usr/local/share/fliperos/bios-pack).

Its torrent is only read, never downloaded: it gives the archive item and the name of its 1.1 GB .zip, and the Internet Archive serves each file inside that .zip on its own, so only the missing BIOS are downloaded (on the cabinet, 13 files and 22.6 MB for PS1, Naomi, Atomiswave and Neo-Geo games).

A BIOS already in place, also one put next to the games, is never downloaded again, and nothing is overwritten. Files over 64 MB (the DSi NAND, the PS3 and Vita updates) are left out.

The check also runs by itself each time the FliperOS menu opens, in the background (fliperos-setup --bios-check), so a game folder copied over the network gets its BIOS without anyone asking.

It only runs when a folder of ~/roms or ~/bios changed since the last check (a deleted BIOS comes back); without network it tries again 10 minutes later. Check when the menu opens turns it off (bios_auto=off in fliperos.conf).

The screen shows how many were downloaded, how many were already there and which ones aren't in the pack, which you put in ~/bios yourself. The pack is Batocera 36's: a newer MAME may want a BIOS file it doesn't have yet. State in /var/lib/fliperos/bios (config/fliperos-bios, lib/downloader.sh).

Scraper

Setup > Games > Scraper has four items: Scrape the games, Scrape with a site (Skyscraper), Scraper provider and Art packs by torrent.

Scrape the games is the FliperOS scraper, the same one the FliperOS frontend runs by itself in the background. For every game in the folders (or one folder), it fetches only what the game still lacks, with no account: - arcade: the information, screenshot, flyer, marquee and logo from the Arcade Database; - consoles: the cover and screenshot from libretro-thumbnails; - logos and videos: the art packs below, by torrent; a pack kept in one .zip per letter (the MAME videos) is fetched one file at a time from inside the zip over HTTP instead of whole letters.

A bar shows each game and how many are left; at the end it says how many games still lack something no source has. It is gui/fliperos-scrape, run as the player; while it runs, the frontend's own scrape waits. The games it tried are recorded in ~/.local/share/fliperos/scrape-state.json, so the frontend does not try them again for 30 days.

Scrape with a site is the Skyscraper scraper below: the site chosen in Scraper provider (ScreenScraper with your account, for instance), and the game lists of Attract-Mode Plus, ES-DE and Pegasus.

Scraper provider picks where the art and the information come from, and keeps the account of the providers that ask for one, the way ES-DE and Arcadeflow keep the ScreenScraper login in their options:

Provider Has Account
ScreenScraper every system user and password, optional (a free account raises the daily limits)
TheGamesDB consoles and computers none
ArcadeDB arcade games none
progetto-SNAPS arcade screenshots only none
MobyGames every system your API key, required
IGDB consoles and computers a Twitch client ID and secret, required
OpenRetro Amiga and old computers none

The choice is saved in fliperos.conf (scraper_source) and the account in /etc/fliperos/scraper-accounts, a file only root reads; it is what Skyscraper gets in -u. A provider that only works with an account doesn't scrape until it has one.

Art packs by torrent brings logos and videos from torrents, without an account and without the per-day limits of the providers. The screen comes filled with packs from the Internet Archive: logos and videos for MAME (also used by the RetroArch arcade cores), Naomi and Naomi 2, Atomiswave, Model 2 and Model 3.

Each pack belongs to some folders of ~/roms, and it only downloads when those folders have ROMs, and only the files of the games that are in them: the torrent's file list is compared with the names of the ROMs, and the rest of the torrent is never downloaded. A game that already has that art in ~/media is skipped.

Where a pack keeps the files inside .zip archives by letter (the MAME videos), only the archives of the letters your games start with are downloaded, and only your games' files come out of them.

The download is done by the same Transmission service as the Downloader, in the background, even with a game open; when a torrent ends, each file goes to ~/media/logo/<games folder> or ~/media/preview/<games folder> with the name of the ROM, and the torrent is removed.

Add a torrent takes a pack of your own (a magnet link or the address of a .torrent, the kind of art and the folder it is for), and the link of a pack that comes filled in can be changed. The packs are in config/fliperos-media-torrents and the program is /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-mediapacks.

Scrape with a site — covers, screenshots, logos, videos and information for each ROM, with Skyscraper (the same one GroovyArcade packages), from the one chosen in Scraper provider.

What to fetch is a checklist: screenshots (snap), logos, covers (box), marquees, descriptions (texto) and videos (preview, unchecked at first: they take much more space).

Skyscraper only downloads the checked types (--flags noscreenshots,nocovers,nowheels,nomarquees and videos) and only exports those; the choice is remembered. An artwork type the folder didn't have yet makes it fetch again the games already in the cache (--refresh): without that Skyscraper doesn't go back to them.

The folders with games (each one's _info.txt doesn't count) that FliperOS knows how to open are included: ~/roms/mame, dreamcast, ps2, dolphin and the RetroArch core folders (~/roms/retroarch/<core>, by the platform of the systemid in the core's .info).

Artwork and text go to ~/media/<type>/<system> (ROMs, BIOS and artwork): Skyscraper writes each type into a subfolder with a fixed name (screenshots, covers, wheels, marquees, videos), and for it ~/media/.skyscraper/<system> has links with those names to snap, box, logo, marquee and preview; the descriptions come out of the generated list into ~/media/texto.

The list goes to the frontend. With GroovyMAME as the default launcher, the MAME folder only gets the artwork: mame.ini and ui.ini already look in ~/media/<type>/arcade (the first snapshot_directory is still F12's).

In ES-DE (FliperOS's EmulationStation) the list goes to ~/ES-DE/gamelists/<system> (Skyscraper's esde format, relative paths) and MediaDirectory is ~/media/.es-de, with one link per ES-DE type (screenshots, covers, marquees = logo, videos) into ~/media.

Earlier artwork (~/.mame/scraped/mame, ~/.attract/scraped/<folder>, <ROM folder>/media) moves to ~/media in tools/cabinet-update.sh and when the folder is scraped.

The images come out each one as it came (screenshot, cover, logo, marquee; the Setup's artwork.xml), and not composited on top of each other as in Skyscraper's default.

Clones: in the MAME folder the Setup asks whether to also fetch the clones of the existing games (groovymame -listclones: mvscu, mvscj...), which in a merged romset are inside the parent's zip and have no file — the scraped folder becomes one of references in ~/.cache/fliperos-scraper (links to the ROMs and a small file per clone).

Resuming: Skyscraper only writes its cache at the end of each run, so the games go in batches of 20 (--includefrom) and the work is recorded in /var/lib/fliperos/scraper (the folders still to do, the files of each one already saved, the source and the account, readable by root only); if the machine was switched off or the Setup closed midway, Setup > Games > Scraper offers to resume from the batch where it stopped.

In Attract-Mode Plus (the default launcher's, or with no frontend chosen, if it is installed) the Setup creates, like GroovyArcade's efc.sh, any missing emulator in ~/.attract/emulators — with the command that opens the game (fliperos-x11-run groovymame [name], fliperos-kms-run retroarch -L <core>, fliperos-x11-run flycast/pcsx2/dolphin-emu) and the artwork in ~/media/<type>/<system> — and its display in attract.cfg (AdvanceMenu theme); Skyscraper writes the romlist to ~/.attract/romlists and the descriptions to ~/.attract/scraper/<emulator>/overview, a link to ~/media/texto/<system>.

In Pegasus, metadata.pegasus.txt lives in the ROM folder itself, pointing to the artwork in ~/media. What already exists (a display, an emulator changed in Attract-Mode) isn't rewritten — the emulator created by the Setup is redone, so the artwork moves to ~/media —, and a system that fails doesn't stop the others.

progetto-SNAPS (no account) is one of the providers, for the arcade folders only (MAME, Naomi, Atomiswave...): the in-game screenshots of progetto-SNAPS by AntoPISA, the same set GroovyArcade users know.

/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-snaps follows the site's guidelines: the pack names come from its Snapshots page and each pack goes through its download link, one at a time; the monthly update (pS_snap_upd_N.zip) wins over the full set (pS_snap_fullset_N.zip, about 520 MB, with the images in a 7z).

The packs stay in /var/cache/fliperos/snaps (about 1 GB with the 7z unpacked), so scraping another folder later downloads nothing again, and a newer version replaces the older one.

Only the screenshots of the games in the folder are copied, to ~/media/snap/<games folder> (~/media/snap/mame); one that is already there stays.

The site doesn't host logos, covers or descriptions, so those still come from the other sources; the Attract-Mode Plus romlist and the ES-DE/Pegasus lists are refreshed the same way.

Adding games

A step-by-step guide to putting games, names and artwork into Attract-Mode Plus and EmulationStation (ES-DE), to the emulator command lines (KMS or X11) and to adding a new emulator that opens from any frontend. The folders themselves are described in ROMs, BIOS and artwork; the automatic artwork download is in Scraper.

Copy the games

Each emulator has its folder in ~/roms (/home/fliperos/roms; over the network, \\fliperos\roms). Copy the files as they come: MAME sets stay zipped and are never renamed (the frontends and MAME find a game by its set name, sf2ce.zip).

Folder What goes in it Opens in
mame MAME sets (.zip, .7z) and their CHD folders GroovyMAME
naomi, naomi2, atomiswave MAME sets of these systems Flycast
model3 MAME sets of Model 3 Supermodel
model2 MAME sets of Model 2 SM2-Emu
dreamcast .gdi, .cdi, .chd Flycast
ps2 .iso, .chd, .cso PCSX2
dolphin GameCube and Wii (.iso, .rvz, .wbfs) Dolphin
retroarch/<core> Whatever that core opens (the _info.txt in each folder lists the extensions) RetroArch

BIOS don't need to be looked for: Setup > Games > Downloader > Download BIOS brings the ones the games in your folders lack, and the menu checks for missing ones each time it opens (ROMs, BIOS and artwork).

BIOS files of your own go in ~/bios (\\fliperos\bios): ~/bios/mame for MAME (neogeo.zip, qsound.zip), ~/bios/dc for Flycast (naomi.zip, awbios.zip, dc_boot.bin), ~/bios/ps2 for PCSX2 and the folder itself for the RetroArch cores. A BIOS left in a games folder shows up as a game in the frontend.

Make the frontend see the folder

A folder with games becomes a system in the frontend when you pick the frontend in Setup > Games > Frontend. For ES-DE and Pegasus, pick it again (even if it already is the default) every time a folder gets its first games: the Setup only creates what is missing, so nothing you changed is lost. Attract-Mode Plus gets the new folder by itself the next time it opens.

  • Attract-Mode Plus: for each folder the Setup creates an emulator (~/.attract/emulators/<name>.cfg, with the command that opens the game and where the artwork is), a display in ~/.attract/config/displays.cfg (~/.attract/attract.cfg before Attract-Mode Plus first runs), and a game list (romlist, ~/.attract/romlists/<name>.txt) built from the files in the folder.

The display uses the Arcadeflow theme, the default in FliperOS.

It doesn't come with FliperOS, because its repository has no license that allows redistributing it: when you pick Attract-Mode Plus, Setup > Games > Frontend downloads version 17.7 from its GitHub (55 MB) to ~/.attract/layouts/Arcadeflow.

Every display is on Arcadeflow by default: each time the launcher opens, the displays on Basic or BasicPlus (the layout Attract-Mode Plus gives the displays it creates itself) move to it; a display you put on another layout (Attract-Mode's menu, Tab > Displays) stays there.

The theme keeps its options and its game database in its own folder; FliperOS turns off one of its options, the check for new versions (it waits for an answer on the keyboard).

The select button keeps the theme's default: the first press opens the context menu over the game (information, favourite, tags) and the second one opens the game; to open the game at the first press, set Context menu button: None in the theme's options.

Clones are grouped, Attract-Mode Plus's default (Group Clones, in Tab > General): the list has one tile per family, and opening a game that has clones shows the list of its clones — pick one to play, or press back to return to the whole list.

FliperOS adds one line to the theme for this: Attract-Mode Plus swaps the list for the clones instead of starting the game, and the theme, which had already cleared the screen for the game, was left showing only its background, with the clone list there but unseen until another press.

To have every clone as a tile of its own, turn Group Clones off. FliperOS also turns off the theme's Game not available indicator: it marks with a red cross, and refuses to open, a game with no file of its own in the folder, and in a merged romset a clone lives inside its parent's zip (GroovyMAME opens it by name).

Arcadeflow is drawn for high-resolution screens and uses shaders on every frame: on a 15 kHz tube (320x240) turn on Small screen and Low Spec mode in its options, or go back to Basic if the text is too small.

On a 15 kHz tube in a wide-pixel mode such as 640x240 (8:3 in pixels, shown as 4:3 by the tube) FliperOS makes the theme draw in 4:3 at the same height (320x240, the theme's own Resolution W x H option) and stretch to the width of the mode (200%), like the emulators do; left alone it arranges itself for an 8:3 screen and everything comes out twice as wide.

This is set each time the launcher opens, from the mode the console is in, and undone in a 4:3 mode; a size you typed there yourself in a 4:3 mode is kept.

Without Arcadeflow (no network at that moment; pick the frontend again to retry) the display uses the Basic layout, FliperOS's version of the one that comes with Attract-Mode Plus (config/attractplus-layouts/Basic, in ~/.attract/layouts, where it wins over the packaged one): the same look, drawn at the screen's real resolution with slightly larger letters.

The original draws at a fixed 640x480 and Attract-Mode scales it, which blurs the text at 320x240 and 640x240.

Every display also gets the default filters: All Games, Most Played (the 25 most played), by genre (Category, from catver.ini: Driving, Fighting, Shooting...), by manufacturer (© Capcom, © SNK, © Sega...) and by release year.

The Setup adds them to any display that has no filter, including the ones Attract-Mode itself created; a display with filters of its own is left as it is. - ES-DE: the Setup writes every system to ~/ES-DE/custom_systems/es_systems.xml (folder, extensions, command and theme). ES-DE reads the folders itself each time it starts.

New games in a folder that is already a system. ES-DE finds them the next time it opens (or right away with Main menu > Utilities > Rescan ROM directory). Attract-Mode Plus doesn't look at the folder: its list is the romlist.

FliperOS brings the romlist up to date each time the launcher opens (and in Setup > Games > Frontend, Folders and AttractPlus ROM List): a file with one of the emulator's extensions that is not in the list goes in, under its file name, and a game whose file is gone leaves; the other lines stay as they are, with the title and year the Scraper wrote.

A folder with its first games gets its emulator and display the same way. A file still being copied (.part) only enters when the copy ends.

The exception is an arcade list with real game names: it leaves the BIOS sets out and has the clones that live inside the parent's zip, so it is only redone in Setup > Games > AttractPlus ROM List. To rebuild a list yourself:

  • Setup > Games > AttractPlus ROM List (arcade folders, below);
  • Setup > Games > Scraper (any folder; it also fetches the artwork);
  • in Attract-Mode itself: Tab opens the configuration, Emulators > (the emulator) > Generate Collection/Rom List;
  • or delete ~/.attract/romlists/<name>.txt and pick the frontend again in Setup > Games > Frontend.

Real game names

A game list made only from the files shows the file name: mvsc2u instead of Marvel Vs. Capcom 2 New Age of Heroes.

Attract-Mode Plus. The name is the second field of each line in the romlist (Name;Title;Emulator;CloneOf;Year;Manufacturer;...). Two ways to fill it in:

  • Setup > Games > AttractPlus ROM List ? for the arcade folders (mame, naomi, naomi2, atomiswave, model2, model3 and the RetroArch arcade cores: mame2010, mame2003_plus, fbneo, hbmame...).

No internet needed: the name, year, manufacturer, players, controls and emulation status of each game come from GroovyMAME's game list (groovymame -listxml), and from the MAME 0.139 list for the mame2010 folder. Clones and bootlegs come in with their own names and with their parent in the CloneOf field.

In the MAME folder the list also gets the clones that only exist inside the parent's zip (a merged romset), because GroovyMAME opens a game by its name and finds the clone there. The other emulators open a file, so in their folders only the clones that have their own file are listed.

A set that isn't in MAME's list keeps its file name, and BIOS sets are left out. The category comes from the catver.ini that ships in the image (/usr/local/share/fliperos/romclean), or from one of your own in ~/roms/mame. The Setup also creates an Arcade display with all those folders together. The first run reads GroovyMAME's list (about a minute); the next ones take a second. - Setup > Games > Scraper ? for every folder, with names and descriptions from ScreenScraper, ArcadeDB or TheGamesDB, plus the artwork.

Each of the two rewrites the list of the folders it works on, so whichever ran last wins. The artwork is found by the set name, so it is kept either way.

Setup > Games > AttractPlus ROM List also goes through every other folder with games (consoles, the arcade folders you left unmarked) and gives it the emulator, the display and the game list it is missing, so a system whose display was removed comes back.

At the end it cleans up: a romlist with no game in it is deleted, with the displays that show it, and so is an emulator left without a romlist.

Those are mostly the ones Attract-Mode Plus creates by itself on its first run, one for each program it finds (mame, flycast, pcsx2...), pointing at its own ROM folders instead of FliperOS's — empty displays next to the Setup's.

Arcadeflow's collections (AF ...) are left alone, and nothing is removed while Attract-Mode Plus is open.

Arcadeflow keeps its own copy of the list. The theme reads the title, year, manufacturer and genre of each game once, into ~/.attract/romlists/<name>.db1, and after that only adds the games that are missing from it.

So when a romlist is rebuilt (by the ROM List, the Scraper or Attract-Mode), FliperOS empties the .db1 that is older than its romlist, before Attract-Mode Plus opens: the theme reads the whole list again the next time the display opens.

Favourites, play counts and last played (<name>.db2) are kept; what Arcadeflow's own scraper had fetched for that list is not.

A game scraped inside Arcadeflow keeps its romlist data. The theme's scraper replaces the title, year, manufacturer, genre, players, rotation, control and button count with what ArcadeDB answers, and writes them empty when it gets no answer — the game then shows no name and no players/control/buttons indicators at the top.

Before Attract-Mode Plus opens, FliperOS puts the romlist's value back into every one of those fields that is empty in the .db1; what the scraper did fill is kept.

The logo of each display. In its displays menu Arcadeflow shows the logo and the picture of a system (system_images, system_bgs) when the display's name is one of the names it knows for that system, listed in the theme's data_systems.txt.

It knows Model 2, Naomi and MAME, but not Supermodel or Arcade (various) (MAME 2010 (0.139)), the names FliperOS gives the displays of those folders.

Before Attract-Mode Plus opens, FliperOS adds the name of each of its displays to the system it belongs to in that file (fliperos-arcadeflow systems): Sega Model 3 for the Supermodel folder, GameCube for Dolphin, FBNeo for its core, and for the other cores the platform of the folder (PlayStation, SNES...).

A RetroArch MAME core is a system of its own, named after the core without its version, so the MAME 2010 display is MAME 2010 and not a second MAME next to GroovyMAME's.

In the menu the logo of a system is a glyph of the theme's font (fonts/font_Roboto-Allcaps-EXT4X.ttf), numbered by the position of the system in data_systems.txt; a system added at the end has no glyph and showed as a dot.

So FliperOS adds one to the font: the MAME logo with "2010" beside it, tilted (the theme's own font is kept next to it as .fliperos-orig). Its picture is the theme's MAME one with "2010" written across it.

Both are made on the machine by fliperos-arcadeflow-art, with fontTools and Pillow, which are installed from apt together with the theme; without fontTools the display stays a plain MAME, and without Pillow it uses the plain MAME picture.

What FliperOS added is listed in the theme's fliperos_systems.txt and taken out again when a display goes away. The logo under each game's title is another thing: it follows the system line of the emulator's .cfg, which is arcade in every arcade folder.

ES-DE. In systems with the arcade platform (mame, model2, model3 and the RetroArch MAME cores), ES-DE already shows the full name of each MAME set from its own list.

Everything else shows the file name until it is scraped: Setup > Games > Scraper writes the names, descriptions and artwork to ~/ES-DE/gamelists/<system>/gamelist.xml. ES-DE's own scraper (Main menu > Scraper) also works and saves to the same places.

Artwork

All artwork lives in ~/media (\\fliperos\media), one folder per type and, inside it, the same folders as ~/roms.

The file name is the ROM name without the extension: the screenshot of ~/roms/mame/sf2.zip is ~/media/snap/mame/sf2.png, and the video of ~/roms/retroarch/mame2010/tekken3.zip is ~/media/preview/retroarch/mame2010/tekken3.mp4.

Setup > Games > Scraper fills these folders, but you can also copy images and videos there yourself (from a MAME artwork pack, for example).

~/media folder What it holds Attract-Mode Plus (artwork line) ES-DE
snap Screenshots (.png) snap screenshot
preview Videos (.mp4) snap (videos sit in the same line) video
logo Logos, wheel art (.png) wheel marquee
box Covers and flyers (.png) flyer cover
marquee Cabinet marquees (.png) marquee ?
texto Descriptions (.txt) overview (~/.attract/scraper/<emulator>/overview is a link here) ? (descriptions come from gamelist.xml)

Each games folder has its own art folder in every type, with the same name: mame, model2, model3, naomi, naomi2, atomiswave, dreamcast, ps2, dolphin and retroarch/<core>. So two folders with the same game (Daytona USA in mame and in model2) can each have their own video, and each art folder can be on another disk (Setup > Games > Folders).

Shared arcade artwork. In Attract-Mode Plus, the other arcade folders (Model 2, Model 3, Naomi, Atomiswave, the MAME and FBNeo cores...) look in their own folder first and then in the mame one: the artwork of a set you have for MAME also shows for the same set in the other emulators. You can see it in the emulator's .cfg:

artwork    snap            /home/fliperos/media/snap/naomi;/home/fliperos/media/preview/naomi;/home/fliperos/media/snap/mame;/home/fliperos/media/preview/mame
artwork    wheel           /home/fliperos/media/logo/naomi;/home/fliperos/media/logo/mame

Coming from the layout by platform. Before, ~/media/<type> had one folder per scraper platform (arcade, snes, psx...), shared by every games folder of that platform.

FliperOS moves them the next time the launcher opens: arcade goes to mame, and the folder of another platform to the first games folder of that platform (snes to retroarch/snes9x). The other games folders of the platform get the art of the games they have (a hard link, no extra disk space).

A platform folder that was a custom folder becomes the same custom folder in each of its games folders, and nothing is written inside a custom folder. A platform folder whose games folder is not there at that moment (a disk that is off) waits for the next time.

ES-DE reads the artwork from ~/media/.es-de/<system>/<type>, where each type is a link to the right folder in ~/media. It only looks in the system's own folder.

Emulator command lines: KMS or X11

What KMS and X11 are

Linux has two ways to put a program on the screen, and FliperOS uses both.

  • KMS (Kernel Mode Setting, through the kernel's DRM driver) means the program draws directly on the video card, without any window system. It is the lightest and fastest path, with the least input lag, and the program changes the video mode itself.

RetroArch (with its CRT SwitchRes, one mode per game) and the frontends (Attract-Mode Plus, ES-DE, Pegasus) run like this. The FliperOS wrapper is fliperos-kms-run: it starts the program on the console and, for RetroArch, adds the FliperOS settings (video driver, button mapping) on top of the user's. - X11 (Xorg, the classic Linux window system) is for programs that only know how to open a window: Flycast, PCSX2, Dolphin, Supermodel, SM2-Emu (Model 2), Hypseus, GroovyMAME.

The FliperOS wrapper is fliperos-x11-run: it starts an Xorg just for that program, has Switchres create a video mode for the monitor chosen in Video Setup (640x240 at 15 kHz for the 480-line systems, so nothing flickers), opens the program full screen and closes Xorg when the program exits. Nothing else runs in that X: no desktop, no panel.

Rule of thumb: RetroArch, in KMS; any other emulator, in X11. If a program says "Cannot open display" or doesn't start in KMS, it needs X11. Both wrappers must be started from the console, as the frontends do: inside the LXDE desktop (which already is an X session), run the emulator directly.

The commands, as a frontend calls them:

# KMS: RetroArch with a core
/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-kms-run retroarch -L /opt/fliperos/retroarch/cores/fbneo_libretro.so "/home/fliperos/roms/retroarch/fbneo/sf2.zip"

# X11: the mode comes from /etc/fliperos/emulator-modes.conf
/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run flycast "/home/fliperos/roms/naomi/mvsc2.zip"

# X11 with a mode chosen on the spot (width x height @ Hz)
/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run --mode 640x240@60 pcsx2 "/home/fliperos/roms/ps2/game.iso"

# GroovyMAME opens a game by its set name
/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run groovymame sf2

The X11 video mode of each program is in /etc/fliperos/emulator-modes.conf (one column for 15 kHz, another for 25/31 kHz and LCD; a program not in the table gets 320x240@60). Add a line there for a new program instead of repeating --mode everywhere. More on the modes in Emulators.

Attract-Mode Plus

Each emulator is a file in ~/.attract/emulators/<name>.cfg (in the cabinet's ~/config/attractmode). The lines that matter:

executable           /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run
args                 supermodel "[romfilename]"
workdir              $HOME
rompath              /home/fliperos/roms/model3/
romext               .zip
system               arcade

[romfilename] is the full path of the game file (keep it in quotes: file names have spaces), and [name] is the name without the extension, for emulators that open a game by name (GroovyMAME, Model 2). For a KMS program, executable is /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-kms-run and args starts with the program (retroarch -L <core> "[romfilename]").

To add an emulator of your own: copy a .cfg from the folder with a new name, change those lines, give it a romlist (Emulators > (the emulator) > Generate Collection/Rom List in Attract-Mode's configuration, or Setup > Games > AttractPlus ROM List for an arcade folder) and a display (Displays > Add new display, with that romlist).

The Setup rewrites the .cfg files it created itself (the ones whose first line is # Criado pelo FliperOS Setup), to keep the artwork paths up to date: to change the command of one of them and keep your change, delete that first line.

ES-DE

Each system is a <system> block in ~/ES-DE/custom_systems/es_systems.xml:

<system>
  <name>model3</name>
  <fullname>Supermodel</fullname>
  <path>/home/fliperos/roms/model3</path>
  <extension>.zip .ZIP</extension>
  <command label="Supermodel">/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run supermodel %ROM%</command>
  <platform>arcade</platform>
  <theme>model3</theme>
</system>

<platform> is what the scraper searches as (Model 2, Model 3 and the MAME cores are MAME sets, so arcade); <theme> is the system's folder in the ES-DE themes, which gives it its logo and background. The Setup gives Model 2 and Model 3 their own (model2, model3), the RetroArch MAME cores (mame2010, mame2003_plus...) the MAME one (mame), FBNeo fbneo, and the GroovyMAME folder arcade.

%ROM% is the game's path (ES-DE adds the quotes) and %BASENAME% the name without the extension (/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run groovymame %BASENAME%). A system can have more than one <command> with different labels: ES-DE lets you pick one per game (Edit this game's metadata > Alternative emulator). <platform> decides the scraper's platform and <theme> the system's look.

Setup > Games > Frontend rewrites the whole es_systems.xml every time ES-DE is picked, so a system added by hand disappears. Keep a copy of your blocks and paste them back after using Setup > Games > Frontend.

Custom games

The quick way for a game or program that is not a ROM (a PC game through Wine, a native Linux game, your own emulator with one game, a script): Setup > Games > Custom games.

Each entry has a group, a name, the command (as you would type it in a terminal) and the video mode: 240p (640x240), 480i (640x480, interlaced on a 15 kHz monitor) or any WIDTHxHEIGHT@HZ.

The frontends show each group as a system and each entry as a game in it, and the entry can also be the game that opens at boot (Setup > Games > Frontend).

Behind it, a group is the folder ~/roms/custom/<group> and each entry a script <name>.sh in it, which opens the command in its own Xorg in that mode (fliperos-x11-run --mode). The mode and the command are also in the script's first lines, which is what the Setup reads to edit it.

A .sh you put in one of those folders by hand shows up in the frontends too (with the mode and the command empty in the Setup). The Scraper skips these folders: there is no art to look up for a script.

Adding a new emulator

FliperOS sets up the emulators it ships by itself. For any other emulator (an AppImage, a package, something you built), there are four steps. If you follow them, the same command works in Attract-Mode Plus, ES-DE, Pegasus or the console.

Step 1: install it and test it by hand

Put the program where the system finds it: a package (sudo apt install ...), or the binary or AppImage in /usr/local/bin (chmod +x). Then, in the console (Exit to shell in the FliperOS menu), open a game through the wrapper:

/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run myemu "/home/fliperos/roms/myemu/game.bin"

If it opens full screen, plays and returns to the console when you quit it, it will work from any frontend. Use fliperos-kms-run instead only if the program runs without X (most don't; see What KMS and X11 are).

Step 2: make the command frontend-proof

A frontend only knows how to run one command with the game's path and then wait for it to finish. The command must therefore follow a few rules:

  • Absolute paths: start with /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run (or fliperos-kms-run), never just the program name. The frontends don't run a shell with your PATH.
  • The program right after the wrapper: fliperos-x11-run [--mode WxH@HZ] program [options] game. The wrapper accepts a name in the PATH or the full path of an executable.
  • Full screen and no questions: pass the emulator's own options for full screen, for skipping its welcome or update dialogs and for loading the game directly. Nobody should need a mouse.
  • It has to quit and stay in the foreground: the emulator needs a way to exit with the panel or the keyboard (a hotkey or a menu), otherwise you are stuck in it. It also must not hand off to another process and exit: when the program the wrapper started ends, the wrapper closes its X and the frontend comes back.
  • The game path in quotes: file names have spaces. Each frontend writes the path with its own placeholder (table below).

If the emulator needs more than that (environment variables, a config file chosen per game, a cd to its folder, Wine), write a small launcher script and point the frontends to it. The frontend then only passes the game, and every detail stays in one place:

#!/bin/bash
# /usr/local/bin/myemu-run GAME
export MYEMU_BIOS="$HOME/bios/myemu"
cd /opt/myemu || exit 1
exec /opt/myemu/myemu --fullscreen --no-gui "$1"

sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/myemu-run
/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run myemu-run "/home/fliperos/roms/myemu/game.bin"

The exec keeps the emulator as the program the wrapper waits for. This is how FliperOS opens SM2-Emu for a frontend (fliperos-model2).

Step 3: the video mode (X11 only)

fliperos-x11-run takes the mode from /etc/fliperos/emulator-modes.conf by the program name (the first word after the wrapper, without its path). Add a line:

# program           15 kHz          25/31 kHz and LCD
myemu-run           320x240@60      640x480@60

Without a line, the program gets 320x240@60. Use 640x240 at 15 kHz for systems that draw 448 or 480 lines, and the system's own refresh rate when it isn't 60 Hz (Model 2 and 3: 57.524).

Step 4: one folder and the command in each frontend

Create the game folder, for example ~/roms/myemu. Setup > Games > Frontend only creates the systems FliperOS knows about, so a new emulator has to be added by hand in each frontend you use. The command is the same everywhere; only the placeholders change:

Frontend Where Game path Name without extension
Attract-Mode Plus args in ~/.attract/emulators/<name>.cfg "[romfilename]" [name]
ES-DE <command> in ~/ES-DE/custom_systems/es_systems.xml %ROM% (ES-DE adds the quotes) %BASENAME%
Pegasus launch: in metadata.pegasus.txt in the game folder "{file.path}" {file.basename}

The same emulator in the three of them:

# Attract-Mode Plus: ~/.attract/emulators/My Emulator.cfg
executable           /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run
args                 myemu-run "[romfilename]"
rompath              /home/fliperos/roms/myemu/
romext               .bin;.zip

<!-- ES-DE: inside <systemList> in ~/ES-DE/custom_systems/es_systems.xml -->
<system>
  <name>myemu</name>
  <fullname>My Emulator</fullname>
  <path>/home/fliperos/roms/myemu</path>
  <extension>.bin .zip</extension>
  <command label="My Emulator">/opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run myemu-run %ROM%</command>
  <platform>arcade</platform>
  <theme>arcade</theme>
</system>

# Pegasus: ~/roms/myemu/metadata.pegasus.txt
collection: My Emulator
extensions: bin, zip
launch: /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run myemu-run "{file.path}"

Then, in Attract-Mode Plus, generate the romlist and add a display (as in Attract-Mode Plus above). In Pegasus, add the folder to the list in ~/.config/pegasus-frontend/game_dirs.txt. For the artwork, use a ~/media/<type>/<platform> folder (Artwork) in the emulator's artwork lines; for ES-DE, use the <platform> that the scraper should use.

What the Setup keeps and what it rewrites. A .cfg you created yourself, without the # Criado pelo FliperOS Setup line, is never touched, and neither is a metadata.pegasus.txt that already exists. Setup > Games > Frontend does rewrite ES-DE's es_systems.xml and Pegasus's game_dirs.txt with only the folders it knows, so add your system again after using it.

Quick checks

  • The system doesn't show up: the folder must have at least one game file (the _info.txt doesn't count) and the frontend must be picked again in Setup > Games > Frontend.
  • The game doesn't open: with debug mode on (Setup > System > Debug mode) the emulator's output shows on the screen; otherwise it is saved in /opt/fliperos/logs. Try the same command in the console (Exit to shell in the FliperOS menu).
  • No artwork: check the name (exactly the ROM name, without the extension, case included) and the platform folder, and in Attract-Mode the emulator's artwork lines.

Controls

Controllers on FliperOS: what the Setup offers in Joysticks and in System > Quirks and how the emulators see each controller. Using the controller in the Setup menus is covered in Installed system.

Light gun (GunCon 2)

FliperOS plays light gun games on the tube with Namco's GunCon 2 (the PlayStation 2 gun, USB 0b9a:016a), with nothing to install. The gun reads the beam of the CRT, which is exactly the screen FliperOS is made for; on an LCD it doesn't aim. What ships with the system:

  • The driver. GunCon 2 has no driver in the mainline kernel. The build compiles beardypig/guncon2 through DKMS for the system's kernel and loads it at boot (/etc/modules-load.d/fliperos-guncon2.conf): plug the gun into USB and it shows up as an input device.
  • The calibration. The raw position the gun reports depends on the tube and on where the cabinet's gun sits, and evdev forgets the range on every reconnection. Setup > Joysticks > Calibrate GunCon 2 measures it on your monitor once (below), and the udev rule 99-fliperos-input.rules reapplies it (fliperos-guncon2-calibrate) every time the gun is plugged in.
  • The menus. The controller-as-keyboard of the Setup menus leaves light guns out, so aiming doesn't move through the menu.
  • The games. In the MAME ROM Cleaner, tell it the cabinet has a Light gun among its controls, and the gun games of the romset are kept along with the others.

Setup > Joysticks

Calibrators and the parallel port (config/fliperos-calibrate, screens/joysticks.sh):

Button mapping (all emulators)

The first question is what is wired to the panel.

Keyboard encoder (MAME default keys) is for an encoder that types keys (I-PAC and the like) in MAME's layout: nothing is pressed, only the number of players is asked, and every emulator below gets MAME's default keys for each player (fliperos-buttons keyboard; player 1: arrows, Left Ctrl, Left Alt, Space, Left Shift, Z, X, 1 Start, 5 Coin; player 2: R F D G, A S Q W E, 2, 6; players 3 and 4 have only the stick and buttons 1 to 3, as in MAME).

RetroArch's own shortcuts that sit on those keys (Space fast-forward, F fullscreen, K frame advance...) are turned off in buttons.cfg, and Supermodel drops its own default keys, which would be another player's. Controllers (press each control) is the mapping below.

Each player's panel, input by input: up, down, left, right, buttons 1 to 6 in panel order (1 2 3 on top, 4 5 6 below), Start and Coin.

The first input pressed tells which controller belongs to the player (on a V-USB panel with two identical devices, one per player); with nothing pressed for 8 seconds the input is skipped; the controller-as-keyboard for the menu is off meanwhile.

Each button does one thing: a button already given to another input (of this player or another one on the same controller) is refused, and the screen says which input has it and asks for another one.

It is read through SDL (config/fliperos-buttons), and the result goes to both: in RetroArch, each player's binds in /etc/fliperos/retroarch/buttons.cfg, which fliperos-kms-run adds to the config (--appendconfig) on top of the controller's automatic profile, with the buttons in the arcade cores' layout (Y X L / B A R, Start and Select on the coin); in GroovyMAME, the ctrlr ~/.mame/ctrlr/fliperos.cfg (each player's JOYCODEs, together with MAME's default keys) and in mame.ini ctrlr fliperos and joystickprovider sdljoy — with sdlgame, the default, MAME sees the panel through SDL's game controller mapping (A, B, X, Y...), which doesn't follow the button order.

It also applies to the other emulators: the device's SDL game controller mapping (GUID), in fight stick layout (X Y RB on top, A B RT below, coin on Back), in /var/lib/fliperos/gamecontrollerdb-user.txt, which fliperos-controllers puts last in gamecontrollerdb.txt (PCSX2, with Pad1/Pad2 on SDL through fliperos-x11-run while PCSX2 has no SDL bind; DuckStation the same way — it points SDL to its own database, but SDL_GAMECONTROLLERCONFIG_FILE takes priority; KOF Final Attack's Ikemen GO, which adds its own external/gamecontrollerdb.txt after SDL starts, so fliperos-kof hands it that database with the FliperOS one last, save/gamecontrollerdb-fliperos.txt, on every launch; AntiMicroX); in Dolphin, GCPad1 to GCPad4 in GCPadNew.ini with that mapping (4 = A, 1 = B, 5 = X, 2 = Y, 3 = Z, 6 = R, coin on the Triforce Coin) and each player's port enabled in Dolphin.ini; Flycast by device name (Dreamcast through SDL; arcade, Naomi and Atomiswave, with the panel's button N on the game's button N and coin on D; a hat D-pad becomes Flycast's hat button code and a trigger goes in its triggers list), and the same files in Fightcade's Flycast Dojo; Attract-Mode Plus, the joystick entries of input_map in attract.cfg: each player's directions, Select on button 1 and Back on button 2, plus its default shortcuts (Up + button 1 and so on) for player 1, replacing the old controller's entries (keyboard entries and other commands stay; it is written again every time Attract-Mode opens, so one installed after the mapping gets it too); Supermodel, Start, coin, directions and buttons 1 to 4 for players 1 and 2 in Supermodel.ini; Hypseus Singe, the [KEYBOARD] of ~/.hypseus/hypinput.ini (buttons 1 to 3 and skill 1 to 3, Start and coin for both players); and OpenBOR, in each player's keys of Saves/default.cfg and of each pak's .cfg (the s_savedata struct: 1 attack, 2 jump, 3 special, 4 to 6 the other attacks, coin on Esc).

The map lives in /etc/fliperos/buttons.map, and a system update writes everything again.

A trigger (an axis resting at one end, like an Xbox 360 controller's LT/RT) can only be pressed one way: if the capture started with it still held, it used to record the release, and the button then counted as pressed at rest in every emulator; the capture now ignores that release, and saving fixes the direction from the controller's resting position, also in a map saved before.

Buttons layout (games of 1 to 5 buttons)

Where the buttons of a game go on the panel, by how many buttons the game uses. Pick the number of buttons (1 to 5) and then, for button 1, button 2 and so on, its place on the panel (top row or bottom row; left, middle or right). The panel is drawn as you go, and the list shows the layout of each number:

3-button games   [1][2][3] / [ ][ ][ ]
4-button games   [1][2][ ] / [3][4][ ]      or      [1][3][ ] / [2][4][ ]

Without a layout, the game's button N is on the panel's button N (1 2 3 on top, 4 5 6 below); Default layout goes back to that. Six-button games always use the whole panel. It needs the Button mapping done first: the layout moves the buttons mapped there.

The choice is saved in /etc/fliperos/buttons.layout (one line per number of buttons: the panel position of button 1, of button 2...).

How many buttons each game has comes from GroovyMAME's game list (-listxml) with the real counts of controls.xml on top (fliperos-romclean buttons writes the table /var/lib/fliperos/game-buttons.txt; the first time it reads the list, about a minute).

The MAME 2010 core has a table of its own, game-buttons-mame2010.txt, from the game list of MAME 0.139: that version gives some games the generic button block of their board instead of the buttons the game has. Tekken 3 and the other System 12 games are buttons 1 2 4 5 of a block of 6 there, and 1 2 3 4 in today's MAME.

Such a game (0.139 lists more buttons than the game has, and today's MAME lists only the game's) counts as its whole block, so no layout moves it: the punches stay on the top row and the kicks under them, as on the original panel.

It applies where the panel's button N is the game's button N: in GroovyMAME, a <system> per game in the ctrlr fliperos.cfg (a clone follows its parent's); in RetroArch's MAME and MAME 2010 cores, a buttons-N.cfg next to buttons.cfg, which fliperos-kms-run adds to the config of a game with N buttons; in Supermodel (Model 3), the buttons of the game in its own section of Supermodel.ini ([ vf3 ]), which Supermodel adds to [ Global ] when the game opens — the fighting games (Punch, Kick, Guard, Escape), the Virtua Striker series (Short Pass, Long Pass, Shoot) and Spikeout (Shift, Beat, Charge, Jump), by the input type of each game in Games.xml; other settings you keep in that section stay; in SM2-Emu (Model 2), a game controller mapping of its own, /var/lib/fliperos/gamecontrollerdb-model2.txt and a gamecontrollerdb-model2-N.txt per layout, which fliperos-x11-run puts on top of the system's gamecontrollerdb.txt for that launch.

SM2-Emu reads game buttons 1 to 4 from A B X Y and always takes RB as button 4, so the fight stick mapping of the other emulators put button 1 on the bottom row; its own mapping puts the panel's button N on the game's button N, layout or not. The Model 2 mapping is written with the panel connected (it goes by the device's GUID).

The other emulators keep the Button mapping order: FBNeo arranges the buttons of each game by itself, and the others have one mapping for all games.

Calibrate GunCon 2

The screen turns white (the gun needs light where it aims) with a target in each corner; three shots at each (the median counts; a shot off the screen is rejected), and the calibrator computes the gun's real range on the tube — GunCon 2 is linear, so two known points give the edges.

A shot at the center checks the result before saving /etc/fliperos/guncon2.conf, which the udev rule reapplies on every connection (evdev forgets the calibration).

Calibrate wheel, pedals or analog stick

The axes show live; turn the wheel from end to end and press each pedal all the way, then leave everything at rest. An axis that rests in the middle (wheel, analog stick) gets a symmetric range around the rest position — the center gives 0 and both sides reach the end — and a 1% dead zone; a pedal keeps the range seen.

It goes to /etc/fliperos/calibration.conf (one line per axis) and udev reapplies it on every connection.

LPT joysticks

Joysticks and pads on the parallel port, through the kernel's own drivers: gamepad adapter (gamecon: NES, SNES, N64, PlayStation, DDR mat, Multisystem; up to 5 per port, on pins 10, 11, 12, 13 and 15), DB9 adapter (db9: Atari/Amiga/Master System, 3/5/6-button Genesis, Saturn, CD32; needs the port in EPP or ECP mode in the BIOS) and TurboGraFX interface (turbografx: up to 7 Multisystem joysticks).

The adapter can't be detected: you say which one it is and what is connected to each input, and the setup writes /etc/modprobe.d/fliperos-lpt.conf (the module options, plus blacklist lp: the printer driver would claim the port, and the joystick drivers want it for themselves) and /etc/modules-load.d/fliperos-lpt.conf (loads at boot), loads the driver right away and shows the joysticks created.

The kernel finds the port itself (parport_pc) when it exists — on the motherboard it often comes disabled in the BIOS (Super I/O > Parallel Port); without one, a PCI/PCIe parallel card. Parallel port joysticks also move the menus.

Setup > System > Quirks

Kernel fixes for USB devices that arrive wrong. It sits in System, not in Joysticks, because it is about any USB device. Two kinds, told apart by the code:

  • Controllers, guns, keyboards (the usbhid.quirks parameter): code 0xVENDOR:0xPRODUCT:0xFLAGS;
  • Disks and pen drives (the usb-storage.quirks parameter): code VENDOR:PRODUCT:LETTERS, without 0x, for example 152d:0578:u, where u turns UAS off for a SATA adapter that hangs or drops off.

Each quirk has a name you give it and a code, for example 0x16c0:0x05e1:0x40 for a dual Xin-Mo encoder to show up as two players. Choosing one from the list deletes it; USB devices connected now shows the vendor:product of each connected device.

Useful flags: 0x40 one device per player (MULTI_INPUT, dual encoders), 0x8 no GET requests (NOGET, an encoder that hangs), 0x400 always poll (ALWAYS_POLL).

The kernel reads at most 4 controller quirks (disk quirks have no such limit), and only at boot: the list lives in /etc/fliperos/quirks.conf, goes into the kernel line (/etc/default/fliperos-boot) and applies after a reboot. Done on the installation media, it goes along to the disk.

Controllers in SDL

AntiMicroX, PCSX2, Dolphin, Flycast and RetroArch use SDL2, which maps a controller outside its database automatically and incompletely: it leaves out the buttons without a counterpart on a modern controller (BTN_C, BTN_Z, extra buttons — in controller mode AntiMicroX doesn't even show them) and puts on the analog stick a digital D-pad that the device sends as axes from −1 to +1 (common in arcade encoders and V-USB projects), and then a game that moves with the D-pad doesn't move.

fliperos-controllers (at boot and whenever a controller is connected, through udev) asks SDL itself how it sees each controller and, only for those with an automatic mapping or with no mapping and a digital D-pad, completes it: leftover buttons go to triggers, misc1 and paddles, and the digital axes become the D-pad.

Controllers in SDL's database (Xbox, DualShock...) stay as they are; real analog ones (wheel, flight stick) too. The result goes to /var/lib/fliperos/gamecontrollerdb.txt (cumulative), pointed to by SDL_GAMECONTROLLERCONFIG_FILE in /etc/environment and in the launchers.

Flycast builds its default mapping from SDL but doesn't understand a D-pad wired to a half axis; for those controllers it also gets mapping files (Dreamcast and arcade, in Flycast's own convention), only if there isn't one yet.

It also ships with player 2 (port B) with a controller — its default leaves only player 1 — and with linear interpolation off (rend.LinearInterpolation = no in emu.cfg; the Linear Interpolation option in its settings): Flycast's default blurs the image when taking it to the tube's mode, and without the filter the pixels come out sharp.

In an earlier emu.cfg, the option is only turned off if it isn't saved yet; once saved, the choice is yours.

Texture Filtering comes as Force Nearest-Neighbor (rend.TextureFiltering = 1) for the same reason; Flycast saves its default (0) when it closes, so in an earlier emu.cfg it is changed once (marked in /var/lib/fliperos/flycast-texture-nearest) and after that the choice is yours.

RetroArch is compiled with SDL2, so the sdl2 joypad driver shows in Drivers > Input next to udev, and the choice is kept (the system retroarch.cfg doesn't pin the joypad driver).

The default is still udev, which shows in the menu the real number of each controller button; with sdl2 the same mappings as the other emulators apply, a controller without a profile falls back to the built-in "Standard Gamepad", and the numbers become SDL's (A = 0, B = 1...).

SDL reads the mappings when it opens: a controller connected for the first time with RetroArch open only works correctly after reopening it.

With udev, arcade panels and encoders were "not configured" (there's no factory profile for them); fliperos-controllers writes one in /opt/fliperos/retroarch/autoconfig/udev for every controller with a digital D-pad and no analog stick that no profile covers, with the buttons in panel order in the arcade cores' layout (FBNeo): 1 2 3 = Y X L (top row), 4 5 6 = B A R (bottom row) — the MAME cores read the RetroPad's Button 1-6 in another order (MAME, B A Y X L R; MAME 2010, A B X Y L R), and a core remap (config/retroarch-remaps, in ~/.config/retroarch/config/remaps/<core>; one saved from RetroArch's menu stays) takes the panel's button N to the game's Button N, as in GroovyMAME; on a panel with up to 9 buttons the 7th is Start and the 8th Select (coin); with 10 or more, 7 and 8 are L2/R2 and Select/Start move to 9 and 10, as on USB encoders.

The profile carries the name and VID+PID (V-USB's VID+PID is the same across different projects) and isn't rewritten: one saved from the menu (Save Controller Profile) stays.

RetroArch's menu always names the buttons after the RetroPad's (A, B, X, Y...); with an arcade core open, Quick Menu > Controls shows the game's names. An encoder whose D-pad is axes only and which the kernel merges into a single controller may need a quirk (Setup > System > Quirks).

Desktop and theme

LXDE desktop

GroovyArcade's LXDE: full lxde with openbox-lxde, panel at the bottom (menu, file manager, terminal, tasks, CPU, volume, tray, network, clock), no compositor, no DPMS or screensaver, Sans 10 font and the Video Setup orientation.

The wallpaper is /usr/share/fliperos/wallpaper.jpg (config/wallpaper.jpg, a pixel-art city at night), stretched to the screen, which is 4:3 in every CRT mode. Everything in the Dracula theme (see below).

Terminal: Alacritty. lxterminal and xterm (the system's default terminal, with bitmap fonts the image doesn't even have) didn't draw Gum's borders; they were removed, and the terminal in the panel, the menu and FliperOS Setup is Alacritty, which always works in UTF-8 and draws borders and blocks by itself, without depending on the font.

Dracula theme with the console palette (config/lxde/alacritty/alacritty.toml), DejaVu Sans Mono, non-blinking cursor (blinking redraws the screen, which flickers in interlaced modes). The font size doesn't follow the DPI from the CRT's EDID (it would give 50 DPI or less): fliperos-lxde exports WINIT_X11_SCALE_FACTOR=1.

Since the lxde metapackage depends on lxterminal, the image installs its components one by one.

App Store: GNOME Software with the Flatpak plugin and Flathub as a source, in the menu (System Tools), on the panel and on the desktop as App Store: Ubuntu packages and Flatpak apps (emulators, games, programs). Ubuntu 24.04's App Center depends on snap, which isn't in the image.

No automatic update downloads and no welcome screen (config/fliperos-software.gschema.override): disk and network activity in the middle of a game hurts latency, for the same reason the apt timers are masked. Installing asks for the user's password (fliperos), through lxpolkit.

Disks on the desktop: every disk is mounted by itself, at boot and when it is plugged in (a second hard disk, a USB stick, a Windows partition), in /media/fliperos/<label>, and gets a hard disk icon on the desktop to open it.

A disk without a label is named after its model, like /media/fliperos/TOSHIBA_HDWD110 (from its second partition on, with the number: TOSHIBA_HDWD110_2), instead of a code like 5E2C-4AEF. The old code path still works: it is a link to the new folder, so a game set to open at boot or a frontend list that saved it keeps working.

The mount is done by udisks2 as the fliperos user, so FAT, exFAT and NTFS disks belong to the user (NTFS through the kernel's ntfs3): a udev rule (config/99-fliperos-disks.rules) starts fliperos-automount@<device>.service for each file system, and config/fliperos-automount leaves out what is already mounted, swap, encrypted, LVM and RAID volumes, and system partitions (EFI, Windows recovery and reserved).

A polkit rule (config/50-fliperos-udisks.rules) lets the user mount, unmount and eject internal disks without a password; formatting and partitioning still ask for it. The icons come from PCManFM (show_mounts=1) with gvfs, which also offers Unmount and Eject in the icon's menu.

Nothing is mounted on the installation media, where a mounted disk couldn't be erased by the installer.

Browser and torrents: Falkon and Transmission ship in the image and appear in the menu (Internet) as Falkon (browser) and Transmission (torrent): fliperos-rootfs.sh copies each package's entry to /usr/local/share/applications, which takes precedence, with the name changed in every language.

Emulators in the menu (Games): RetroArch, GroovyMAME, Flycast, PCSX2, Supermodel, Dolphin, OpenBOR, Model 2 and, once downloaded through the Setup, Fightcade 2, with the projects' own icons.

GroovyMAME, Model 2 (SM2-Emu) and Fightcade don't bring one into the image, so their official icons come from config/icons; Supermodel has no icon of its own and gets a FliperOS monogram.

None of them runs inside the desktop's X — RetroArch and GroovyMAME use KMS, the others start an Xorg of their own in the mode from the modes table (Emulators) —, so the shortcut (fliperos-launch) saves the request and closes the desktop (with a confirmation if there are open windows), fliperos-session opens the emulator on the CRT and, when it closes, the desktop comes back.

An emulator that wasn't built (--skip-*) doesn't show in the menu. Model 2 always does: it is not compiled into the image, and the first click clones and builds it (Emulators). Steam and Heroic (GOG), once installed through Setup > Games > Extras, also live in Games, but open inside the desktop itself.

GroovyArcade's tools also ship: AntiMicroX and QJoyPad (controller as keyboard/mouse), xterm, htop, evtest, joy2key, hwinfo, lshw, read-edid, i2c-tools. FliperOS Setup lives in System Tools (and on the panel), like gasetup.desktop. The terminal uses the Dracula colors. Leaving the desktop goes back to the menu.

Screen Resolution (Preferences): changes the desktop resolution on the fly. The list is the resolutions of the monitor chosen in Video Setup, plus Other resolution... (any WIDTHxHEIGHT@HZ).

Switchres computes the mode within the ranges of /etc/switchres.ini (switchres --calc, the same calculation the emulators use) and xrandr applies it, adjusting the screen size; the window opens maximized and follows the change. Without confirmation within 15 seconds, the previous resolution comes back.

Use every time the desktop starts saves the mode in ~/.config/fliperos/desktop-mode, which fliperos-lxde applies when the desktop opens; choosing the boot resolution forgets the saved one. Only the desktop changes: the console, the setup and the frontends keep the Video Setup resolution. With an LCD monitor, the list is the modes from its EDID.

Dracula theme

Dracula is the theme of everything FliperOS draws:

Where How
Console and fliperos-setup VT palette (below) and Gum with its indices
LXDE — GTK 2/3 windows and programs official dracula/gtk theme, pinned by commit (fliperos-dracula.sh), with GTK 2's murrine/pixbuf engines
LXDE — Openbox borders and menus config/openbox-3/themerc (dracula/gtk has no Openbox theme), selected in lxde-rc.xml
LXDE — panel, background, terminal colors in config/lxde (lxpanel, pcmanfm, lxterminal)
