Terminal (zsh) Oh My Zsh with the official dracula/zsh theme, both pinned by commit in /usr/local/share/oh-my-zsh (fliperos-dracula.sh), without automatic updates; ~/.zshrc is config/zshrc. On the Linux console the arrow and git's ✓/✗ become >, ok and * (the console font lacks those symbols)
RetroArch the Dracula theme built into RGUI (rgui_menu_color_theme = 17)
GroovyMAME UI colors (menus, game list, sliders) in /etc/fliperos/mame/ui.ini (config/mame-ui.ini, ARGB)

On the console

The Linux console only has 16 colors, and the background only accepts the first 8.

The VT palette is reprogrammed with the Dracula tones at boot (/etc/vtrgb, applied by Ubuntu's setvtrgb.service, with config/vtrgb-dracula as a higher-priority alternative) and again by fliperos-setup; Gum's styles use the palette indices, not hexadecimal colors.

That way the tube and a graphical terminal show the same thing. The console font (Lat15/Uni2) has the rounded borders, the bar blocks and the arrows the screens use.

Latency

What weighs most in the delay between pressing the button and the picture changing is the same on FliperOS and on GroovyArcade: the same kernel patches (the same video output on radeon/amdgpu), the same Switchres and GroovyMAME, and the CRT, which doesn't process the image.

FliperOS applies the tweaks GA already makes and adds others, in two modes chosen in Setup > System > Latency (fliperos-setup/lib/latency.sh).

Tweak GroovyArcade FliperOS Standard FliperOS Low latency
mitigations=off audit=0 in the kernel yes yes yes
USB polled at 1000 Hz (usbhid.jspoll=1 kbpoll=1 mousepoll=1) no yes yes
CPU on the performance governor while the frontend runs while the frontend runs always, from boot
Kernel preemption linux-15khz (there is also a linux-rt) 6.18 PREEMPT_DYNAMIC, voluntary mode preempt=full
GroovyMAME lowlatency 1, autoframedelay 1, framedelay 0 lowlatency (the rest is default) yes yes
RetroArch video_max_swapchain_images = 2 yes yes yes
RetroArch video_threaded off, input_poll_type_behavior = 2 default yes yes
RetroArch automatic frame delay no no yes
RetroArch preemptive frames (1 frame) no no yes
apt and man-db running by themselves don't exist (Arch) masked masked

What each tweak does:

  • mitigations=off audit=0 — GA's default line. Turns off the kernel's Spectre/Meltdown protections, which cost the most on the older CPUs (without hardware fixes) typical of cabinets. It trades security for performance, acceptable on a machine that only runs games.
  • USB at 1000 Hz — a full-speed controller is polled every 8 ms (125 Hz); the average wait drops from ~4 ms to ~0.5 ms. It applies to whatever uses the usbhid driver (Zero Delay/Xin-Mo style encoders, I-PAC as a keyboard, trackball); Xbox controllers use xpad and don't change.

If a controller misbehaves, usb_poll=default in /etc/fliperos/fliperos.conf and applying the mode again restores the original polling. - performance governor — frame delay counts on a fixed emulation time per frame; with the CPU raising its clock only after the load appears, that time varies. In the standard mode it only applies during the session (fliperos-session calls fliperos-setup --session-start/--session-end, like galauncher's cpu_governor.sh); in the low latency one, from boot (fliperos-latency.service). - preempt=full — FliperOS's 6.18 kernel is PREEMPT_DYNAMIC; with this parameter it interrupts any kernel work to run the emulator, which Ubuntu's old lowlatency kernel did. It reduces the variation (jitter) more than the average. - Frame delay (GroovyMAME's autoframedelay, RetroArch's video_frame_delay_auto) — the emulator waits part of the frame before emulating, and reads the controls closer to when the picture goes out: up to almost a frame (16.7 ms) less. The automatic one backs off by itself when the CPU can't keep up. - Preemptive frames — removes the game's own internal delay (1 frame), redoing the last frame only when the input changes (lighter than run-ahead, which redoes every frame). It needs a core with savestates; those without turn the feature off with a warning. - apt and man-db — Ubuntu's timers would run apt update and the man reindexing in the middle of a game. Updating lives in Setup > System > System Update, as in GA.

What was left out, and why: a PREEMPT_RT kernel (GA has a linux-rt), because preempt=full covers cabinet use and RT trades throughput for predictability, which is only worth it with measurements showing a gain; limiting the CPU C-states, because the gain would be microseconds when the CPU wakes up, against more power draw and heat; and RetroArch's video_hard_sync, because in KMS the 2-image swapchain already waits for each flip.

Compared with GA: on the same hardware, expect a tie in Standard mode (with an advantage of a few ms from USB at 1000 Hz) and up to 1 to 2 frames less in RetroArch games in Low latency mode. A hand-tuned GA gets to the same place; the difference is that FliperOS ships this way out of the box.

Recommended hardware

Use CPU Memory and disk GPU
Standard (up to PS1 and most of arcade) x86-64 with 2 cores 4 GB, 16 GB of disk AMD with VGA or DVI-I output, within CRT_EmuDriver's range (HD 2000 to R7/R9 GCN 1.0)
Low latency AVX2 (x86-64-v3: 4th-generation Intel Core, AMD Ryzen or newer), 4 threads, 3.0 GHz or more 4 GB (8 GB better) same
Everything (PS2, Model 3, Dreamcast) 4 physical cores with AVX2 and single-thread PassMark ≥ 2000 (Core i7-7700, Ryzen 5 3600 or newer) 16 GB, SSD same: at CRT resolutions even the R7 240 exceeds PCSX2's minimum (G3D ≥ 600)

The "Everything" tier follows the Moderate level of the PCSX2 requirements, the heaviest emulator in the ISO; the stronger GPU PCSX2 asks for at that level is for upscaled resolution, which doesn't exist on a CRT. Cards without analog output (AMD RX and newer, recent NVIDIA) need a converter: see Converters.

The CPU's speed decides more than its cores. For arcade games a faster clock is what lets MAME run heavier games. GroovyArcade notes that above 8 cores MAME generally gains nothing.

Checking the machine: Setup > System > Latency shows the CPU, cores, clock, instruction level, memory, GPU and analog outputs, and Check this computer compares them with the Low latency mode minimum (lib/hardware.sh: x86-64-v3, 4 threads, 3.0 GHz, 4 GB). Choosing Low latency on a machine below that asks for confirmation.

Small machines

A cabinet doesn't need a tower. GroovyArcade benchmarked these with GroovyMAME, listed from fastest to slowest; its page has the results, photos and manuals. None has been tried on FliperOS. Check that the outputs suit your monitor: many of them have DisplayPort or a bridged VGA (Video cards).

To benchmark your own, GroovyArcade's mamebench runs a list of games and reports the speed and the frame delay each one reached. It is written for GroovyArcade's folders, though -m and -r set the GroovyMAME program and the ROM folder. It hasn't been tried on FliperOS.

Network

Use a cable if the cabinet is near the router: the live screen of the web panel with sound needs it. For Wi-Fi, GroovyArcade recommends Atheros chipsets on Linux, and 802.11n is enough for updates and remote work.

The test cabinet uses an Atheros AR9271. Of the TP-Link TL-WN722N, only version 1 has an Atheros chip.

Measuring

The only reliable comparison is measuring, on the same cabinet, the same game and the same emulator version. Film the button and the screen together with a phone in 240 fps slow motion (~4 ms per video frame), 20 to 30 presses per configuration, and count the video frames between the button going down and the picture reacting.

Multiple monitors

Multiple monitors

Some arcade games were built for two or three monitors side by side or stacked: Darius and The Ninja Warriors (3 screens in a row), Punch-Out!! and Super Punch-Out!! (2 screens, one above the other), Ferrari F355 Challenge, Airline Pilots and Sega Strike Fighter (3 screens in a row, one NAOMI board per screen).

FliperOS drives two arcade CRTs from the analog outputs of one video card, and up to three with a second video card or an active converter on a digital output (both experimental). When a game has 2 or more screens and the multi-screen mode is on, the emulator sends each screen to its own monitor. Every other game stays on monitor 1.

What you need

  • A video card with one analog output (VGA, DVI-I) for each monitor, supported by the 15 kHz kernel. The tested way is every monitor on the same card as monitor 1; a second card is experimental (below).

Older Radeons with VGA + DVI-I (HD 5000, 6000 and 7000 series, like the HD 5450 or HD 6450) are the tested way to get 2 CRTs. These cards usually have two DACs, so even with VGA + 2 DVI-I outputs only two analog monitors work at the same time. - Check the DVI connector: only DVI-I (the 4 extra pins around the flat blade) carries analog VGA, and works with a passive DVI-to-VGA adapter. DVI-D is digital only. For example the Radeon R7 240 has VGA + DVI-D + HDMI: only one analog output. - You are not limited to one video card. The outputs can also come from more than one card: each card brings its own outputs (and its own DACs), so how many cards you can use only depends on how many free PCI/PCIe slots the computer has. Monitor 1's card draws the picture and the others only add outputs (see A second video card). - Monitors of the same type as monitor 1 (Setup > Video Setup > Monitor Type): they get the same video mode. - Monitor 1 already chosen by the output test (boot menu or Setup > Video Setup).

Digital outputs with an active converter (experimental)

An HDMI, DVI-D or DisplayPort output can drive a CRT through an active converter to VGA (one with a DAC chip inside; passive adapters don't work). The Setup lists these outputs as digital, active VGA converter, experimental. This is not tested yet on a cabinet: - An HDMI or DVI-D link can't go below about 25 MHz of pixel clock. GroovyArcade reports no such limit on DisplayPort, but the Setup treats every digital output the same: the extra monitor boots in the super resolution of the monitor's preset (video=HDMI-A-1:1280x480iSe at 15 kHz: the same lines and frequencies, with thinner pixels), and the Xorg configuration doesn't give it monitor 1's low-dotclock modeline. - Many cheap converters refuse non-standard modes, interlaced modes or low frequencies. If the monitor stays black, try another converter; see Converters for the ones the community recommends. - GroovyMAME's Switchres makes each game's mode for every screen with the card's own limits; on an AMD card these can go below the converter's minimum, and that screen goes black. Flycast's 3-screen games only use analog outputs for now.

A second video card (experimental)

The extra monitors don't have to be on monitor 1's card: they can be on another video card, or on several. If one card doesn't have enough analog outputs, add another; the only limit is how many free PCI/PCIe slots the computer has.

The Setup lists the outputs of every card it finds, as card1:VGA-1 (AMD Radeon ...), and fliperos.conf saves them with the card in front (screens=VGA-1,DVI-I-1,card1:VGA-1). This is not tested yet on a cabinet: - Monitor 1's card draws everything. X opens on it (its BusID is in /etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/10-fliperos.conf) and adds the other card as a GPU screen (AutoAddGPU, AutoBindGPU): its outputs join the same desktop, and the picture is copied to them (reverse PRIME).

In XRandR they get another name: VGA-1 of the first extra card is VGA-1-1, of the second VGA-1-2. fliperos-multiscreen xnames makes that translation for GroovyMAME and Flycast, and binds the card (xrandr --setprovideroutputsource) if X didn't. - The kernel's video= goes by connector name, on every card. video=VGA-1:640x480iSe sets the VGA-1 of both cards, so an extra monitor on a second card's VGA-1 gets monitor 1's mode, and an unused output with the same name on the other card is also forced on (with nothing plugged in, it does no harm). - Use a card the 15 kHz kernel supports with low dotclocks (AMD/ATI, radeon or amdgpu). On a card without them (Intel, NVIDIA; the NVIDIA low resolution test only covers the main card) the monitor boots in the super resolution, and GroovyMAME's per-game modes may not reach it. - Programs in KMS (RetroArch, the frontends) only see monitor 1: the others are turned off while they run, as on one card.

Reports from anyone testing a converter or a second card are welcome in the issues.

Step by step

  1. Plug the monitors in. Monitor 1 is the one the boot menu and the output test found. Plug the others into free analog outputs (VGA, or DVI-I with a passive adapter), on the same card or on a second card. Turn them all on.
  2. Open the Setup: Setup > Video Setup > Multiple Monitors. The top shows monitor 1, monitors 2 and 3 (off) and the game screen order.
  3. Monitor 2: choose its output from the list (analog outputs of monitor 1's card first; digital outputs and other cards are marked experimental). The Setup asks if a monitor of the same type as monitor 1 is plugged in there. The first time it also prepares the GroovyMAME games with 2 or 3 screens (about a minute).
  4. Monitor 3, if you have one: same thing.
  5. Leave Video Setup: the Setup writes the kernel line (each extra monitor with its forced 15 kHz mode) and the Xorg configuration, and offers to reboot. The new monitors only light up after that.
  6. Identify Monitors: each one turns off for 3 seconds, in the game screen order. If the order is wrong (Darius' left screen on the right), fix it in Game Screen Order: left to right for Darius and F355 Challenge, top to bottom for Punch-Out!!.
  7. Play. Open a game with several screens from any frontend or the Games menu: GroovyMAME and Flycast send each screen to its monitor. Single-screen games, RetroArch and the frontends stay on monitor 1.
  8. Multi-Screen Games: Off puts every game back on monitor 1 without removing the monitors; Monitor 2/3: Off removes them (another reboot).

Setting it up

Setup > Video Setup > Multiple Monitors:

Item What it does
Monitor 2, Monitor 3 Picks the output of each extra monitor. The list shows the free outputs of monitor 1's card, the analog ones first and the digital ones marked as experimental; Off removes the monitor. Before saving, the Setup asks if a monitor of the same type is plugged in there.
Multi-Screen Games On (default): games with 2 or 3 screens use one monitor per screen. Off: every game opens on monitor 1, and the extra monitors stay on but unused.
Game Screen Order Which output shows each screen of a game: from left to right (Darius, F355 Challenge) or from top to bottom (Punch-Out!!).
Identify Monitors Turns each monitor off for 3 seconds, in the game screen order, so you know which is which.

New monitors only turn on after a reboot: the Setup offers it when you leave Video Setup. FliperOS never turns on an output that didn't get its 15 kHz mode at boot, since the kernel would send 31 kHz to the tube.

Which emulators use it

Emulator Games Monitors
GroovyMAME Every MAME system with 2 or more screens (Darius, Darius II, The Ninja Warriors, Punch-Out!!, Super Punch-Out!!, Vs. Tennis...) 2 or 3. With 2 monitors, a 3-screen game opens on the first 2
Flycast NAOMI multi-board games: Ferrari F355 Challenge (deluxe, twin, twin 2), Airline Pilots, Sega Strike Fighter 3 (left, center, right), all analog

The other emulators (RetroArch, PCSX2, Dolphin, Supermodel, Model 2...) and the frontends stay on monitor 1. It works from any launcher: the frontends, LXDE's Games menu, GroovyMAME's own game list and the terminal all go through the same commands.

How it works

Boot. Each extra monitor gets the boot mode of monitor 1, forced on, in the kernel line (video=DVI-I-1:640x480iSe; with an EDID boot, the preset's mode; on a digital output, the preset's super resolution). Rotation (Monitor Orientation) applies to all of them.

The fliperos.conf keeps the outputs in the game screen order (screens=DVI-I-1,VGA-1,DVI-I-2) and the multi-screen switch (multiscreen=off when off).

X. Each output of monitor 1's card has its own Monitor section in /etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/10-fliperos.conf, side by side in the game screen order, with monitor 1 as the primary screen: single-screen programs open there. Outputs of a second card come in as a GPU screen (see above).

KMS. RetroArch, Attract-Mode, EmulationStation and Pegasus open on the first connected output, which could be an extra monitor. So fliperos-kms-run turns the extra ones off (fliperos-setup --outputs main), and every X server (fliperos-x11-run, the desktop) turns them back on (--outputs all).

GroovyMAME. fliperos-mame-screens reads GroovyMAME's own -listxml and writes one .ini with numscreens per system with 2 or more screens in /etc/fliperos/mame/screens (limited to the number of monitors).

This takes about a minute the first time and only runs again when the GroovyMAME binary or the number of monitors changes. The groovymame command adds that folder to the -inipath after the main one, so a user .ini in the main folder wins, and sends each window to its output (-screen0 screen1...).

GroovyMAME's Switchres finds screenN in XRandR order and SDL counts the primary screen first; for both to agree the command makes the first output primary, and on the desktop restores the previous one when GroovyMAME closes. Switchres sets the mode of each game on every monitor.

Flycast. Flycast runs each NAOMI board of these games as its own process, with its own window (network:MultiboardSlaves=2): the main board where window:left says and the others one window width to each side.

For the F355 Challenge, Airline Pilots and Sega Strike Fighter sets (f355, f355twin, f355twinp, f355twn2, alpilot, alpilotj, sstrkfgt, sstrkfgta), with 3 monitors and the switch on, fliperos-x11-run puts fliperos-multiscreen in front of Flycast.

Inside the X server it gives the three outputs the mode Switchres made for monitor 1, side by side with no gap, and places the main board on the middle one; in full screen SDL puts each window on the monitor it falls on.

The other boards are new Flycast processes that only read ~/.config/flycast/emu.cfg, so full screen and the stretch are saved there. The board BIOS (f355dlx, airlbios, naomi...) must be in a Flycast content folder, next to the game.

Problems

  • The Setup offers no output for monitor 2: no other output is free on any card. A DVI-D connector is not analog (see above).
  • An extra monitor stays black: check that you rebooted after choosing it, and use Identify Monitors. On a digital output, try another active converter. On a second card, xrandr --listproviders (in a terminal on the desktop) must show both cards, and xrandr must list its outputs (VGA-1-1...). The kernel line must have its video= (Setup > System > Debug mode shows /proc/cmdline).
  • The screens are swapped: change Game Screen Order.
  • A game opens on one monitor only: check that Multi-Screen Games is On. For GroovyMAME, /etc/fliperos/mame/screens/<game>.ini must exist (the Setup makes them when you add a monitor; groovymame remakes them otherwise). For Flycast, it needs 3 monitors.
  • Logs: /opt/fliperos/logs/groovymame.log and /opt/fliperos/logs/flycast.log (the fliperos-multiscreen lines show the layout used).

See also Emulators and Installed system.

DIY hardware

Open-source projects you can build yourself, with an Arduino, a Raspberry Pi Pico or an ESP32, and use on a FliperOS cabinet. Most of them plug into USB and show up as a standard joystick, mouse or keyboard, so FliperOS needs no driver for them. This page says, for each one, what FliperOS does with it and whether it has been tried.

Only two of these have been used with FliperOS so far: the V-USB MamePanel, which is the control panel of the test cabinet, and the ZeDMD, which connected on a user's cabinet in October 2026 once its firmware was updated to 5.1.8. The others are listed because of how they present themselves to the computer, not because they were tested.

Control panel (joysticks and buttons)

After plugging the panel in, map each player's buttons once in Setup > Joysticks > Button mapping; the mapping goes to every emulator (Controls).

Project Board What the computer sees
GP2040-CE (documentation) Raspberry Pi Pico and other RP2040 boards A gamepad, in the mode you choose (XInput, DInput, keyboard and others); one board per player. MIT license
DaemonBite Arcade Encoder Arduino Pro Micro (ATmega32U4) A USB joystick with up to 12 buttons, made for low latency. GPL-3.0
Arduino Joystick Library Arduino Leonardo, Micro and other ATmega32U4 boards A joystick or gamepad you describe in your own sketch (32 buttons by default). LGPL-3.0
V-USB MamePanel ATmega8 (18 inputs) or ATmega32 (30 inputs, two joysticks), with the V-USB software USB driver Joysticks with up to 8 buttons each. This is the panel of the FliperOS test cabinet
  • Two players on one board: an encoder that carries both players may arrive as a single joystick. Setup > System > Quirks has the kernel flag that splits it (0x40, one device per player); see Controls.
  • Latency: Setup > System > Latency reads USB at 1000 Hz, which only helps if the board also answers at that rate (Latency).

Spinner and trackball

Project Board What the computer sees
Arcade Spinner Arduino Micro or another ATmega32U4 board, with a rotary encoder A mouse (the spinner is the X axis) and a joystick (the buttons). GPL-3.0

GroovyMAME and the MAME cores of RetroArch read a mouse as the spinner or trackball of the game. FliperOS has no screen to set this up: it is done in the emulator's own input menu.

Light gun

FliperOS ships the driver and the calibration for the GunCon 2, which reads the tube itself (Controls). The projects below work another way: an infrared camera in the gun looks at LEDs placed around the screen, so they don't depend on the kind of monitor.

Project Board What the computer sees
OpenFIRE Raspberry Pi Pico and other RP2040 or RP2350 boards An absolute-position mouse, a keyboard and a gamepad
SAMCO IR Light Gun Arduino boards (ATmega32U4, M0, M4) The project OpenFIRE came from; its page now points to OpenFIRE. GPL-3.0

The GunCon 2 calibration of the Setup is for the GunCon 2 only. These guns are calibrated in their own firmware and used as a mouse in the emulator.

LED display (marquee, DMD)

Project Board With FliperOS
ZeDMD ESP32 (the ESP32-S3-N16R8 is the recommended one) or Raspberry Pi Pico, driving HUB75 LED panels of 128x32 or 256x64 Setup > Games > Extras > ZeDMD installs the support: the display shows the selected game, the game that is open, its high scores and the achievements (Frontends). Needs ZeDMD firmware 5.1.0 or newer: older firmware, like the one that works on Batocera 41, doesn't connect (how to check and update it). GPL-2.0
libdmdutil (runs on the PC) The library, from the Visual Pinball project, whose dmdserver FliperOS uses to talk to the ZeDMD

The Pixelcade marquee, which FliperOS also supports, is a commercial product with closed software; it is on the Frontends page.

Game outputs: lamps, recoil, motors and button lights

Arcade games drive things outside the screen: start lamps, gun recoil, motors, digit displays. GroovyMAME, Flycast, Supermodel and SM2-Emu (Model 2) can publish these outputs over the network (TCP port 8000, one name = value line per change). On Windows the program that reads them is MAMEHooker. FliperOS has three readers, each one an extra in Setup > Games > Extras. They can be installed together.

Project What it drives With FliperOS
Hook Of The Reaper Light guns with recoil and lights (OpenFIRE, GUN4IR, Blamcon, Fusion, RS3 Reaper, Alien, AimTrak, Sinden and others), boards on a serial port or USB HID, Ultimarc light boards Setup > Games > Extras > Hook Of The Reaper. A Windows program, run through Wine. Its source isn't public at the moment
QMamehook Light guns on a serial port only: OpenFIRE, GUN4IR, Blamcon, RS3 Reaper Setup > Games > Extras > QMamehook. Native, without Wine: its source is built on the cabinet. LGPL-2.1
LEDSpicer Ready-made LED boards: Ultimarc (PacLED64, PacDrive, Ultimate I/O, NanoLED), LED-Wiz 32, Howler, Adalight Setup > Games > Extras > LEDSpicer, from its author's Ubuntu repository. It lights the buttons each game uses. GPL-3.0

The emulators only open port 8000 when one of them is installed, because the port is reachable from the network and accepts a pause command.

None of them has been tried with a real gun or board on a FliperOS cabinet yet. QMamehook was built and run against a simulated game: it connects to the port, looks for the game's .ini and closes with the game.

Hook Of The Reaper was run under Wine against a simulated game: it connects to the port, loads the game's file and closes with the game.

On the test cabinet it was installed from the Extras and opened with a Model 2 game (The House of the Dead in SM2-Emu, on a virtual screen): it stayed connected to the game's port for the whole run and closed with it. Whether Wine reaches each gun's serial port or USB HID interface still has to be seen on hardware.

Model 2 game outputs

A Model 2 gun cabinet has no recoil, so the board never says that a shot was fired, and SM2-Emu on its own only publishes the lamps. FliperOS adds a patch to it (config/sm2-emu-patches, to be offered to the SM2-Emu project) that reads the game's own memory and publishes it as outputs. The gun games use the names Hook Of The Reaper's game files already listen for:

Game Outputs
Virtua Cop (vcop), Virtua Cop 2 (vcop2), The House of the Dead (hotd) P1_CtmRecoil (a pulse per shot), P1_Ammo, P1_Clip, P1_Life, P1_Damaged (a pulse per life lost), P1_LmpStart, the same for P2_, and Credits
Gunblade NY (gunblade) P1_CtmRecoil, P1_GunMotor (the cabinet's own gun motor), P1_Life, P1_Damaged, P1_LmpStart, the same for P2_, and Credits
Behind Enemy Lines (bel) P1_CtmRecoil, P1_Ammo, P1_Clip, P1_Life, P1_Damaged, the same for P2_, and Credits
Rail Chase 2 (rchase2) P1_Life, P1_Damaged, P1_LmpStart, the same for P2_
Virtua Fighter 2 (vf2), Fighting Vipers (fvipers), Sonic the Fighters (schamp), Last Bronx (lastbrnx), Dead or Alive (doa) P1_Wins and P2_Wins (the rounds each side has taken in the match being fought, back to zero when it ends), and Credits
Desert Tank, Dynamite Cop, Indianapolis 500, Over Rev, Pilot Kids, Sega GT 24h, Sega Ski Super G, Sky Target, Top Skater, Virtua Striker, Zero Gunner Credits

Each was checked with a reader on port 8000 through a game played by a script: a credit, a start, shots until the magazine is empty and lives lost, for player 1; the fighting games with two scripted two-player matches, one won by each side. Player 2 in the gun games and a real gun haven't been tried.

The wins feed the versus score on the LED display. The addresses were found in the sets of the MAME 0.289 romset, and belong to the revision that set opens as.

The games on two coins a credit that start by themselves when the credit completes (Daytona USA, Sega Rally, Sega Touring Car, Motor Raid, Manx TT, Wave Runner, Sega Water Ski, Virtual On) have no Credits: it is spent the moment it exists. The two baseball games and the credit counter of Rail Chase 2 weren't found.

The patch reaches a cabinet that already built Model 2 the next time Games > Model 2 opens, which offers to update and rebuild.

Hook Of The Reaper

Hook Of The Reaper is the current successor of MAMEHooker. It has no Linux version yet (its author plans one after the program is complete), so FliperOS runs the Windows program through Wine.

  • What is installed: 64-bit Wine and a virtual screen (xvfb) from apt, and the program from its own website (pinned version and hash) into ~/hotr. It gets its own Wine folder, separate from Fightcade's. Nothing of this is in the image.
  • Setting it up: on the desktop, Preferences > Hook Of The Reaper opens its window. Add your light guns and assign each one to a player, as its tutorial shows. The settings stay in ~/hotr/data.
  • Game files: it comes with its own files for over 200 gun games (~/hotr/defaultLG), which work with any gun it supports. MAMEHooker .ini files go in ~/hotr/ini/MAME. The folder is also at ~/config/hotr, shared on the network.
  • When it runs: it opens with each game of GroovyMAME, Flycast, Supermodel and SM2-Emu and closes with it. It runs on the virtual screen, so none of its windows or warnings appear over the game. Installing it again from the Extras updates the program and keeps your guns, players and .ini files.
  • USB HID guns and boards: the install lets the fliperos user open the USB HID devices (/dev/hidraw*, group input), which is how Wine reaches them. Serial boards already belong to the user's dialout group.

LEDSpicer

  • The install adds the packages for every board it supports, but doesn't turn the service on: LEDSpicer needs /etc/ledspicer.conf describing your boards and which LED is which button, as its wiki explains. Then sudo systemctl enable --now ledspicerd.
  • With the service running, FliperOS tells it which game opened (emitter LoadProfileByEmulator <game> arcade, or the console's folder for the others) and when it closed, from any frontend or emulator.

QMamehook

QMamehook is an open-source (LGPL-2.1) reader that runs natively on Linux, without Wine, and uses MAMEHooker's .ini files unchanged.

It is small on purpose: it only writes to serial ports and only accepts the USB IDs of a few gun boards (OpenFIRE, GUN4IR, Blamcon; the RS3 Reaper after sudo modprobe usbserial vendor=0x0483 product=0x5750). It has no window and nothing to set up.

  • What is installed: its author publishes only the Windows program, so the install builds version 2.2 from source (pinned by hash) into ~/qmamehook. The compiler and Qt 6 come from apt; it takes about two minutes. Nothing of this is in the image.
  • Game files: MAMEHooker .ini files go in ~/qmamehook/ini, one per ROM set (sf2ce.ini). The folder is also at ~/config/qmamehook, shared on the network. For a game without a file, QMamehook writes one there listing the outputs the game sent, for you to fill in.
  • Players: the guns are numbered in the order of their USB product IDs, so the .ini writes to port 1 for the first gun, 2 for the second.
  • When it runs: it opens with each game of GroovyMAME, Flycast, Supermodel and SM2-Emu and closes with it. What it says (the guns it found, the file it loaded) is in /opt/fliperos/logs/qmamehook.log.
  • With Hook Of The Reaper also installed, only one of the two opens with the game, because a gun's serial port can't be shared: Hook Of The Reaper, unless /etc/fliperos/fliperos.conf has the line outputs_reader=qmamehook.

Adding a project to this page

A project fits here if its firmware or software is open source and it works on Linux without a closed driver.

If you use one of these on your cabinet, or another one, open an issue in the repository saying which board, what the Setup showed in Setup > System > Quirks > USB devices connected now, and whether it needed a quirk: that is what turns a line of this page from "should work" into "tested".

15 kHz kernel

fliperos-kernel.sh downloads kernel.org 6.18.54, applies patches/kernel-15khz/6.18/ (D0023R's 01 to 09, plus FliperOS's own 10, which lets nouveau take modes under 25 MHz on analog outputs: see Video cards) on top of the .config of Ubuntu 24.04's own kernel and builds the .debs. No module signing and no debug info. Compiling takes hours, so the .debs stay in a cache keyed by version and patch hash (/output/kernel-cache/<key>/): the next build reuses them.

Switchres (v2.2.1, the same version as GroovyArcade's package) is compiled with grid and geometry, and at build time generates one EDID per monitor preset plus the two super resolution ones used by the boot's EDID entries (fliperos-rebuild-edids, GroovyArcade's rebuild_edids). The initramfs hook carries all of them into the initramfs.

Build and tests

Build

Always in Docker (CLAUDE.md forbids chroot with the host's /dev on WSL).

docker build -f Dockerfile.fliperos -t fliperos-builder .
docker run --rm --privileged --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/output,target=/output" fliperos-builder bash /build/fliperos-mkiso.sh --output /output/fliperos-0.16.iso
Option Effect
--skip-groovymame, --skip-retroarch, --skip-flycast, --skip-pcsx2, --skip-supermodel Leaves the emulator out of the image (the compiled ones take minutes to hours; GroovyMAME and PCSX2 are the official releases)
--skip-skyscraper Without the Setup's Scraper
--skip-switchres Without Switchres: no per-monitor EDIDs, geometry or EDID boot entries
--skip-input-drivers, --skip-wheel-drivers Without the input drivers (GunCon 2 and wheels), or only without the wheel ones. By default guncon2, hid-tmff2 (Thrustmaster T150/T300/TX/T248...) and new-lg4ff (Logitech with full force feedback, replacing hid-logitech) ship, through DKMS — validated on the cabinet's 6.18
--kernel-cache DIR Where to store/reuse the kernel .debs (default /output/kernel-cache)
--splash fliperos-text\|fliperos\|evangelion\|none Plymouth theme (default fliperos-text)
--wifi-ssid NAME --wifi-psk PASSWORD Saves a Wi-Fi network in the image (the password is stored as plain text in the ISO; don't distribute it)
--repo DIR APT repository of the frontends carried into the image (default /output/repo, if it exists)

What doesn't exist in Ubuntu 24.04 is downloaded with a pinned version and hash: Limine 11.4.1, Gum 2.0.2 (the .deb stays for the man pages; the binary is built from the same version's source with patches/gum, compiled with Go 1.26.7: ▲/▼ arrows instead of dots in the menus' pagination, the menu sounds and Space toggling in checklists — gum 2.0.2 only knows the key as " ", and its library calls it space —, put in place of /usr/bin/gum with dpkg-divert), AntiMicroX 3.6.1 (official .deb for 24.04), Skyscraper 3.21.0 (Gemba fork, compiled with Qt6).

Audit of the generated ISO (read-only): checks the boot menu, kernel, setup files, libraries of the compiled programs, EDIDs and BIOS/UEFI boot.

docker build -t fliperos-vmtest -f tools/Dockerfile.vmtest tools
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/w:ro" -w /w fliperos-vmtest bash tools/verify-iso.sh /w/output/fliperos-0.16.iso

Release

Every new ISO goes to GitHub Releases, with the version's changelog, like GroovyArcade's releases (substring/os): the text by area (system, packages, fliperos-setup, tools) and, next to the ISO, the package list.

  1. Write in CHANGELOG.md the ## VERSION section with what changed since the previous release (git log PREVIOUS_VERSION..HEAD lists the commits). A new ISO after a release needs a new version (FLIPEROS_VERSION in fliperos-mkiso.sh).
  2. Commit and push.
  3. Tag the version and push the tag (the name is the version, without "v"):

powershell git tag 0.16 git push origin 0.16

Pushing the tag triggers the GitHub Actions Release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml). It checks that the tag is FLIPEROS_VERSION and that CHANGELOG.md has its section, builds the frontends repository (Dockerfile.packages) and generates the ISO with the same Dockerfile.fliperos as the local build.

Then it publishes through tools/release-publish.sh, with the workflow's own token. The kernel and frontend .debs stay in the Actions cache, so they only recompile when the version, a patch or a recipe changes. Without the cache, the build takes about 3 hours on a 4-core runner (the limit is 6 h).

If it fails, fliperos-mkiso.log is kept as a workflow artifact. Run by hand (Actions > Release > Run workflow), it generates the ISO of the current version and keeps it as an artifact for 3 days, without publishing.

To redo a version that was just tagged, move the tag and push it again (git tag -f 0.16, git push -f origin 0.16): the build of the old tag that is still running is cancelled, and its release, if it was already published, is replaced.

To publish an ISO generated here, in the audit container:

docker build -t fliperos-vmtest -f tools/Dockerfile.vmtest tools
docker run -it --rm -v fliperos-gh:/root/.config/gh fliperos-vmtest gh auth login
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/w:ro" -v fliperos-gh:/root/.config/gh -w /w fliperos-vmtest bash tools/release-publish.sh /w/output/fliperos-0.16.iso

gh auth login is a one-time step: the login stays in the fliperos-gh volume.

tools/release-publish.sh only publishes what can go public:

  • the ISO goes through the audit (tools/verify-iso.sh), so it is the one from the current repository — an old ISO, generated before the latest commits, is rejected;
  • an ISO with a saved network (--wifi-ssid, --wifi-psk) is rejected: the password would go with it;
  • without the version's section in CHANGELOG.md, nothing is published;
  • an existing release isn't replaced without --replace (deletes and publishes again); the workflow passes it, because there a release only exists again when the tag was moved on purpose.

GitHub accepts up to 2 GiB per file, and the ISO stays below that. The build's slim_rootfs_chroot removes the -dev packages and the build tools, but keeps build-essential, dkms and the kernel headers, which the DKMS drivers use.

No autoremove, because the Qt plugins and Vulkan come in through dlopen and don't show in ldd; the libraries ldd shows are marked as manually installed, and an ldd before and after fails the build if any is missing.

Switchres opens libX11.so, libXrandr.so and libdrm.so by those unversioned names, which belong to the -dev packages: config/fliperos-dlopen-links scans the binaries in /usr/local and /opt for such names and links them in /usr/local/lib to the installed version, and tools/verify-iso.sh checks the three.

The packages left with nothing depending on them once the -dev are gone (Qt SVG, sndio, hidapi, OpenAL) are marked as manually installed too, so an apt autoremove on the installed system doesn't take them.

The apt cache and lists also go, as does the out-of-scope firmware (Mellanox, Marvell Prestera, Qualcomm, QLogic), through a dpkg path-exclude so an update doesn't bring it back. The GPU firmware stays, NVIDIA's included: nouveau needs it to accelerate the newer cards. The squashfs is xz.

Wine, Steam and Heroic aren't in the image: Setup > Games > Extras installs them (config/fliperos-extras). If the ISO goes over 2 GiB, it is split into 1900 MiB parts (fliperos-0.16.iso.001, .002...), and the release text gets the instructions to join them (copy /b on Windows, cat on Linux).

Also published: fliperos-0.16.sha256 (the whole ISO and each part) and fliperos-0.16-pkglist.txt (package, version and architecture of what's in the image).

--prerelease marks it as a pre-release; --to FOLDER only prepares the files and the text (notes.md), without touching GitHub; --notes VERSION shows the version's text.

Tests

docker build -t fliperos-tests -f tests/Dockerfile tests
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/w" -w /w fliperos-tests python3 tests/test_setup.py
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/w" -w /w fliperos-tests python3 tests/test_build.py
  • tests/test_setup.py — the logic of fliperos-setup with fake DRM sysfs, EDIDs, lsblk, nmcli and aplay, on the same Ubuntu (and the same mawk/jq) as the ISO.
  • tests/test_build.py — boot menu, kernel and patches, pins, image files, the installed disk's Limine, fliperos-video-check.
  • tools/ui-snapshot.sh SCREEN [WIDTH HEIGHT] — captures a screen as text in an 80x30 tmux (or 64x24, 25 kHz's 512x384), with a fake system (tools/ui-demo.sh).
  • tools/vm-test.py install ISO — in QEMU: installs through the setup's lib onto a disposable disk and boots the disk on BIOS and UEFI. tools/vm-test.py screens ISO and tools/vm-monitor.py capture the real tty1 (Gum on the Linux console) screen by screen.

tools/vm-test.py desktop ISO opens LXDE on the installed disk (from boot and from the menu, with the 15 kHz xorg.conf).

tools/vm-test.py dev ISO takes the current repository's files to the installed disk, without a new ISO, and drives the menu with a fake gamepad (tools/vm-fakepad.py, uinput) up to the desktop, the resolution change and the quirks. - Updating the cabinet without a new ISO (over the network, with the default user fliperos and password fliperos):

powershell docker build -t fliperos-ssh -f tools/Dockerfile.ssh tools docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/w:ro" -w /w fliperos-ssh sh tools/cabinet-push.sh 192.168.1.111

tools/cabinet-push.sh sends the setup, config/, fliperos-rootfs.sh and the frontends repository; there, tools/cabinet-update.sh keeps a copy of what changes in /root/fliperos-backup-DATE.tgz, runs the same fliperos-rootfs.sh as the build and applies what comes from outside it: fliperos-limine-update, automatic login, DNS, clock, new packages (through apt), kernel line and services. At the end it restarts tty1.

Website

The project website lives in website/ (Next.js, server-rendered, English and Portuguese). npm run dev inside the folder serves it locally; the Dockerfile there builds the standalone server that Coolify (or any Docker host) runs on port 3000. Its README has the details.

Architecture

fliperos-setup

fliperos-setup/
├── fliperos-setup        entry point (media or installed system)
├── lib/                  logic — no file here calls gum, except ui.sh
│   ├── common.sh config.sh progress.sh speech.sh
│   ├── drm.sh video.sh monitor.sh xorg.sh bootloader.sh
│   ├── disk.sh install.sh recovery.sh
│   ├── launcher.sh audio.sh network.sh status.sh scraper.sh update.sh
│   ├── romclean.sh netshare.sh  MAME ROM Cleaner; network shared folder (SMB)
│   ├── downloader.sh     romset and CHDs by magnet link (Transmission)
│   ├── folders.sh        custom folder (external disk) for ~/roms, ~/bios, ~/media
│   ├── hardware.sh latency.sh   CPU/memory/GPU and the latency modes
│   ├── quirks.sh padkeys.sh     usbhid quirks; controller in the menus
│   ├── lpt.sh            parallel port joysticks (db9, gamecon, turbografx)
│   └── ui.sh             Gum, theme, screen frame
└── screens/              screens — they only combine ui.sh with the logic
    ├── output-test.sh (test + Testing Results)  main-menu.sh  setup-menu.sh
    ├── video-setup.sh  disk-selection.sh  install-progress.sh  progress.sh
    └── recovery.sh  first-boot.sh  latency.sh  lpt.sh  rom-cleaner.sh  downloader.sh

Long operations (install, repair, update, scraper) don't know about the screen: they write events (@step, @pct, @msg, @fail) that screens/progress.sh draws. Everything goes to /var/log/fliperos-setup.log.

Launch commands and wrappers

Nothing on FliperOS opens a frontend or an emulator by calling its binary directly. Between the boot and the game there is a short chain of scripts, each one with a single job. All of them are in /opt/fliperos/bin, except fliperos-menu and groovymame, which are in /usr/local/bin so they can be typed in the shell.

Command Called by What it does
fliperos-tty1 ~/.zprofile, at the tty1 login The boot flow: first boot or update notice, then the default launcher, then the menu loop
fliperos-menu You, in the shell Back to the menu: runs fliperos-tty1 --menu and, on leaving, shows the MOTD again
fliperos-session [name] fliperos-tty1 Opens one launcher from the sessions table and returns when it closes
fliperos-kms-run program [arguments] fliperos-session, frontends, you Runs a program straight on KMS/DRM, without Xorg
fliperos-x11-run [--mode WxH@HZ] program [arguments] Frontends, fliperos-launch, you Runs a program in an Xorg of its own, in a video mode made by Switchres
fliperos-x11-client fliperos-x11-run, through xinit Inside that Xorg: window manager, then Switchres switches the mode and launches the program
fliperos-launch name The Games menu of the desktop Closes the desktop, opens the emulator, brings the desktop back
fliperos-escquit PID fliperos-session, fliperos-fightcade Esc closes the frontend when no game is open
fliperos-powerkey triggerhappy, on the power button Closes the open game; with no game open, powers off

From the boot to the launcher

fliperos-tty1 is the only entry point. At boot it runs fliperos-session with no argument, which opens the launcher chosen in Setup > Games > Frontend (/etc/fliperos/session); when that closes, it enters the menu loop.

In the loop the Setup never opens anything itself: Start frontend and Start desktop write the launcher's name to /run/fliperos/launch and exit with code 20, and fliperos-tty1 then calls fliperos-session <name> from the login shell, where tty1 is the controlling terminal (Installed system explains why). fliperos-menu is the same loop without the boot part.

fliperos-session looks the name up in /etc/fliperos/sessions.conf (and in sessions.custom.conf, the frontends you registered), one launcher per line as name|backend|binary|package|description. The backend decides how it opens:

  • kms: fliperos-kms-run <binary>. For the frontends (Attract-Mode Plus, ES-DE, Pegasus and your own) it also starts fliperos-escquit and marks the process with FLIPEROS_POWERKEY=frontend.
  • x: xinit <binary> on the same VT. Only the LXDE desktop uses it.
  • none: opens nothing; the boot goes straight to the menu.

Around the launcher it sets the CPU governor to performance and restores it afterwards (fliperos-setup --session-start and --session-end).

The two wrappers: KMS and X11

Every emulator is opened through one of them, and both refuse to run inside an X session (DISPLAY set): they need the console. Which one to use for each emulator is in Adding games.

fliperos-kms-run is for what draws on KMS by itself: RetroArch and the KMS frontends. The video mode is the one from the boot, and RetroArch switches it per game on its own. Before the program starts, the wrapper:

  • tells the Pixelcade marquee and the game outputs (fliperos-pixelcade launch, fliperos-outputs launch) which game is opening;
  • for RetroArch, stacks the system configuration on top of the user's with --appendconfig (the FliperOS retroarch.cfg, the gl fallback for cards without OpenGL 3.2, the Button mapping, DOFLinx and the versus score);
  • turns off the extra monitors, leaving only the main one;
  • exports the console drivers: SDL_VIDEODRIVER=kmsdrm, SDL_AUDIODRIVER=alsa and Qt's eglfs;
  • gives the program the session's terminal as its input when a frontend handed it /dev/null;
  • sends the program's output to /opt/fliperos/logs/<program>.log (to the screen in Debug mode).

fliperos-x11-run is for what needs X: Flycast, PCSX2, Dolphin, Supermodel, Model 2, OpenBOR, Hypseus. It starts an Xorg just for that program and closes it when the program exits.

The mode comes from --mode, or from the program's line in /etc/fliperos/emulator-modes.conf (one column for a 15 kHz monitor, another for 25/31 kHz and LCD), or is 320x240@60.

It also adds each emulator's own full-screen and stretch options, turns the extra monitors back on, exports SDL_VIDEODRIVER=x11, and writes the same log.

The Xorg's client is fliperos-x11-client: it starts Openbox (which fits the window to the screen at every mode switch) and hands over to switchres WIDTH HEIGHT HZ --switch --launch "<program>", which creates the modeline for the monitor in /etc/switchres.ini, switches to it and runs the program. More in Emulators.

Commands that wrap themselves

Two launchers are kms in the sessions table but need X. Their own command notices it is on the console and opens itself again through fliperos-x11-run:

  • groovymame (config/fliperos-groovymame): the real binary is /usr/local/libexec/groovymame. Commands with no screen (-listxml, -verifyroms...) run directly.
  • /opt/fliperos/fightcade/fightcade (a link to fliperos-fightcade, see Fightcade 2).

So choosing Fightcade in the menu runs this chain, each line starting the next:

fliperos-tty1                                    the menu loop
└─ fliperos-session fightcade                    the row in sessions.conf, CPU governor
   └─ fliperos-kms-run /opt/fliperos/fightcade/fightcade      log, Pixelcade, outputs
      └─ fliperos-fightcade                      no DISPLAY: opens itself in X
         └─ fliperos-x11-run /opt/fliperos/fightcade/fightcade    mode from the table, xinit
            └─ fliperos-x11-client               Openbox, Switchres switches the mode
               └─ fliperos-fightcade             DISPLAY set: Wine prefix, emulator settings
                  └─ Fightcade2.sh               the Fightcade client

From the desktop

The desktop is itself an X session, and the wrappers don't run inside one. fliperos-launch <name> (the items in Games, see Desktop and theme) writes the full command, already with its wrapper, to $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fliperos-next and closes LXDE.

fliperos-session, which was waiting for the desktop's X to end, runs that command with FLIPEROS_POWERKEY=game and then opens the desktop again. It only accepts a request that starts with fliperos-kms-run or fliperos-x11-run. fliperos-launch --mode 640x240@60 program does the same for any program.

Which one to type

On a console (tty1 after leaving the menu to the shell, or another VT), not over SSH: an SSH session has no VT for the screen.

To Type
Return to the FliperOS menu fliperos-menu
Open a launcher exactly as the menu does /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-session fightcade (or retroarch, attractplus, lxde...)
Open the default launcher /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-session
Run RetroArch with a core /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-kms-run retroarch -L <core>.so <game>
Run an X emulator in its table mode /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run flycast <game>
Run any program in a chosen mode /opt/fliperos/bin/fliperos-x11-run --mode 640x240@60 <program>
Open GroovyMAME or Fightcade groovymame [game], /opt/fliperos/fightcade/fightcade

Other components

Splash. Plymouth.

The default fliperos-text theme is text only, in the style of a modern terminal: the name scrambles into place and then waves through a gradient, a prompt types the subtitle, a gradient progress bar with a moving shine, the last systemd units with a spinner (SetUpdateStatusFunction) and faint falling characters.

It draws everything with JetBrains Mono (OFL, config/fonts), which goes to /usr/share/fonts/truetype/fliperos and, through the fliperos-fonts initramfs hook, into the initramfs: the Ubuntu plymouth hook only copies the Ubuntu font.

fliperos is a full 640x480 image scaled to the boot mode (640x480, 640x240, 320x240...) with an animated bar.

Three themes from Gnome-look come too: cogwheel (by DUKE93, GPL 3), into-it and windoze95, adapted to scale to the window, with the pixel twice as tall in the double-width modes (640x240), and Windoze 95's art reduced to 640x480.

All of them live in config/splashscreen and go to /usr/share/plymouth/themes and to ~/splashscreen, where Setup > System > Splash screen also lists the user's themes (more on Gnome-look).

Setting one (lib/splash.sh) copies its folder with ImageDir and ScriptFile rewritten, points the default.plymouth alternative at it and runs update-initramfs (the initramfs hook takes the new initrd to the ESP); the preview runs plymouthd with plymouth.splash=NAME.

tools/cabinet-update.sh rebuilds the initramfs when the boot theme's files change. The build can also use evangelion (202 frames, with a seizure risk declared by the author and no license in the package) or none.

Network. Samba (\\<ip>\FliperOS → /opt/fliperos, and \\<ip>\roms, bios, media, nvram, save and config → the folders of the same name in ~, writable only with the fliperos user; config/smb.conf), SSH/SFTP and Avahi (fliperos.local).

Default user fliperos with password fliperos, like GroovyArcade's user arcade with password arcade (see Installed system).

NetworkManager handles Wi-Fi and wired (the empty 10-globally-managed-devices.conf overrides Ubuntu's, which only managed Wi-Fi) and writes /etc/resolv.conf itself with the DNS from DHCP (90-fliperos-dns.conf: Ubuntu would hand DNS to systemd-resolved, which isn't in the image).

The clock comes from the network (systemd-timesyncd). On the first test on the cabinet all three were missing: resolv.conf was the build container's, the BIOS clock was two months behind, and apt didn't work (neither System Update nor frontends).

Diagnostics. sudo fliperos-video-check --json reads the active mode of each output (current CRTC through libdrm, read-only): connector, resolution, kHz, Hz, interlaced.
